master-class-character-the-canary:
The Canary: The Small Life the World Rested On

← Mr. Chandelier · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

After the murder plot and the pearls and the invented chauffeur are all set aside, the book names the thing the mother's life actually hung on, and it is not a person. "It had not been her chauffeur upon whom her life depended, however." It was "a plain little bird," "a yellow canary with a glassy eye and ruffled wing," "sleeping in a gilded cage at her elbow," and on this, her life and everything else depended.

The rule is absolute, and she believes it completely. "So long as this bird lived, she could not die." The canary is "all that had ever stood between her and tides of death," and if it ever went she must go too, "searching through all the realms of death with an empty bird cage." So she tends it like a shrine, a silken bed, a marble bath, "three gold-edged mirrors for the phantom birds," and she guards its sleep, because if it stays calm and unaged then she will stay "as preserved as she had been when she was young and beautiful." "It never sang." The whole delusion of her deathlessness perches on one drugged bird that makes no sound.

Ask the wrong question and the canary is a pathetic detail, an addict's pet. Ask the right one and it is Radical Immanence's load-bearing case, the small real thing at the dead center of a constructed world. Miss MacIntosh could not admit her wig was a wig because the admission was load-bearing, and the mother cannot look closely at her canary for the same reason, because the one glance that told the truth would bring the whole cosmology down.

And the truth is that there is no one bird. The canary "had died already many times without her knowledge," "as changeable as her own dead selves," and it was Mr. Spitzer who arranged "this substitution of the living for the dead," "another canary always in the house, a spare." He warns the servants she must never see "the canary's funeral in the wave-washed garden," or "the whole universe might topple." So the faithful companion on which everything depends is a rotation of interchangeable birds presented as one, "an unbroken continuity of one small life," though "there had been many little yellow canaries in this cage." The mother gives the single bird many names, Juniper and Cellini and Methuselah and Marco Polo, and among them Solomon, the same name Vera hung on her turtle, as if wisdom kept getting handed to the small dumb creatures. She thinks the names are moods of one bird. They are closer to headstones.

The canary is Spitzer's keeping-faith-with-the-dead performed as mercy. He pays a dead man's debts out of his own pocket, and he keeps a dead bird's post filled out of the same refusal to let the dead be gone, and both are done so the survivor need not know. It is the gentlest lie in the book and the most total, a man burying a bird by starlight so a woman can go on believing she cannot die. And when the deceit finally slips, the horror lands the wrong way up. She sees "Marco Polo flying out through an open transom" into a storm, a real bird escaped at last, and instead of terror she is "quite calm, resigned hopelessly" to the fact that now she "must certainly live, of course, forever," because "who could locate one lost canary in a hurricane." The rule she built to keep death away has trapped her in a life she can no longer end. The small life the world rested on has flown, and the world does not topple. It simply goes on, which is worse.

The turn for a writer is where to set the thing everything depends on. A tidy story would rest the mother's survival on her grand invention, the chauffeur with the loaded gun, the drama she authored. Young rests it instead on a bird the mother barely sees, drugged and silent in a cage at her elbow, and then reveals that even the bird is not one bird but a quiet succession no one is allowed to notice. The load-bearing thing is never the vivid thing. It is the small, overlooked, endlessly replaced thing at the edge of the frame, the canary and not the chauffeur, and a writer who wants to know what a character truly cannot lose should look away from the drama she performs and toward the plain creature she keeps without attention. The mother spent her invention on a murderer at the wheel. Her life hung on a bird that never sang, that she never really looked at, that Mr. Spitzer buried again and again in the dark so she would not have to learn what everyone learns, that the thing you cannot live without was mortal all along, and small, and already gone several times over while she slept.
master-class-03-brief-overview-of-radica:
Brief Overview of Radical Immanence

← The Wheel That Turns Around Nothing · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Plot →

You are not one self.

Reality is constructed.

Grief doesn't end.

Witnessing is the core ethical act.

Build anyway, knowing it's temporary.

Unfinished is honest.

The margins reveal the truth.

The past doesn't go away.

Language shapes what's possible.

The sacred is here.

The crossing point is the place where a person stands, the exact here-and-now of a life.

For the writer: I am not suggesting that you need to develop an entire philosophical system to embed in your writing and I am also saying your writing needs to say something and/or be based on something. It does not need to be traceable to some school of thought. You can also use your imagination.
master-class-character-friday:
Friday: The Blind Dog Who Saw the Angel

← Solomon · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Mrs. Hogden →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Old Friday · The Chicago Detective · The Stone Deaf Man

Old Friday is Miss MacIntosh's dog, "the old sheep dog following always this shepherd of the surf," and he is blind. This matters, because Friday is blind and sees what his sighted mistress cannot. He goes "barking always at her heels as if, though he was blind and could not see the fringes of departing light, he saw what could not be seen, some other being in the purple fog and shadow, some golden, feathered angel soft as fog and dusk and woman's hair." Miss MacIntosh, walking right through that fog, "though herself she might seem the vision, could not see it." She had spent her life refusing the dream, bristling "like the porcupine" at the very thought, ready to beat back "with her stout umbrella, tides of angels wearing golden crowns." The blind dog perceives exactly what the clear-eyed woman has trained herself not to.

He is the book's image of the witness as pure faithfulness, and he holds together the two things the book will not let resolve. He has "known the denudation and the dream, the reality and the illusion, how each must live by some pretense." The bald truth under the red wig and the golden angel in the fog are both real to Friday, and he does not need one to defeat the other; he barks at both. This is exactly the attention the philosophy asks for, the holding of two contradictory truths at once without forcing a winner, and it is a blind dog who manages it while the humans around him choose one side and go blind in the other eye.

And when Miss MacIntosh walks into the sea and does not come out, Friday does the truest thing in the chapter. He keeps barking. After she has drowned, "the old dog to bark much as if he might still be aware of her, a moving shadow, a shadow of a black umbrella moving over water and sand, as if perhaps she had never gone or had returned." He keeps his vigil at the tide's edge, at the crossing point where the land meets the water that took her, "old Friday barking by the waves which return with all but her." He is grief that will not be told the loss is over. He barks for the drowned as if barking could call her back, or as if he can still see, in the fog he was always better at barking than seeing the shadow of her umbrella moving.

The turn for a writer is brief and steadying. Friday is faithfulness itself, the blind companion who attends to the invisible thing, who perceives the angel the clear-eyed refuse, who keeps barking at the shore long after the sensible have accepted that she is gone. He is the maker's stubborn attention to what has vanished, the refusal to file the loss as finished, the holding of the bald reality and the golden dream in the same breath without making them fight. Set him beside the Chicago detective, who has perfect eyes and sees a corpse, and beside the stone deaf man, who cannot hear and hears the fishes in the river. Friday cannot see and sees the angel. The book keeps handing its truest witnessing to the ones whose ordinary channel is closed, and the blindest, most faithful of them is a dog barking by the water for a woman who is not coming back, keeping her, in the only way left, by not letting the barking stop.
master-class-character-doctor-justice-ol:
Doctor Justice O'Leary: The Witness Who Stopped Seeing

← Mr. Weed · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · James the Chauffeur →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Justice O’Leary · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Vera Cartwheel

The reader meets him first as a reflection, a dead man in a bus driver's rear-view mirror, and only later, through the thin wall of an Indiana inn, learns his full story. Both meetings are the right because being a reflection, a haunt, a voice raving through a wall, a man half in the grave and still practicing medicine, is the whole of what he is.

Dr. Justice O'Leary, so he calls himself, announcing his name and his greatness to anyone within earshot, the best medical practitioner the country ever saw, left to grow old among ungrateful clients. He is the baby doctor of a poor country town, the one who brings the babies in. He has blown his breath into the mouths of dead men whose mouths stank. He is drunk, reeling, borrowing a nickel for the next drink, paid for his deliveries in turnips and rotten walnuts with the worms still crawling in them, a cancer eating into his own face. He was killed earlier that same evening in an illusory traffic accident, and by rights should be pinned under a steering wheel in a flooded meadow, and he is up all night anyway, practicing. And he keeps a dead woman in his room. Her name is Sarah, his sister, who died at the age of one and lies under a stone in the vegetable garden, and who has come back, silent, perhaps imaginary, to disgrace him, and whom he cannot make leave.

Radical Immanence makes witnessing the central act, staying present with what one cannot fix or resolve, and it gives that act its clearest keeper in Vera. O'Leary is the same act turned inside out. He is the professional witness of the threshold, the man stationed at both doors of the world, the one who ushers the living in and watches the dying go out. The question the book asks through him is not why he is so ruined, but what becomes of a witness who has seen too much. The answer is that he goes blind to the very thing he witnesses.

The first time O'Leary watched a man die, he saw something steal out of the room, a mist, a vapor, the soul going out by the door. He has watched and listened ever since, at deathbed after deathbed, and never once seen or heard anything leave again. Death, he says, has ceased to be a drama. That is the exact reverse of Vera, who comes close to each person and refuses to conclude, who keeps every mystery open by never solving it. O'Leary has stood nearer than anyone to the central mystery of the whole book, the passage between the living and the dead, and standing there for a lifetime has worn it smooth. He is the witness who witnessed until there was nothing left to see. Where Vera's long looking keeps people alive and unfinished, O'Leary's long looking has closed the door on wonder itself.

The numbness has a body. He cannot feel the pulse of another, the book says, because his own pulse has failed and his own artery has hardened. A doctor is a person whose whole art is to lay a finger on another life and feel it beating, and this one cannot, because the beating has stopped in him first. It is the plainest image in the novel for what a witness becomes when the witnessing empties out. He is present at every threshold and can feel none of them. He has so much faith in the past, the book says, that he has none in the future. A man that full of the dead has no room left in him for the living to register.

Sarah is the proof. The numbed witness of a thousand deaths cannot make his own single dead sister go. He knows she is dead, says so, insists he has put her out of his memory and devoted his life to hard work, and still she is there every night, silent, on the floor, in the bed, her feet cold as ice, and he argues with her until the walls shake and the slop jar dances and he never wins, because there is no winning against a grief that will not end. He calls her an impostor, the wrong woman, a senile baby dead at the age of one, and none of it makes her leave. The man who lost the power to see the soul steal out of the room is haunted by the one soul that will not. His deadness to death and his helplessness before this single death are the same condition. He went numb, it seems, precisely because he could not bear the door Sarah keeps propping open.

His name is the book's flat joke and its deepest one. Justice O'Leary presides over a world with no justice in it, women brought to child-bed against their will, help asked for and never given, a good doctor paid in worm-eaten walnuts, a cancer eating the face of the man who might have been a Mayo brother curing cancer, a God who has deserted him. He is named for the thing his world most lacks and he can least supply. The name is not a label the reader is meant to trust. It is a claim the book raises in order to bring it down, the way it raises Miss MacIntosh's sensible reality and Catherine's madness and then quietly swaps their places. A man called Justice who cannot feel another's pulse is the novel saying, in a single name, that the grand words people give themselves are the last thing anyone should believe about them.

He belongs, in the end, to the book's company of the not-quite-living, alongside the clam-digger who buries himself in the sand and Moses Hunnecker who drives too long after he is dead. O'Leary was killed in the accident and is up all night practicing; he is the doctor of the threshold who lives on the threshold. It is fitting that the one physician stationed between birth and death cannot say which side of his own doorway he is on. He keeps the crossing not as its guide but as its longest resident.

The lesson for a writer is in how to build the dark twin of a virtue. Vera's witnessing is the book's ethical center, and a lesser novel would have left it there, admired and unopposed. Young sets against it a man who does the same thing for a living and has been ruined by it, so that the reader sees at once what witnessing is worth and what it looks like when it fails. O'Leary is not the opposite of Vera the way a villain is the opposite of a hero. He is what her gift becomes when it is spent, when the looking has gone on so long that nothing looks back. To place that figure a few rooms down from the one who witnesses well is to show, without a word of argument, both the worth of the thing and its cost. A writer who wants a virtue to carry weight can build, somewhere in the same house, the person it destroyed.
master-class-character-moses-hunnecker:
Moses Hunnecker: The Driver of the Crossing

← The Old Clam Digger · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Madge Capehorn Edwards →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Vera Cartwheel

He is the first person in the book, at the wheel, whistling, drunk, driving badly through the mist because he is the one steering the whole thing, the vehicle that carries Vera and the two sleeping lovers and the reader into the novel, and he is doing it half blind, toward a place that will not turn out to be the one anyone meant to reach.

Moses Hunnecker drives the Grey Goose bus into interior America, his long hair streaming like a curtain over his eyes, his fat shoulders sloping over the wheel, a whiskey bottle he drinks from openly with many calls upon God and the angels and the angel Gabriel. He whistles the mating calls of birds and sings that the old grey goose is dead, died in the morning with a pillow under her head. He talks the whole way about his old woman waiting at home, who will take his head off when she sees him, and Vera cannot tell whether the wife and the children and the ordinary happiness are his or something she dreamed up out of her own hunger for it. He may be a family man going home. He may be a bachelor, a nobody, a mad Don Quixote chasing windmills. He drives erratically through a mist that blots out the road, and he says he can see better drunk than the sober can see, because he has the rear-view mirror and can watch what comes from before and behind at once.

Ask the wrong question and he is a bit of local color, a comic driver to open on before the real story starts. Ask the right one and he is piloting the book's deepest claim. Radical Immanence holds that the meaning is not at the destination set out for but at the actual place a person ends up, the exact here-and-now, the crossing point where she happened to be standing. Moses is the man at the wheel of that idea. The question the book asks through him is not where is he taking her, but what is it to be carried, half blind, toward a place that will not be the one she was looking for, and to find that the wrong place is the only place there is?

Vera boards to find Miss MacIntosh, or the dead, or the truth, a journey with its destination out ahead of it. Moses does not take her there. He plows nowhere, through the mist, on a road that turns and seems to go back the way it came, and he sets her down in southern Indiana, a state as yet unknown to her, a place she never meant to reach. The bus was supposed to arrive somewhere. It arrives here. And here, the ordinary misted plain of the Middle West, the low fields, the toy train crossing the toy bridge, turns out to be the whole point, the real ground under the real moment, which is the only ground anyone ever stands on. Moses is the one who drives her off the map she was reading and into the place she is. He does not reach the destination because there is no reaching a destination. There is only being carried into the present, and he is the one doing the carrying.

His name says it twice. Moses is the man who leads the people the whole long way toward a promised land and does not himself set foot in it, who dies in sight of the country he spent his life crossing toward. Moses Hunnecker drives the same errand. He steers everyone toward an arrival that is always one more lap ahead. We are on the next to the last lap now, he says, and the next step is the end, or maybe it is the beginning, but which of us will live to know. He is the guide to a place the guide does not enter. The infant Moses was drawn out of the water and set adrift among the reeds, and this Moses pilots his bus across a plain the book keeps calling oceanic, a sea of mist with no boundary and no shore, ferrying his few passengers over the ambiguous waters of the first creation. The name is not decoration. It is the job.

And he is himself on the border he drives across. The whole ride he rages at old Doc, the doctor who brought him into the world and is dying now, or dead, killed by the revenge of all the patients he could not save, come back for him and riding in the rear-view mirror above the driver's shaggy head. Moses says he is living too long after he was dead, that some new mortal complication is on him, cold and burning at once, that he ought to be driving in his shroud. His cheeks have gone wooden and the woodpeckers bore holes in them, so that the living driver is turning into a carved effigy as he steers. He is the clam-digger's brother and Spitzer's, one more figure who cannot be called clearly alive or clearly dead, and it is exactly right that the crossing between those two states should be piloted by a man who is himself in the middle of making it. The one who drives the border belongs to both shores.

There is one more turn, and it is Vera's. She cannot verify a thing about him. The wife with the ample figure, the children, the home, the happiness she could not imagine to be real, may all be his, or may all be hers, laid over a stranger's back because she wants a world where people go home to someone. His ordinary life is either a fact she witnesses or a dream she builds, and the book refuses to say which. So even the man driving the crossing is himself a place where reality is made instead of found, a screen for the longing of the person he carries. He is real, and he is also whatever the passenger needs him to be, both at once, which is the condition of everyone in this book seen at their plainest.

The lesson for a writer is about who to put at the wheel. Young opens her enormous novel not with the sea-blackened mansion or the famous beauty or the lost governess but with a drunk bus driver singing about a dead goose, and she does it because the frame of the whole book, the journey that never arrives, needs a driver who is it rather than a symbol who stands for it. Moses does not represent the crossing. He drives it, half blind, into the present, toward a home he may or may not have, named for the guide who never reached the land. Put a figure like that at the very start and the reader is already inside the book's hardest claim before a single door of the great house has opened: that the reader is not going where she thinks, that the wrong place is the only place, and that someone not quite seen is carrying her there.
master-class-character-rosemary-longtree:
Rosemary Longtree: The Perfect Child Who Was Never Born

← Esther Longtree · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Walter →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Esther Longtree · Rosemary

She is the most loved person in the Longtree house, and she was never alive for a single minute. Rosemary was Esther Longtree's twin, "stillborn," while "Esther lived, a reproach to her mother." From that first morning, when the mother "had not known there were two until the first one came and was laid out upon a tiny lace pillow," Rosemary became the daughter the mother wanted and Esther became the one she got. Rosemary is built entirely out of the mother's speech. She exists as the one "of whom her mother had spoken ever since Esther Longtree's earliest memory," and everything about her is perfect because nothing about her was ever tested by being real. "Rosemary's hair was golden, soft as moth's silk, and Rosemary's little feet were perfectly formed." She "would have grown to perfection and would have been a daughter to lean upon." She is the one "who had grown not but who would have been perfect."

Grief is the engine here, and the philosophy's words for it are exact: grief does not resolve, "it accumulates," "you carry it." But the mother carries it in the worst possible way, by turning it into a weapon against the child who lived. She has decided that Esther killed her twin in the womb, that she "kicked Rosemary out into the cold winds, the snows, the starlight, straight out of the womb into the grave," and she says so, over and over, all of Esther's life. The stillborn daughter becomes the standard the living daughter can never meet, because the dead do not track mud on the parlor floor or break the furniture or "smell to high heaven." Rosemary would have been considerate, would have learned her lessons "quick as a flash," would never have talked back. She is perfect by the simple mechanism of never having had to be anything at all.

The cruelest turn is that no one can say for certain which twin was the shadow. The mother tells it so that Esther "had seemed the shadow herself until she was born dead and killed by Esther," and the words fold back on themselves until the living daughter and the dead one trade places, "one seeming a shadow or a reflection." Esther grows up believing her "soul was the soul of Rosemary," half convinced that the real child died and the wrong one lived. She digs in the ground "for Rosemary with an old, earth-colored spoon," under one pear tree and another, because the mother will never say which pear tree holds the grave, "there being so many now, so many little pear trees." She turns up thimbles and wooden beads and a teething ring and "a long gold hair," the buried evidence of a child who may be her sister or may be her own first stillborn, and she cannot tell them apart. The alphabet book she digs out of the ground spells the whole thing: "M for murder, murder, murder, M for mother."

This is where Rosemary explains Esther, and the book knows it. A woman raised to believe she murdered the perfect child in the womb, and that the perfect child is buried somewhere in the ground waiting to be found, will spend her life trying to give birth to her, to undo the first death, to at last deliver the golden daughter who lived. Esther's everlasting pregnancy is the attempt to produce Rosemary. Every stillborn is another failure to bring the first one back. The mother built a flawless dead child out of words and hung her over the living one, and the living one has been trying ever since to make the words come true.

The turn for a writer is the one that stings most, because every writer keeps a Rosemary. She is the perfect version, the flawless thing that exists only in the telling, the book that "would have been perfect" and shames every actual page. She costs nothing and she ruins everything, because she never had to survive contact with the world, never tracked mud, never broke the furniture, never smelled to high heaven, and so she wins every comparison with the real, mud-tracking, furniture-breaking work actually made. She is built entirely of speech, of would have, and she is more beloved than anything finished. Set her beside Esther, the living daughter, big and awkward and bruised and alive, and the book's whole moral is in which one the mother chose. To love Rosemary is to love the thing that was never born over the thing that is. It is the writer's oldest cruelty, turned inward, and the book lets Esther dig for the golden child under all the little pear trees, forever, spoon in hand, looking for the sister she is accused of killing and may only have dreamed.
master-class-character-mr-weed:
Mr. Weed: The Life Made From a Knot

← The Tavern Landlady · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Doctor Justice O'Leary →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Mr. Weed · Vera Cartwheel

The other man signing in at the Tavern, the one who takes so long at the register, is "the Christian hangman, Mr. Weed, a respectable citizen with a large family," on his way home from a hanging. He is the landlord's twin at the counter. The landlord ties the knot that marries people and swears it cannot be undone. Weed ties the knot that ends them. Between the two of them the whole trade of the book stands at the front desk, one man binding and one man severing, and by the time the night is over it is not easy to say they were doing different work.

His day job is death and his real living is a dairy farm. The hangman, the landlord lets slip, is secretly a prosperous farmer with a model dairy, and he ties the noose only because, as the phrase goes, "he got paid to tie it." "Every hanging represented an improvement on the farm." He calls himself "the soul of tolerance," condemns nobody, and dresses for a hanging in the same good suit he wears to church, because to him the two are equally official occasions. He is proud of his method. He "rehearses every hanging," practices with a sandbag the exact weight of the man, and holds that "the rehearsal is more important, from my point of view, than the actual hanging." He is, in his own mind, a merciful technician, offering a painless drop as a Christian kindness.

And he never once meets the person he kills. He writes each condemned man a form letter asking for "his weight and measurements and his permission to tie the official knot," and beyond that he "never talked to any of the parties concerned." This is the thing that makes him more terrible than any butcher in his own stories. He spends his life in the room with death, closer to it than anyone, and he sees no one. He reduces each man to a weight, a drop, a knot, and calls the reduction mercy. Where Mr. Bonebreaker fled the real the instant it stood revealed, Weed does the opposite and never has to flee, because he arranged never to look at the person in the first place. He is attention emptied of contact, procedure standing in for witness.

He is also where the book says its own deepest thing out loud, and it comes out as dread. The most terrifying murders, Weed believes, are the subtle ones, "like murdering a mouse in your dreams, and then the next morning when you got up, you found a mouse with a crushed skull in your coat pocket." That is the whole novel in one sentence, spoken by the hangman: the thing imagined becomes the thing that is real, and the body is found in the pocket. Where the mother dreams a chauffeur into being and the landlord makes coffee cups speak, Weed dreams of a killing and wakes up to a corpse. He knows, better than anyone in the book, that a thing made in the mind does not stay in the mind, and it does not comfort him. He once stood in his own orchard, saw small bodies hanging in the peach tree, nearly cut a branch to beat his children with, and only then realized he had been "walking in his sleep" and that the branch was from the tree where their mother died.

Because there is a death he did not manage cleanly, and it will not close. His first wife, Marie, hanged herself one snowy night, fearing she had conceived again, and when he went to cut her down he was "a split second too late." He was late, he cannot stop saying, because "he had stopped to put on his galoshes." Out of that split second he has built a riddle he will never answer, "Was the hangman a murderer because he put on his galoshes?" The man who makes death painless and efficient for strangers botched the one death that was his own, called it "an unskillful hanging," and it is the reason he "cannot sleep at night." Her children play at hanging themselves in the orchard. His whole professional calm is built over the one knot he tied too slow, and the calm does not reach it.

His surface, like everyone's in this book, is made of the dead. He wears "a dead man's hat." His Parker pen was a souvenir. He carries a tiny globe-shaped watch on a black ribbon, given to him by a man who shoved his own family off a cliff, and the watch stopped the instant the car went over, so that among all the broken things "the crystal was not broken." He keeps the exact moment of a murder wound down in his pocket, the smooth face intact over the catastrophe, and he takes it out to show, because "he was determined to show us everything." He collects the relics of other people's deaths the way Miss MacIntosh keeps a fled man's umbrella, and he displays them with a technician's pride, the stopped watch that tells no time and keeps perfect time, the surface that holds while everything under it is smashed.

And he is not even one man. When Vera cannot square the confessing, dancing, endlessly talking hangman with a respectable dairy farmer, the landlord explains that the rambler was "the hangman's shadow, who got loose after every hanging" and said the things the close-mouthed hangman never would, and then closes the split back up, "the two were one." So Weed performs the book's divided self as helplessly as everyone else, the silent farmer and the loosed shadow, one person and two. By the time his feet are dancing their soft tattoo on the ceiling over Vera's room, she is no longer sure he was ever there at all, and she asks the question the book asks of all its figures, "Had I dreamed the hangman?"

The connection for a writer is the darkest turn in the whole set, because Weed holds the maker's power and feels it as guilt. To bring the imagined to life is the same act as finding the dead mouse in the pocket the next morning. The book has spent itself insisting that dreaming makes real, that a sleeping stranger can be given a whole marriage and a cried name a whole death, and Weed is the figure who says the quiet cost of that power plainly, that what is made in the mind leaves a body. He is also the anti-witness in his purest form, not the man who runs from the real like Bonebreaker but the man who stares at death for a living and never sees a single person, who takes the weights and measurements and ties the knot and calls it mercy. A writer can do exactly that, reduce people to their uses, collect them as material and souvenirs, tie the neat knot and never talk to any of the parties concerned. That is the hangman's craft, and it is efficient, and it improves the farm. The book sets it beside the other kind of making, the kind that stays in the room and looks at the person, and it lets Weed dance alone on the ceiling all night, a good father who cannot sleep, to show what the tidy version costs.
master-class-character-joe-goldberg:
Joe Goldberg: The Champion Who Could Not Be Remembered

← Walter · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Chicago Detective →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joe Goldberg · Miss MacIntosh

He writes from the top of a frozen mountain to the one person who has forgotten him. Joe Goldberg, "the golden cock, the featherweight champion who had worn a crown of golden feathers," is dying of tuberculosis in the Colorado snow, and he spends his last strength on letters to Esther Longtree, begging her to remember one night in a graveyard years ago when he "took her against her will" and, he believes, fathered her child. She was "the peak of his existence," he tells her, greater than any crowd in Chicago or St. Louis, the one triumph "that God could not take away." And she cannot place him. She reads his letters "with squinting eyes," she cannot finish them because they are "too long and fine to read to the end," and for the life of her she cannot remember the champion, because, the book says with terrible simplicity, "she could remember the weak but not the strong."

Esther holds every sterile, weeping salesman who ever cried in her arms, the puny fathers, the ones who lost. The one man who came to her strong and victorious, who wanted to be remembered for his strength, is the one man she cannot find in her memory at all. He weighs nothing there, "too much like an angel's feather for her to know him." He staked his immortality on being witnessed by her, and she is the witness who keeps only the defeated. His demand to be held for his victory is the very thing that makes him unholdable.

His last fight is with God, in an arena the book strips from everyone else. "There was no umpire," "no audience, no crowd," "the bleachers were empty and white as bones," and he is "boxing with shadows," "fighting with his imagination only." God is "a professional, fighting with weak amateurs," there are no rules in the game, and Joe is losing to soft blows he cannot even feel until he is on his knees. He fought his whole life to see "the surprised look in the other guy's eyes" as they fell and glimpsed the empty heaven, and now God is giving him that look, feinting and slow and absent-minded, knocking out the man light as a feather. This is the wheel of fortune the book reads its own way, the champion who was spread wide at the top now stripped to the vertical line, alone, in contact at last with what he is made of. And Joe cannot accept the bottom. He keeps insisting he "won every battle but the last," keeps reaching for the crown "of dove feathers" and the roaring crowd, keeps framing his death as a bout he might still take. The one thing the philosophy asks, that a person stand honestly at the bottom and witness where he actually is, is the one thing the champion will not do. He wants the horizontal back. He wants the applause.

His deepest hope is the one the book denies him with the most tenderness. He believes he left "the only real mark he had ever made on anyone" in Esther, a child, a piece of himself carried forward. And the child "was never born and were never conceived, so far as she could recall." She remembers the graveyard, the tombs, the angel whose nose he knocked off as they struggled, all "the details that she knew so well," but she cannot attach the details to the man. The mark is there; the maker is gone from it. She was marked and cannot name what marked her, and so his one bid to survive himself dies in the memory of the only woman who could have carried it.

The turn for a writer is the nakedest fear in the whole set, because Joe Goldberg is the artist who works for posterity and is forgotten by the reader he worked for. He sends his self out in letters, "with trembling fingers, with bleeding eyes," a speck of his own blood on the white paper, and the reader cannot finish the pages, cannot tell him from any other man who passed through, "travelling salesman or tramp." He fights the blank and holy opponent in an empty arena where no one watches, which is the writing life. And his one consolation, that he left his mark, that the work touched someone, is answered by a woman who kept the mark and lost the man. Set him beside Miss MacIntosh's fled lover, whose umbrella is kept while he is forgotten, and beside Esther, who mourns the weak and cannot see the strong. The champion learns what the book keeps teaching, that memory holds the ones who suffered and lets the victors fall through, that the surest way to be forgotten is to demand to be remembered for having won. He wanted to be the golden cock crowned in feathers. He is remembered, if at all, as the weight of a feather, drifting, that no one caught.
master-class-character-lorena:
Lorena: The Life Made From a Confession

← Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Mr. Bonebreaker →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Jacqueline White · Lorena · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Lorena is not summoned out of nothing the way the others are. She was real, and she was loved, and she comes into the book by accident, pulled out of Miss MacIntosh one morning by a question Vera did not expect to matter. Vera had always been "certain that Miss MacIntosh could have no past," that the plain, red-haired nursemaid who stood for truth to nature was exactly as much as she appeared and no more. Lorena is the past that certainty had erased. She is the one love of the one person in the novel who was supposed to have no secrets, and she is the crack that runs straight through the book's idea of the real.

She was a dancer. Dark, "very dark, fat and not thin," with black hair "like the midnight curtain concealing the star until the star was revealed," she was in the orphanage that Miss MacIntosh worked in, laughed at her, and ran off to become a strip-tease artist, a fan dancer with a feather fan. Years later she came back into Miss MacIntosh's life the way the lost come back in this book, by chance and by force, paroled into her care, so that the nursemaid was now the parole officer of the girl she loved. Then Lorena ran again. "I loved only once," Miss MacIntosh says, and it was this, a beautiful girl who laughed at her and left twice.

Losing Lorena is what unmade the one steady person in the novel. Miss MacIntosh cannot chase her, because she is the officer sworn to hold her, and so she does the only thing left, which is to come apart. "I wandered. I wandered on and on. I broke my nose. I lost my breast. I had no place. I walked into the traffic flow." The woman who was the moral guide, the anchor, the one who told Vera not to let her mind wander from reality, wandered herself, out of her post and into the road, because a fan dancer left her twice. The rock of the reality that Miss MacIntosh was supposed to represent turns out to have been cracked from the start by a love it could not hold.

The secret Lorena knew is worn on Miss MacIntosh's head. Miss MacIntosh is bald and hides it under a wig, and the wig is the truest object in the portrait, a made surface pulled over a bare truth, put on quickly when footsteps come and thrown off when they recede. She wore it black at first because Lorena's hair had been black, and only later red, so that the concealment was also a memorial, the beloved's color kept on the head that lost her. The novel's one figure of truth to nature spends her days managing a false surface over a real absence, which is as exact a picture of how this book thinks reality works as anything in it. The plain woman is a construction too, and the construction is where the grief is kept.

Lorena and Miss MacIntosh are opposite faces of one longing. "She sought the light as I have sought the shadow," Miss MacIntosh says, the dancer under the spotlight and the nursemaid under the umbrella, the one who took everything off and the one who could not take off even her wig. But the two orientations meet at the same bare place. Lorena "snatched them all bald until she became old and bald herself, bald as an old man," and Miss MacIntosh was bald all along, so that exposure and concealment arrived at the identical naked head. And it was Lorena who had seen that head first, who "had known, laughing behind her fan," the one person who looked under the cover and stayed long enough to laugh. The love and the exposure were the same act.

Vera never meets her. Everything of Lorena reaches the reader through Miss MacIntosh's guarded, self-interrupting telling, a confession she keeps trying to stop, breaking off when "she stopped herself suddenly as if she were going to tell me too much," saying they have talked long enough, wondering why she should think of Lorena dancing in the spotlight at all. To know Lorena is to receive the version a bald, grieving woman will allow, drawn out of her by a girl's persistence and pushed back down again. She is the known built by the knower one more time, except that here the known was real, and loved, and the knower would rather not build her at all, and does anyway because she cannot help it.

This is where the method turns on its own foundation. Miss MacIntosh was the reason Vera went searching, the solid thing at the bottom of a dreaming world, the one who was not to be taken in. Lorena is the proof that the anchor was a wig. If even the woman who stood for the plain and the real is a concealed surface over a bare and grieving head, kept in the color of a girl who laughed and left, then the real in this book is not the opposite of the made. It is a thing worn. The most trustworthy person in the novel is trustworthy the way a wig is, a careful cover pulled over a loss, and the truest fact about her is the one she spent her whole life keeping under it, which has a name, and the name is Lorena.

The turn for a writer is about excavation rather than invention. Madge was made from a blank sleeping face and Jacqueline from a name cried in sleep, both conjured out of nearly nothing. Lorena is the reverse operation. She was real, and loved, and she has to be dug out of the one person who would rather not speak of her at all, drawn up against that person's own resistance, and given only in the version a bald, grieving woman will permit before she "stopped herself suddenly as if she were going to tell me too much." That is the other half of the work, not building a figure out of air but drawing a buried real thing out of a guarded source, and accepting the partial, self-interrupting account, because the reticence is itself true to the teller. The deepest material is almost always the thing the source least wants to give, kept under the wig, worn in the black of a girl who laughed and left and later in memorial red. And Lorena turns the whole method back on its own foundation, because Miss MacIntosh was supposed to be the solid ground, the one figure who was not made up, the floor the invention stood on, and she proves to be a careful surface pulled over a loss like everyone else. A writer who trusts that some characters are simply the real ones, the reliable floor beneath the dreaming, should remember that the floor is wearing a wig, and that the steadiest person in the book was assembled over a grief she would not name until a patient listener drew it out of her one guarded sentence at a time.
master-class-16-literary-devices:
Literary Devices

← The Symbolism · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Epilogue →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

A note on method

What follows groups Young's devices into families rather than cataloguing them one by one, because she never uses them one by one. A single sentence will run alliteration through a chiasmus while a phrase repeats at its head and its tail, and to pull those apart into separate entries is to describe a chord by naming its notes in different rooms. Each family below leads with a passage rather than a definition, because the passage is the argument; the naming comes after. Quotations are cited by chapter, since the novel has appeared in more than one edition and page numbers would depend on what edition.

Repetition

Of a bull frog's voice coming out of the dark, Young writes that it croaked "too deep, too deep" (ch. 61), and the doubling is the whole of her method in miniature. The phrase does not describe depth. It sinks, the second "too deep" carrying the first down with it, so that the reader arrives at the bottom of the sound before arriving at its sense. This is what repetition does everywhere in the novel, and it is worth treating the several named devices, anaphora, epistrophe, epanalepsis, anadiplosis, refrain, as one family, because Young runs them together and they all serve a single end. Her repetition does not clear a word for reuse. It thickens the word with everything it has already carried.

That end is the exact opposite of the one repetition usually serves in modern prose, and the distinction is the key to reading her. As the discussion of her education noted, the contemporary whose surface most resembles hers is Stein, and Young declined the kinship for a precise reason. Stein repeats to strip a word of its associations and make it land clean in the present. Young repeats to make the past accumulate in the word until it can barely be lifted. Every device in this family is a way of refusing to let something go.

Anaphora, the repeated head, is her instrument for a mind circling a question it cannot answer. Catherine, staring down the golden archer, asks "Am I the anvil? Am I the hammer?... Am I the horseshoe? Am I the horseman or the horse?" (ch. 43). The repeated "Am I" does not build toward an answer; it multiplies the identities the questioner might be until the self dissolves into the asking. The same head-repetition drives Mr. Spitzer through space in a passage where every clause begins "He passed," and by the end he "passed the same place twice, or else the place had moved" (ch. 54), the anaphora itself enacting the loop it describes, so that the reader cannot tell forward motion from return any better than he can.

Anadiplosis, the tail that becomes the next head, is where the family shows its deepest logic, because it makes the sentence physically circle. "For years collapsed into a moment of sighing. Or a moment of sighing was extended to many years" (ch. 54): the second sentence takes the first apart and reassembles it backward, "years" and "a moment of sighing" trading places across the period, so that time itself is shown to be reversible at the level of the clause. Young does the same with Spitzer's music, where "the unconscious music" becomes "the conscious music," and then, in the next breath, "the conscious music became the unconscious" (ch. 55). The chain does not advance. It hands each term back to its opposite, which is the novel's whole picture of a mind that cannot keep its states sorted.

Set against these circling figures is the flat declaration that they are not accidents of style but law. "Anything which was worth happening at all was worth happening twice" (ch. 62), Spitzer reflects, and the sentence is the family's charter. In a novel governed by that principle, nothing occurs once. Events double, the dead return, the pearls that are lost come back more numerous than before until, as Catherine explains, "the more pearls there were. It was infinity" (ch. 71). That is repetition's strangest turn here: it is not loss but increase. The thing repeated does not wear thin with each return. It gathers.

What makes the technique bearable across so many pages, rather than merely insistent, is that the doubling carries the book's grief. "Everything seemed to repeat and double before his eyes, even in this sad world so like the next that it was perhaps the next" (ch. 51). The repeated world and the world to come blur into each other because, for a man who has lost his twin, every present thing is haunted by its double, and the prose that keeps returning to the same phrase is performing the same refusal to let the dead be gone that Spitzer performs with his two watches and Catherine with her crowded bedroom. The refrain, in this novel, is grief's own grammar: the line that will not stop coming back because the person it mourns will not. It is no accident that the flat statement underwriting the whole family, that the living and the dead are not to be sharply divided (ch. 2), is also the statement underwriting the book's treatment of death. Repetition is how a sentence keeps the dead in the room.

So the several devices resolve into one gesture. Anaphora circles a question, anadiplosis circles a clause, the refrain circles the whole book, and each does it by returning rather than advancing, by gathering the past into the present phrase rather than clearing it away. A reader who wants to feel why the novel is as long as it is, and why its length is not a flaw, need only watch what its repetitions do: they do not move the book forward, because the book's deepest conviction is that nothing that mattered ever fully passes, and a prose faithful to that conviction cannot, in good conscience, stop coming back.

Sound

Young sets the whole family's terms in a single clause, calling her own prose "weavings of the threads of sound upon the loom of time" (ch. 58). That is not a description of a scene; it is a description of what her sentences are made of. Sound in this novel is not decoration laid over meaning but the material the meaning is woven from, and the several devices usually kept apart, alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, cacophony, and the book's peculiar musicality, are better read as one loom, because Young works them all at once and toward one end. That end is the novel's deepest paradox about hearing: that the truest sound in the book is silence, and the truest music is the music no one can hear.

The soft devices come first, and they do the work of the trance. In "whispering presentiment of rain in a distant street" (ch. 58) the repeated breathy consonants and the long vowels running under them slow the line to the pace of the thing described, so that the sentence does not report a hush but produces one. This is the hypnotic register that carries a reader through a book of this length, the alliteration and assonance functioning less as ornament than as tempo, a way of making the prose move at the speed of reverie rather than the speed of information. When Young writes of "fading ripples begetting fading ripples, merged whispers and movements" (ch. 62), the sounds enact their own sense: the phrase fades as it repeats, each soft cluster begetting the next exactly as the ripples do, so that the reader hears the dying-away the words name.

Against this hush she sets the noise, and the noise is where the family turns harsh on purpose. The novel is full of "buzzings, hummings, hammerings, ripplings of sounds" (ch. 61), and of "the demented sea shells singing to themselves" and "the shriekings of the silken skies" (ch. 56), clusters of grinding, clashing consonants that break the trance the soft passages induce. This cacophony is not a lapse from the music; it is the music's necessary opposite, the discord that the fragile order of the prose is always holding at bay. Young even personifies it, giving the racket a keeper: a "sound effects man" (ch. 54) who imitates the chaos of the world, foghorns and slamming doors, so that the noise has an author the way the silence does. Between the whispering and the shrieking the novel maps its whole acoustic range, and the range is the same as its thematic one, the fragile made thing and the chaos it is built against.

Then comes the turn that makes Sound more than a matter of ear, and it is the reason to treat the family as a unit rather than a checklist. The book is crowded with the deaf and the mute, and its central musician, Mr. Spitzer, hears his music only as "a crystal droning, buzzing in his dead ear, his deaf ear" (ch. 55), a sound that is not sound, arriving through the organ that cannot receive it. Young pushes this until the paradox states itself outright: "what was sound but the dream of communication in worlds where none should speak?" (ch. 62). Sound, in that formulation, is not the real thing but the dream of it, and silence is where the real communication lives. The novel's highest musical value is therefore an oxymoron it returns to like a refrain, "the music of the perfect silence" (ch. 14), the music beyond the reach of the falling stars, audible to no living ear and truer for it. The stone deaf man Vera finally marries is the figure this whole family has been building toward: the one who hears with his eyes, for whom all the world's noise is silent, and who is offered, without irony, as the book's deepest listener.

So the loom's two threads, the hush and the din, are woven toward silence rather than sound. The onomatopoeia that seems at first to be Young reveling in noise, the trolley bell that goes "Ding, dong, ding" (ch. 54) long after the last trolley has passed, turns out to be haunted: a bell ringing where there is no bell, sound persisting past its source exactly as the dead persist past their lives. Every device in the family finally points the same way. The soft sounds lull, the harsh sounds jar, the imitated sounds haunt, and all of them are measured against a silence the novel holds to be more musical than any of them, because in a book where the truest things are said by the mute and the truest music is heard by the deaf, sound itself is only the dream of a communication that silence, in the end, keeps better.

Opposition and reversal

The front of this book gave two chapters to the novel's largest refusal: the Dialectics chapter, on how Young invokes the machinery of thesis and antithesis and then withholds the synthesis it promises, and the Paradox chapter, on the two-things-at-once condition the book is left holding once that synthesis fails. Those chapters argue the theme across the whole length, because the refusal to resolve is a thing you can only feel over 1,198 pages. This family does the opposite. It watches the same refusal happen inside a single sentence, in the grammar, before any theme has been stated, and its whole claim is that the philosophy the chapters describe was never laid over the prose but built into its smallest joints. Antithesis, chiasmus, and oxymoron are the theme worked at the scale of the clause.

Antithesis is the balance the novel refuses to tip. When Young writes that Mr. Spitzer "was this soul divided, for he was this twin, and one was dead, and one lived" (ch. 25), the mechanism to watch is not the meaning but the missing word. The natural sentence would join those halves with "but," ranking one over the other, one the true brother and one the shadow. Young joins them with "and," and the two clauses sit at equal grammatical weight, neither subordinated, so that the sentence itself declines to say which twin is the real one. The refusal the Dialectics chapter traces across the book is here performed in the choice of a single conjunction. She does it again with Catherine, who "was both living and dead" (ch. 25): the word "both" is doing the antithesis's whole work, holding two states the mind wants to sort into one register and forbidding the sort. What a reader feels in these lines is not an idea about unresolved opposites but the small grammatical fact of an opposition that the sentence structurally will not resolve.

Chiasmus is the same refusal made to circle. Its mechanism is the mirror: a clause reverses its own order so that its end throws its beginning back, and the sentence arrives where it started. When the world "was a mad man's dream" (ch. 22) recurs across the novel, the surrounding sentences keep folding their terms back to front, past becoming present becoming past, until the line has no forward direction left in it. The device does something no theme-statement can do: it makes the reader's eye travel out and back within a single sentence and end at the beginning, so that the book's claim about time's non-progression is not asserted but enacted in the act of reading the clause. The chapters can tell you the novel does not advance. Chiasmus makes a sentence not advance while you watch.

Oxymoron is the collision compressed until it fits in a breath, and it is where the family does its most distinct work, because it operates faster than thought. "Wakeful sleep, of sleeping wakefulness" (ch. 4): the two words are pressed so close that the mind cannot hold them apart long enough to reject the contradiction, and the fusion registers before the objection can form. This is precisely what a sentence can do and a chapter cannot. The Paradox chapter can describe a state in which sleep and waking are one condition; the oxymoron makes you experience the two meanings refusing to merge in real time, in the half-second it takes to read two words. When Young writes that "there should be nothing certain but uncertainty" (ch. 2), the paradox is not a theme she is introducing, it is a torque she puts on a single sentence, the statement undoing its own claim to statement even as it makes it. The mechanism is the point: the contradiction is delivered too fast to be argued with, which is exactly why it lands as felt rather than proposed.

Juxtaposition is the family's device turned outward from the clause to the paragraph, the same balancing carried up one scale. Where antithesis holds two terms in one sentence, juxtaposition sets two images side by side and, again, withholds the connective that would rank them: the half-eaten breakfast apple beside the phantoms thickening in the air, the plain fact laid next to the impossible one with no "but" to tell you which to believe. It is the bridge between this family and the whole book's method, the point at which the sentence-level refusal becomes the structural one the Dialectics chapter describes.

Figuration

Young's densest single image is a definition of her whole figurative method: a world that is, she writes, "the spectre of the spectre, the dream of the dream" (ch. 49). Look at what the figure does rather than what it says. It offers a thing, then the copy of the thing, and removes any original the copy could have been made from, so that the metaphor has no ground floor. This is the trait that unifies the devices usually separated here, metaphor, simile, analogy, personification, anthropomorphism, allegory. In ordinary prose a figure borrows the solidity of the literal to illuminate the figurative: the real bridge lends its realness to the metaphor. In Young the direction reverses. Her figures do not stand on a literal ground; they dissolve it, so that the comparison and the thing compared turn out to be equally provisional.

Metaphor and simile, in her hands, tend to unmake the solid rather than fix it. When Mr. Spitzer becomes "a poor puppet dancing on its strings, but who held the spindle?" (ch. 56), the simile does the expected work of rendering his helplessness, and then the question dismantles the whole figure by asking after a puppeteer the novel refuses to supply. The comparison opens onto an absence. The same reversal runs through the marble statue "sculptured by man dreaming that he was other than he was" (ch. 1): the figure of solid stone is immediately undercut by the dream inside it, so that the most literal object in the sentence, carved marble, is revealed to rest on a fantasy. Young's figures characteristically point at the drawn thing and then at the hand that drew it, and find the hand uncertain.

Personification and anthropomorphism are the same gesture turned on the inanimate world, and they should be read together because Young makes no working distinction between them. She grants agency to objects, forces, and abstractions indiscriminately, and always to the same end: the erasure of the line between what is alive and what is not. The earth "swelled, heaved like a woman in child labor" (ch. 56); the sea lies "paved with human faces and luna moths and glow-worms" (ch. 2). These are not decorative animations of a dead landscape. They are the figurative arm of the novel's deepest claim, that the boundary between the living and the dead, the animate and the inanimate, is one the book does not honor. When the furniture dreams and the tides obey and the statues open their eyes, personification is doing philosophical work: it is enacting, at the level of the individual image, the dissolution that the whole novel argues.

Allegory sits above these as the same principle organized at book scale, the house as psyche, the journey as quest, the black coachman as conscience, but it works the way the small figures do, refusing to let its vehicle settle into a stable one-to-one key. The coachman is death and conscience and fate and simply a coachman, and the allegory will not resolve to any single reading, exactly as the metaphors will not resolve to any single ground. What holds the whole family together, from the two-word "dream of the dream" to the book-long allegory of the wheel, is this consistent refusal of the literal anchor. Young's figuration does not illuminate a solid world by comparison. It is the instrument by which she shows the world was never solid, each figure a small demonstration that the thing compared and the thing it is compared to are made of the same dissolving material.

Amplification and excess

Young sends Cousin Hannah up "Alps exceeding Alps, perhaps the mountains of illusion" (ch. 46), and the phrase names the engine of her whole rhetoric of excess: not a mountain but a mountain beyond the mountain, magnitude that will not stop at any summit. Hyperbole and amplification are the same device at two scales here, the single exaggerated stroke and the sustained accumulation, and both serve the novel's conviction that ordinary proportion is a lie about a world that is actually boundless.

Hyperbole inflates the particular past the point where realism could hold it. Cousin Hannah becomes "the boldest mountain-climber ever known among members of the weaker sex" (ch. 46); the great house acquires more drawing rooms than tideless years. The exaggeration is not decorative overstatement but a claim about scale: that these lives and losses are genuinely too large for the measured sentence, and that a prose faithful to them must break proportion. Amplification is the same impulse extended, the piling of "many drifting mirrors, many cascading stars, stars rushing like streams, tides of faceless memory" (ch. 39), where the repeated "many" and the cascading clauses refuse to arrive at a countable total. The novel does not amplify to emphasize a point already made; it amplifies because its subject, memory, grief, the dead, is inexhaustible by nature, and a finite sentence would misrepresent it. Excess, in this book, is a form of honesty about magnitude. Where a spare prose would imply that experience can be captured in proportion, Young's overflow insists that it cannot, and the surplus that seems like extravagance is the sentence admitting it will never be equal to what it carries.

Understatement and negation

Set against all that overflow is a countervailing family that works by saying less, and Miss MacIntosh is its voice: "Fine words butter no parsnips. Words do not harness the winds. Words are as nothing" (ch. 63). Litotes, apophasis, antanagoge, antiphrasis, and euphemism are the devices of saying-by-not-saying, and in a novel this saturated with excess they do something the excess cannot, they mark the places where the book distrusts its own eloquence, and where the deepest things are the things withheld.

Litotes and its blunt cousins belong mostly to Miss MacIntosh, whose plain negations puncture the surrounding lyricism. Her verdict that the law "was the practice of liars" (ch. 14) is understatement wearing bluntness: it says less than a full denunciation and lands harder for the restraint. The device characterizes her, the flat Middle Western negative set against Catherine's cascades, but it also does thematic work, because her understatement is the book's own skepticism about whether any of its beautiful language reaches the real.

Apophasis and euphemism carry the heavier freight, because they point at what cannot be said directly. The narrator's description of Miss MacIntosh as "nobody's fool, the mirror to no one" (ch. 22) defines her by negation, by what she is not and reflects for no one, and the whole novel's method of approaching its central mysteries, death, identity, the dead brother, is this apophatic circling, naming a truth by refusing to state it. Euphemism does the same for mortality: death arrives as "the music of the perfect silence," as sleep, as a veil, never as the blunt fact, and the softening is not evasion but the book's recognition that the plain word would falsify a thing it holds to be unspeakable. Where the amplification family insists that some things are too large for proportion, this family insists that some things are too deep for statement, and the two families are the novel's two honesties, the overflow and the withholding, the excess that admits it cannot capture enough and the reticence that admits it should not try to say everything.

Syntax and disruption

Young's most famous sentences run without brakes: "Brooklyn Bridge like a purple lace glove reaching through the darkness and Times Square lighted with a thousand lights and Roman fountains splashing in lonely court yards" (ch. 2). Asyndeton and its relatives, the missing conjunctions, the broken clauses, the inverted order, the endless parallel, are how the novel builds and breaks the sentence itself to match a consciousness that does not proceed in orderly steps.

Asyndeton is the rush: images strung with "and" after "and," or with no connective at all, so that the reader is carried through a cascade without the pauses that ranking and subordination would impose. This is the sentence-level form of the novel's refusal to sort, the same refusal the opposition family traced in the conjunction, now extended across a whole breathless period until the images pile faster than judgment can process them. Against this flood Young sets anacoluthon, the sentence that breaks its own structure mid-flight, swerving from one grammar to another: "Sound was life, echo of echo. Death was silence, though it was also figured like a state of mind" (ch. 55), where the thought turns and re-turns and never completes the shape it started. The broken syntax is not carelessness; it is the accurate transcription of a mind losing and refinding its footing, the grammar fracturing exactly where the consciousness fractures. Parallelism and anastrophe complete the family, the one imposing a mirror-order that the content keeps disrupting, the other inverting normal sequence so that the sentence arrives strangely, out of its expected order, the way memory arrives. Taken together these devices make the sentence a working model of the mind the novel renders: accumulating without sorting, breaking without warning, ordered and disordered in the same clause, so that reading the syntax is the closest a reader comes to inhabiting the consciousness from inside.

Structure and time

The larger architecture of the novel is built, above all, to unsettle time, and its governing image is a house where "each clock having been stopped at a different hour" (ch. 12). Foreshadowing, flashback, motif, archetype, and the recurring symbolic image are the devices that operate at this structural scale, and they all serve the book's refusal of linear sequence, the conviction that the past does not lie behind the present but presses up through it.

Foreshadowing here is unusually total, because in a book of reversals nearly everything is a seed for something later. The secret canary substitution, "this substitution of the living for the dead, another canary always in the house, a spare" (ch. 2), planted early and paid off late, is characteristic: the novel seeds its ends in its beginnings so thoroughly that, as the foreshadowing material rightly observes, a second reading becomes a different book, the reader now seeing every early image as the announcement of a reversal to come. Flashback, correspondingly, refuses to stay in the past, because the novel's memory is not retrospective but present-tense, the recalled scene arriving with the same weight and immediacy as the framing one, so that past and present cease to be separable layers.

Motif and recurring image are the threads that bind this non-linear structure, and they behave like the repetition family at book scale: the black coachman, "upon whom all things depended" (ch. 14), the sea, the clocks, the wheel, returning across hundreds of pages, each recurrence gathering the weight of its previous appearances rather than merely reminding. Archetype gives these recurrences their mythic reach, the Dreamer and the Realist, the Quest, the House as psyche, lifting the particular characters toward the universal patterns the Characters-as-Representations material traces. And under all of it runs the novel's treatment of time as stopped, cyclical, and simultaneous, the clocks each frozen at a different hour and starting up wheezing in the dark. What these structural devices share with the sentence-level ones is the single conviction the whole book is built on: that sequence is a fiction the novel will not honor, that the dead coexist with the living and the past with the present, and that a form faithful to this cannot advance in a line but must, like its own stopped clocks, keep the hours all at once.
master-class-02-the-wheel-that-turns-aro:
The Wheel That Turns Around Nothing

← Introduction to the 2nd edition · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Brief Overview of Radical Immanence →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

Marguerite Young told an interviewer that she thought of Miss MacIntosh as the center of a wheel, the hub, with the other characters as spokes radiating out from her, and the wheel itself endlessly expanding like a universe. That is the architect describing the blueprint. She explicitly names it and then takes it away from the reader.

Miss MacIntosh, the practical nursemaid from What Cheer, Iowa, stands at the center. Vera, Catherine, Mr. Spitzer, Cousin Hannah, Esther Longtree, all the others turn around her. Each spoke holds its distance from the others and its attachment to the middle. This is a reassuring shape. It has a center. It promises that if one travels far enough inward, past the outer characters and their orbits, one arrives at something solid, a person who is what she appears to be, who knows what time it is, who cannot be fooled.

Then Miss MacIntosh, who once carried rocks in her pockets “perhaps as ballast,” walks into the ocean and is never seen again. The hub is gone almost before the wheel has finished turning once. The wig comes off. And here is the thing the novel is quietly doing from that moment forward: it is not showing a wheel that lost its center. It is showing that the center was never there to lose. Miss MacIntosh was the still point everyone believed in, the plain reliable ground, and the whole long book is the slow revelation that even she was turning all along, secretly, under her hat, the same as everyone else. The hub was the last illusion to go.

This is the motion the novel was built on. The hub-and-spoke wheel, the one Young described, collapses into a different wheel underneath it. That second wheel is older. Boethius drew it in prison while he waited to be executed: the Wheel of Fortune, which turns as it pleases, raises the low and brings down the high, and does not turn for any one person specifically. It simply turns, and people happen to be on it. The medieval world treated this not as a metaphor but as a diagram of how time actually works. Young built that diagram into the novel from the first page, and she encoded it in the narrator's name before a single chapter unfolds. Vera Cartwheel. Truth, attached to a wheel. Truth turns. It does not stay.

What Young does with the old wheel is the part worth studying, and it is where a writer can learn the most from her. In the traditional Wheel of Fortune, many people ride the rim. Fortune lifts one and drops another; the wheel is crowded with rising and falling figures, each having their turn. Young made one change, and it is the change that generates everything else. She put a single person on the wheel. Not many selves each taking a turn, but one self that is itself the turning, made of the same stuff as the wheel, multiple and contradictory and never arriving. When Vera observes that life must always have these double motions, circles within circles, wheels within wheels, orbs within orbs, she is not describing the sky. She is describing the inside of a single consciousness that contains its own revolutions and cannot resolve them into one center. Mr. Spitzer is the clearest case: always between two streams, unable to decide which way to turn, unable to stand still. He is not a man who lost his center. He is a man made of turning.

That single change is why the novel can be 1,198 pages long without going anywhere in the ordinary sense. A spoke does not travel; it rotates. The book does not build toward a climax; it accumulates revolutions. This is a structural decision with consequences, and any writer who has been told that a novel must advance, must escalate, must arrive, should sit with what Young proves here: that a book can hold a reader by turning rather than by climbing, if the turning is the subject. She built a structure whose deepest architecture is invisible on a first reading, that accumulates across the full length, and that rewards the reader who stays long enough to feel its weight. She learned to do this by reading Tom Jones thirteen times as a student, until she could see how a structure hides itself in plain sight. She spent eighteen years applying that lesson to a novel that looks nothing like Tom Jones.

I have a name for the philosophy the novel enacts by turning this way. I call it Radical Immanence: the conviction that everything which matters is here, in this world, in this turning, and not in some still point beyond it. I want to state clearly that I coined the term for what I found in Young before I knew it had a philosophical history. The word immanence carries other thinkers behind it, Spinoza and others who set the immanent against the transcendent, and when I traced that history afterward I found that Young seems to have arrived at her version on her own, the same way I arrived at the name on mine. Three independent arrivals at the same place is not a weakness in the idea. It is a small argument that the place is real, and that it was waiting in the novel to be found rather than carried in from outside.

One more honest note about what I am claiming. I am arguing that the novel enacts this philosophy, not that Young sat down intending to build it. The documents that might settle the question of her conscious intent are at the Beinecke Library; I have put the question to her official biographer. Until the archive speaks, the claim rests where it should rest, on what the book does rather than on what its author meant, and I would rather stand on firmer ground. This is itself, as it happens, one of the philosophy's own commitments: to name where you are speaking from instead of pretending to speak from nowhere.

Radical Immanence has eleven load-bearing ideas, and I will not walk them here. They have their own chapters, and readers who want the full case, or the chapter-by-chapter mapping to the novel, will find it in the companion volumes listed above. What matters here is how the wheel gathers them. The plural self is the person on the wheel, many and turning. Constructed reality is the recognition that the ground everyone stands on, including the "just the way things are" that Miss MacIntosh insists upon, was built by someone and can be asked who it serves. Grief that does not end is the wheel's emotional weather: it keeps turning even after everyone has gone home, and the losses accumulate rather than resolve. Witnessing is what Vera does, staying present with contradictions she cannot fix, which reframes her so-called passivity as the hardest and most ethical thing the book asks. Building anyway, unfinished as honest, the margins revealing the seams, the past accumulating beneath the present, language shaping what can exist, the sacred found here rather than beyond: each of these is a spoke, and each turns around the same absent center.

The eleventh idea is the one that ties the others together, and it is where Young's reinvention of the wheel finishes its work. I call it the crossing point. The traditional Wheel of Fortune is vast and impersonal; it turns over you and produces awe at its scale. Young's singular wheel produces something else. If there is one self on the wheel, and the self is the turning, then the meaningful place is not the great rim sweeping through the heavens but the exact intersection where this specific past meets this specific moment, here, in this body, now.
