The crossing point is not large. It is precise. It is Vera arriving not at What Cheer, Iowa, the magical center she quested toward, but in Indiana, in the ordinary Middle West, at herself, choosing to marry a stone deaf man and accepting that there is no perfect moment and no hub to reach. “Whatever is average is the dream. Whatever is hidden is the revealed.” The still point she spent the novel seeking was never out on the rim. It was the crossing point she already was.

Young gave us a wheel with a center, and then showed us the center was never there, and in doing so gave us a truer wheel, the old one, with a single turning self on it, arriving nowhere, finding the sacred in the exact and ordinary here. She could not live long enough to write the book about writing she said she would never write. But she left the lesson in the architecture, for any reader patient enough to feel the wheel turn, and for any writer willing to learn how a novel can hold together when the hub is gone.
master-class-character-the-old-clam-digg:
The Old Clam Digger: The Witness the Gulls Mistook for a Rock

← Jock Cartwheel · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Moses Hunnecker →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

The reader meets him the way the seagulls do, by mistaking him for part of the beach. He is Mr. Spitzer's servant, a grey, close-mouthed man out on the salt flats before dawn with his clam buckets and a torn tennis net he drags through the tide pools as if fishing for lost balls, and you would take him for a rock or a heap of eel grass, which is exactly what the birds do because being taken for scenery, being beneath all notice, is the position from which he sees everything.

He is Mr. Spitzer's valet and houseman, a former bookie trained in silence upon the racetrack, a man who knows his master's habits as well as he knows the clam's. He is a hopeless keeper of a house and a faultless keeper of clams, whose economy, the book says, is highly organized, and he goes out at dawn and by starlight to dig them up and to listen to their dying voices. He plucks the broken glass of a fallen chandelier from behind Spitzer's ears without a word. And he digs holes. He digs holes up and down the beach and climbs down into them, buries himself in the sand with only a small opening left for his mouth and nose, sleeps in a hollowed half-shell that rocks like a cradle and would do just as well for a coffin, so that Spitzer, walking at night, is afraid of stepping on him, and the gannets and the herring gulls come down and land on him, taking him for moss or a moving rock. He seemed more native to that shore, the book says, than Mr. Spitzer with his cane and his cape.

Ask the wrong question and he is there for atmosphere, a bit of gothic set-dressing behind the elegant lawyer. Ask the right one and he is the book's plainest bet and its riskiest. Radical Immanence holds that the truth is not at the shining center but at the margin, in the people nobody watches, and the clam-digger is that claim carried to its limit. He is the lowest figure in the whole novel, a mute servant the birds mistake for the ground. The question the book asks through him is whether the truth really does live down there, in the person beneath notice, or whether that is only a consoling idea. His answer is yes, and it is total.

Two things at the end turn the set-dressing into the point. The first is that he knew. On the day of Catherine's funeral, in heavy rain, driving the rickety Packard, he hears Mr. Spitzer confess at last that he is Peron and not Joachim, the largest secret in the book, the thing the whole confession is built toward, and he shows no surprise. He had known all along, or would not have been surprised either way, and he had said nothing for all those years. The secret had been riding in the front seat the entire time, kept by the one man no one thought to look at. The second is that when the great storm comes and only Spitzer survives it, the clam-digger drowned, Spitzer's grief for him runs greater than his grief for Catherine, greater than for anyone, a grief that rises into rage as he stamps his cane on the Boston sidewalks and the traffic lights seem to lower. The book, which uses its length to tell a reader where to look, spends its tenderest late pages not on the famous beauty or the dead lovers but on a drowned servant who dug clams and must, Spitzer says, be counted among his grievous losses. That is the argument, made in the placement itself. The truth was at the margin, exactly where the book kept promising it would be.

And he holds it in the one way the center never can, in silence. He is clam-mouthed, trained to say nothing, and his silence is not emptiness but the shape his knowing takes. Spitzer's whole tragedy is that he cannot stop talking, cannot take the short line to anything, circles and defers and confesses too late for it to land. The clam-digger is his opposite and his completion, the man who carries the same secret and simply keeps it closed, like the clam whose dying voices he rows out to hear. Where language fails Spitzer, holding him forever short of himself, silence serves the clam-digger perfectly. He never has to say that he knows. He knows the way the shore knows the tide.

His burying is the other half of it. A man who spends his nights climbing into graves he dug for himself and sleeping in them, breathing through a hole in the sand, is rehearsing death every night and refusing it every night, and neither the book nor Spitzer can quite say whether the old fellow is fully alive at all. Spitzer half believes he pulled him out of a doorway that was really a tomb and kept his body going by some unusual bargain while the spirit slipped away, so that the clam-digger became a preserved shell with the man gone out of it, a living corpse combing the beach. He held up a dark mirror, the book says, to Spitzer's own illness. He is the crossing point between the living and the dead worn by a servant instead of a gentleman. The two of them are one condition at two heights, the man in the cape who cannot say whether he is himself or his brother, and the man in the sand who cannot be called clearly alive or clearly dead. The margin does not merely hold the truth about the center. It holds the same truth, stripped of the cape.

The lesson for a writer is about where to hide what matters. Young could have handed the book's deepest secret to a major figure and let it go off at the center, in full light. Instead she gave it to the one person the reader was trained to skip, the servant taken for a rock, and let him keep it in silence until the last pages, so that learning he knew, a reader also learned how much is missed by looking where the book told her to look. To place your truth at the margin is to make the reader complicit in overlooking it, and then to turn the overlooking into the lesson. The clam-digger is beneath notice on purpose. He is proof that the person never watched was holding everything, and that when the grief finally comes, it comes hardest of all for him.
master-class-character-walter:
Walter: The Named Child

← Rosemary Longtree · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Joe Goldberg →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Esther Longtree · Rosemary · Vera Cartwheel · Walter

Of all Esther Longtree's stillborn, the eye, the ear, "a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb, nothing," only one has a name, and having a name he has everything the others lack: a voice, a face, a growing body, a red muffler, "his little aviator's goggles, his little boxing gloves, his red sweater," and a reproach. "Walter," she tells Vera, lowering her voice, "was my first-born. He is alive." He was "not bigger than her hand." She "left him in a far-away place, left him as dead," and heard him cry once as she turned away, and hears him now everywhere. The others fell from her as pieces and were buried unmourned. Walter she named, and the name would not let him die.

This is the book's clearest lesson about what naming does, and it is the philosophy's ninth pillar made flesh: language is where a thing gets made real, where it becomes a person who counts. The unnamed stillborn do not officially exist, snowflakes and cobwebs that fall away. Walter exists. Because she said the word, he has an age, or rather all the ages at once, "nine years old," "ten years old," "twelve years old," with a gap where "the eleventh year" went missing in her sieve of a mind. Because she named him, he can speak, and what he says is unbearable. "Mother, why did you kill me?" "Mother, you have led a wicked life." "Mother, you will never find me." The named child is the one who can turn around and accuse.

He is also black, and that is not incidental. "My skin is black, and the snow is white, mother, and I am killed." He is her "black mystery whom the white detective will not find," "black as my true love, black as my heart," the child of a father who "was no salesman," hidden away, "being cared for by nice people in another county, by white people." He is the buried thing the town would judge her for, the loss that carries both her shame and the world's, the child un-findable precisely because he is a black child in a white landscape, with no place in the law. He is the past pressing up from under, the deposit in the ground that will not stay down, and the philosophy's eighth pillar is written across him: the past is not behind you, it is beneath you, and it presses.

He is her reason to live, and the book says so flatly: "This memory was what caused Esther Longtree to live." "Only for him do I live now." He is "the beloved obstacle." She keeps having children in order to have him back, or to have one that will not accuse her, and none of them is Walter, "he was not Walter, though." She calls into the dark for him to wrap his muffler against the cold, to not catch his death, a mother tending a boy who is either lost in another county or lost in the ground or never was, and she cannot tell which, and neither can the book, and it refuses to settle it. "Could not have killed him, because the murder was not finished, he is alive and comes to tell me so." His asking why she killed him is her proof that he lives.

The turn for a writer is the one that cuts closest to the act itself, because Walter is the named creation, the first one, the thing you called into being with a word and therefore made real enough to leave you, real enough to grow on its own, real enough to come back and ask why you killed it. The unnamed pieces cost nothing and stay buried. The named one has a life you did not authorize, ages you cannot account for, a voice that reproaches the maker and then stops its ears when she comes near. To name a thing is to lose control of it. It is also to become responsible for it forever, to live for it, to call into the dark after it. Set him beside Rosemary, who was never named and never lived and stays perfect, and Walter is the opposite kind of ghost, named and flawed and alive and accusing and gone. He is what the writer made and abandoned "in a far-away place," the one work she gave a name and a life and could not keep, and it followed her, and it grew, and it will forgive her, she knows, too late, when she is where he is.
master-class-17-epilogue:
Epilogue

← Literary Devices · Teaching a Writing Masterclass

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

My hope with this survey of Marguerite Young's craft, is that readers will come away seeing Miss MacIntosh, My Darling more clearly, and that writers studying it will find not only a catalogue of the devices available to them but a demonstration of what those devices can be made to do when every one of them is bent to a single vision. The lesson the section has kept arriving at is that Young's techniques are not separable ornaments. Her repetitions, her sounds, her oppositions, her figures, her excess and her reticence, her broken syntax and her stopped clocks all perform the same few convictions, that reality and illusion do not divide, that the self is many, that the dead do not leave, that nothing resolves. A device, in her hands, is never decoration added to a meaning. It is the meaning, worked at the scale of the sound, the clause, the sentence, the chapter, until there is no gap left between what the prose says and what the prose does.

Young's contribution to writing

Marguerite Young's Miss MacIntosh, My Darling expands what the novel can attempt, and it is worth naming these enlargements, because they are the inheritance she leaves to writers willing to learn from her.

She demonstrates, first, that reality and dream can be rendered on one plane without ranking them, that a prose which refuses to sort the hallucinated from the actual can be more honest about consciousness than any realism, because consciousness itself does not sort its contents while having them. She shows that the divided, plural self, Spitzer and his twin, Catherine and her invented company, can be built into the very structure of a book rather than merely described in it, so that fragmentation becomes a form and not just a subject. She proves that poetic density can be sustained at novel length, that the lyric sentence need not be confined to the short forms, and that musicality carried across 1,198 pages produces an immersion no shorter work can reach. She offers, through Miss MacIntosh and Vera and Catherine and Esther Longtree, a range of female interiority (physical, visionary, laboring, grieving) rendered with a psychological depth and a refusal of easy judgment that the tradition had and rarely does extend to such women. She meditates on death and the persistence of the dead not as a theme visited but as a condition inhabited, giving the book a cosmic dimension that never leaves the domestic ground it stands on. And she builds, out of the bus driver and the waitress and the clam-digger and the deaf man, a polyphony that grants mythic scale to the American margins, making an epic out of the people the epic tradition had always left out.

What binds these contributions is the conviction this book has tried to trace: that form and meaning are one thing, that how a novel is made is inseparable from what it knows. Young could not live long enough to write the book on writing she said she would never write. She left the lesson in the architecture instead, for any reader patient enough to feel the wheel turn, and for any writer willing to learn how a novel can hold together when everything the tradition promised, the stable self, the linear time, the resolved ending, the single reality, has been let go.
master-class-09-the-setting:
The Setting

← Characters as Representations · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Regions of the United States →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The settings in this novel are usually read as mirrors. A decaying house for a decaying mind, a frozen waste for a frozen heart, a fog-bound coast for a soul that cannot see its way. That reading is available and it undersells what Young is doing. Setting here is the second pillar of Radical Immanence built out of brick and weather. Reality is constructed rather than found, and the places in this book are the plainest proof of it. They are made by the people who need them, they will not hold still, and in the end they are swept away. Setting is not a backdrop that reflects the self. It is the self's construction, and it fails the way every construction in the novel fails.

The sea-blackened house on the New England coast is the clearest case. It is vast, dark, and almost empty, roofed in "many-colored glass," ringed by roaring surf, and it does not stay where it was put. It "sometimes seems to move in the night from place to place," set down in strange dead cities, its furniture changing, its mirrors "hanging lopsided," its windows "looking out upon a different sea or a different street." A house that relocates while its occupants sleep is not a symbol of instability. It is instability, rendered in the floor plan. The reader is not being told that Catherine's mind is unmoored. The reader is watching the ground itself refuse to be ground, which is the thing the novel keeps insisting: that the solid world is a thing someone built, and a thing that was built can shift, or move in the night, or come down.

Catherine has populated the house the way she populates everything, by making the company she needs. The rooms hold "enchanted clocks stopped at different hours," imaginary servants, guests out of the silent films, "royal sleighs with rusted bells," "giant crabs like monks," "old pontiffs walking in the mist." The servants take these callers for real, and the taking is the point. A dream world is not a lapse here. It is a place, as fully inhabited as any address in the book, and the atmosphere of "snow crystals, halos, mock suns and moons" is not the failure of a real setting but the success of a made one. The house is at once protective and imprisoning, a reality she constructed and cannot now leave.

Whatever moves in the house moves in the cities too. Boston's South Station is "crowded with submarine musicians" and watery apparitions. The Brooklyn Bridge appears as "a purple lace glove reaching through the darkness." Times Square burns with a thousand lights, and Roman fountains splash in courtyards where they do not belong. These are real cities that have stopped behaving like real cities, their streets moving, their buildings changing shape, their landmarks turning up where no map would place them. The polar extremes do the same work by other means, "glaciers like mirrors moving through darkness," the aurora borealis and australis lighting the sky so that the two poles cannot be told apart. So does the Indiana village at night, its "upright houses like coffins," its "pale, dented moon like a skull," a "conspiracy of illusion" filled with amorphous shapes and dead souls. City, ice, and village are not three settings with three meanings. They are one refusal, made three times: the refusal of a place to stay fixed long enough to be trusted.

Against all of this stands Miss MacIntosh, and her world is built to be the exception. Where the house shifts and the cities dissolve, her environment is plain, old-fashioned, and stripped of illusion. She prefers the wind and the hail and the snowstorm to the enclosed, hallucinatory rooms, and her presence is meant to ground the narrative in the solid and the given. It is worth reading her setting as carefully as the book reads her, though, because her plain outdoor world makes the same claim she makes and gets it wrong the same way. She insists that reality is single, found, and reported, that a place is simply there. The novel spends its length demonstrating that even her steadiness is a construction, a self assembled out of a wig and a corset and a rule that there is a place for everything. Her austere world is not the one true setting among the false ones. It is one more built place, kept plain on purpose, by a woman who could not admit that plainness was a choice. The counterpoint holds, but it is not the counterpoint of the real against the unreal. It is one construction that knows itself set beside several that do.

Then the houses come down, and the novel makes its argument in rubble.

Catherine's mansion is a "citadel of dreams and visions and imaginary pretenders to vanished thrones," a "house of shades and monsters," even a "private mad house," the place where her "dreams begot the only realities." After she dies, the sea she dreamed beside all her life reaches up and takes it. The house is "swept over" and "carried away," and the water that filled her visions reclaims the room those visions were kept in. This is not punishment and it is not tidy symbolism. It is the plainest statement of the pillar of reality is constructed. She built a place to survive a life she could not otherwise survive, and the place was temporary, as every built place is, and the tide that was always at the window finally came in.

Mr. Spitzer's houses tell the same story in a lower key. He lives at first in a "grey, impoverished house" of "general confusion" and disrepair, and the novel remembers an earlier house of exact "twin arrangements," the mirrored order that his brother's death shattered. At the end he is in a "beach-comber's shack" with the old clam-digger, and the same storm that takes Catherine's mansion takes the shack. The man who could never say whether he was himself or his brother loses even the walls around him to the one weather. His anchor was always provisional, and the sea does not distinguish between the citadel and the shack.

Cousin Hannah's house is destroyed by a different force, and the difference matters. Her Boston mansion "between two water towers" was "torn down long ago to make space for an asphalt highway," and Mr. Spitzer keeps visiting the empty lot, noting that the place "had disappeared as if by magic." No storm, no sea, only the highway, the ordinary machinery of progress paving over where her life once stood. It fits her, the woman of tent cities and deserts and mountains, whose home was never a structure but the going itself. Her house did not need the ocean to prove it impermanent. The city did it, on schedule, for the sake of a road.

Three houses, three ways of coming down, storm and storm and demolition, and the same lesson under each. The houses in this novel are where memory and identity and the dream are kept, and they are all, in the end, unkept. What survives is not the building. It is the going-on after the building is gone, Spitzer walking the emptied lot, Vera carrying the drowned house forward in the only place it can still stand, which is her telling of it.

The turn for a writer is the one the book keeps making in a new key. A setting does not have to reflect a character to do its work, and it does more when it stops reflecting and starts behaving. Young does not describe a shifting house to signal a shifting mind. She lets the house shift, and the reader feels the ground go before any character explains it. She does not call the mansion fragile. She floods it. The strongest setting is not a mirror held up beside the person. It is a thing the person made, standing on its own until the weather comes, and a writer who learns to build a place that can move in the night, and then be swept away, has learned to make the world of a book carry the argument that the sentences would otherwise have to carry alone.
master-class-15-the-symbolism:
The Symbolism

← The American Literary Tradition · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Literary Devices →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

Young's symbols are not scattered decorations. They organize into a small number of families, and every family points in the same direction: toward the collapse of the boundaries the mind relies on, between life and death, reality and illusion, self and other, past and present. To catalogue the symbols one by one is to miss that they are a system, each object a different instrument playing the same refusal. But before the system can be read, it helps to know where the habit of mind that built it came from, because Young's symbolism is not only a set of images. It is a way of thinking in images, and that way of thinking was trained. She was a scholar before she was a novelist, and the novel is the output of a specific education. What follows traces that education first, from the sentence she inherited to the consciousness she inherited, and then reads the symbols as what that formation produced.

The euphuistic root

Young did her graduate study on John Lyly, whose Euphues gave the language the word euphuism: a prose built on balanced antithesis, elaborate patterning, and above all the relentless drawing of similitudes from the natural world, the beast, the stone, the star, the herb, each pressed into service as an emblem of a human truth. Lyly's prose advances by coupling opposites and by heaping analogy on analogy until the argument is carried less by statement than by accumulated image.

This is Young's method exactly, transposed from the Elizabethan drawing room to the American interior. Her sentences balance opposites the way Lyly's do, and her symbols work the way Lyly's similitudes work, as a hoard of natural and made objects, the sea, the rose, the chessman, the clock, the ship, each standing for a state of the soul. The difference is what she does with the form. Lyly's antitheses resolve into wit; the balanced opposites click shut into a point. Young takes the same balancing habit and denies it the click. Her opposites are coupled and left open, her similitudes multiplied past any single meaning, so that the euphuistic machine, built to produce clarity through pattern, is turned to produce the opposite: a patterned irresolution. The scholar of Lyly learned to think in balanced emblems and then built a novel in which the emblems refuse to balance out. That inheritance, absorbed and inverted, is the engine under everything that follows.

The formal inheritance: how the book is built

If Lyly gave Young the sentence, two English novelists gave her the shape of the book, and she studied both of them as deliberately as she studied Lyly.

The decisive one was Fielding. As a student under the Neo-Aristotelian critic Ronald S. Crane at the University of Chicago, Young read Tom Jones thirteen times, not for pleasure and not for the plot, but to map its invisible, load-bearing architecture, to see how every seemingly casual digression and peripheral character served a grand formal design the novel never announced but always enacted. What she took from Fielding, by way of Crane's exacting functional questions, was a single conviction: that a novel's structure could hide itself completely in plain sight, that the design could be total and yet invisible on a first reading, revealing itself only across the full length to a reader patient enough to feel it. She spent eighteen years applying that lesson to a book that looks nothing like Tom Jones. What reads as oceanic, undisciplined prose is, on this inheritance, a precisely engineered structure whose architecture is meant to stay submerged until the whole has been carried.

The second formal ancestor is Sterne. Tristram Shandy is where the English novel first refused to advance in a straight line, where digression became the method rather than a lapse from it, where time looped and stalled and doubled back and the promised story kept deferring itself. Young inherits the license Sterne opened: the right to build a long book that circles rather than climbs, that treats the tangent as the substance and the arrival as something it need never quite reach. From Fielding she took the buried, total design; from Sterne, the freedom to let that design express itself as circling rather than progress. Between them they account for the paradox of the novel's shape, that it can be enormous and rigorously built and still go nowhere in the ordinary sense, because a structure this deliberate does not have to travel in order to hold.

The consciousness inheritance: what the book believes, and how it repeats

The formal ancestors explain how the novel is made. Two figures from psychology and philosophy explain what it believes about the mind it renders, though one of them enters by being refused.

William James is the genuine ancestor. The stream of consciousness that critics reach for to describe Young's prose is James's phrase and James's discovery, and the deeper inheritance is his method in the Principles of Psychology: the patient, exhaustive description of mental experience as it is actually lived, before philosophy or clinical practice has sorted it into categories. James insisted that every element of the stream is equally real as an element of consciousness, regardless of whether it corresponds to anything outside the mind. The fringe, the half-formed feeling at the edge of attention, the vague and the peripheral, are as much a part of the stream as the clear focal thoughts that respectable psychology had taken as its only subject. This is the philosophical root of Young's refusal to rank. Her prose grants the dead queens the same reality as the knitting needles because James had already argued that consciousness does not, in fact, sort its contents into the real and the negligible while it is having them. The oceanic quality of her sentences, moving outward in all directions at once and carrying everything present in the mind forward together, is James's stream widened until it has no banks. His radical empiricism, in which reality is constituted by experience rather than found beneath it, is a direct ancestor of the novel's conviction that the world is made by the attention paid to it.

Stein is the contrast, and Young drew it herself. The two spent two weeks together at the University of Chicago, and when Young was later asked what Stein's influence had been, she answered: very little. This is worth taking at face value, because Young was declining precisely the kinship a careless reader would assume, and she was right to decline it. Stein is the one contemporary whose surface most resembles Young's, the insistent repetition, the continuous present, the phrase returned to and slightly varied. But the resemblance is a trap, and the two weeks that produced the disavowal are the tell. Stein repeats in order to strip a word of its accumulated associations, to scrub memory off it and make it land clean in the present, a word freed from everything it has carried. Young repeats to do the exact reverse. Her recursion thickens a phrase with everything it has already meant in the book, so that each return deposits more of the past into it rather than clearing the past away. Stein's continuous present erases history from the word; Young's circling is history refusing to leave the word. The two methods look identical on the page and are opposite in their aim, and Young's "very little" is not modesty or evasion but an accurate account of that difference. The one contemporary she most resembles is the one she most needed to distinguish herself from, and the distinction is what her repetition is for: not the erasure of the past but its accumulation, which is the emotional weather of the entire novel.

So the education resolves into a single tendency. From Lyly, a sentence that balances opposites and hoards emblems. From Fielding, a total design that hides itself. From Sterne, the freedom to circle rather than arrive. From James, a mind whose contents cannot honestly be ranked. And from Stein, by way of refusal, a repetition that gathers the past instead of dissolving it. Every one of these points the same way, toward accumulation without resolution, and the symbols are where that tendency becomes visible objects.

Symbols of the dissolving boundary: sea, water, ship

The largest family is water in all its forms, and its work is dissolution. The sea, the tides, the floods, the submerged cities are the novel's image for the unconscious and the infinite, but more precisely they are the image for the loss of edges. Water muffles sound and obliterates boundaries; it merges the separate into the unknowable whole; it is where individual identity goes to stop being individual. When the sea finally takes Catherine's house, it is not just destroying a building but performing what water always performs in the novel, the erasure of the line between one thing and another.

The ship and the voyage belong to the same family, turned toward the journey rather than the merging. Ships, sea voyages, and shipwrecks figure life as navigation through chaos toward a meaning that may not arrive; the lost ships and drowned passengers are the disappearances the whole book grieves. Water dissolves, and the ship is the fragile human attempt to cross the dissolving thing without going under. That most of the novel's ships are lost tells you how Young rates the attempt.

Symbols of decay: the house, the marble statues, the rose

A second family renders the passage of time as ruin, and it centers on the sea-blackened house, with its gilded ballrooms where no one dances, its broken statues, its ruined gardens. The house is grandeur in the act of failing, a physical and psychological space where memory and illusion and ghost all lodge, and its slow slide into ruin is the fading of a life and the dissolution of a self made visible in architecture.

The marble statues inside it sharpen the point. Broken and scattered, they are human aspiration and the idealization of beauty, and their breakage is the failure of those ideals to survive time and nature. Miss MacIntosh's disdain for them is characteristic and, in the novel's final judgment, ironic: she scorns the statues as pretension, the plain woman rejecting the dream of perfection, but she is herself a construction under a wig, an aspiration to solidity as breakable as any marble. The rose completes the family from the other side. Ethereal, ghostly, falling, the rose and its petals are beauty precisely as transience, and the "immortal rose" is the paradox the family turns on: the fleeting thing wished permanent, love and memory persisting past the death that should have ended them.

Symbols of duality held open: black and white, the chessmen

A third family stages opposition without letting it resolve, and it is the most directly euphuistic of the groups, since it is built on balanced pairs. The recurrent black and white, the black coachman, the black and white chessmen, the play of light and shadow, sets life against death, reality against illusion, knowledge against ignorance, and then declines to choose. The pairing is the meaning. Where Lyly's antitheses would resolve to a witty point, Young's stay balanced and unresolved, two colors on one board.

The chessmen make the family's argument fully. Life-sized, moving through shifting clouds and waters, they figure existence as a game of fate whose pieces are moved by forces larger than themselves, and they "move unevenly," which is the tell: the board is not the site of fair contest but of imbalance, individuals caught in a game they do not control and cannot see whole. The black-and-white board promises the clean opposition of a game with rules. The uneven motion takes the promise back.

Symbols of the unstable self and unreliable time: the coachman, Mr. Spitzer's cloak, the clocks

A fourth family attacks the two coordinates a person uses to locate the self, identity and time. The black coachman is the presiding image, driving his carriage through chaos and darkness, his face never seen, never turning to his passengers, the perfect emblem of a fate that steers without revealing itself. He is death and the soul's passage, and the novel names him specifically as Catherine's conscience, so that the unknowable driver of her life turns out to be a part of herself she cannot see the face of. The self is driven by the self and cannot look at the driver.

Mr. Spitzer's cloak does the same work on the body. The mantle that seems to grow and envelop him like a shell is identity as both shelter and prison, the shadowy, ambiguous covering of a man who cannot say whether he is himself or his brother, alive or dead. And the clocks, sundials, and watches with broken or missing numbers dismantle the other coordinate: time here is cyclical, fragmented, suspended, never a reliable line. Between the faceless driver, the enveloping cloak, and the broken clocks, the novel strips a person of every fixed point, who is steering, who am I, what time is it, and leaves the self turning without a coordinate to hold.

Symbols of communication past language: the mute's hands, silence

A last, smaller family points to what lies beyond words, and it is where the novel locates its deepest expression. The mute character's hands, performing their signs of prayer, farewell, flight, and meeting, stand for the ineffable and for the limits of language, communication that succeeds exactly where speech fails. This family runs toward the stone deaf man Vera marries, and it makes the book's quiet claim that the truest things are said in silence, by the hand, by the flower, in the register language cannot reach. In a novel so made of language, these symbols of wordless meaning are Young's admission of where words stop, which is itself a euphuist's confession, the master of patterned speech marking the border past which pattern cannot go.

The whole system

Set the families side by side and the design is plain. Water dissolves the boundary between things; the house and rose and statue dissolve the boundary between grandeur and ruin; black and white and the chessboard hold opposites open without resolving them; the coachman and cloak and clock dissolve the self and its sense of time; the mute's hands dissolve the boundary between speech and silence. Every family is a different assault on the same wall, the wall between the categories a mind uses to keep reality sorted.

And every family traces back to Young’s education. The balanced emblem is Lyly. The buried total design that only the whole reveals is Fielding. The refusal to arrive is Sterne. The unranked contents of the mind are James. The repetition that gathers the past rather than dissolving it is Stein turned inside out. Young learned to think in balanced emblems and pressed the whole inherited apparatus toward a single end none of her models intended: not to sort the world into witty oppositions or clean streams or cleaned-off words, but to show the oppositions bleeding into one another until the sorting fails.

The lesson for a writer is in the discipline underneath the density. Young's symbolism looks like profusion, image heaped on image, but it is governed, every symbol assigned to one of a few jobs and every job serving one argument, and the governance was learned. A writer drowning a page in imagery for its own sake produces only noise; Young produces a system, because each image, however lush, is doing philosophical work, and because behind each image stands a decade of study in how images can be made to carry it. The reader who traces the families rather than the individual symbols finds not a catalogue of pretty things but a single sustained proof that the lines we draw to make the world legible are lines the world does not honor, built by a writer who had studied, more closely than almost anyone, exactly how those lines get drawn.
master-class-character-mrs-hathaway:
Mrs. Hathaway: The Name That Would Not Change

← Musidora · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Beatrice Fitzgerald →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Lisa Lunde · Peron Spitzer

One brother burned to death, and within a few days she married the other, and wore black to the wedding. Mrs. Hathaway is a tale carried in the tavern gossip, a widow twice over, and she is the book's twin knot told in its plainest and cruelest form, because keeping the name while the man beneath it changes.

The facts are few and terrible. One brother, Rudolph, "burned to death and was a long time burning." Before the funeral was cold she married the second, Josh, "still in mourning for his brother," with "only a few days between the marriage and the funeral." Josh married her with his eyes open, "suspicious," wedding her "to make sure, to find out," and what he found out killed him. The town tells his death as a locked room and a frozen face, "the lights went out of his eyes," a door that shut by "nobody's hand," a man who "seemed to die when she came in," his cries "muffled under so many coats" that no one could hear. And it tells her answer, the one thing she is ever reported to say: "I'll still be Mrs. Hathaway."

Ask the wrong question and this is a murder ballad, the black widow and her two dead men. Ask the right one and Mrs. Hathaway is Mr. Spitzer's knot pulled tight and handed to a stranger. The plural self, the person who is not one, is the book's deepest subject, and where Spitzer gets the longest section in the novel to be two brothers in one uncertain body, Mrs. Hathaway gets a paragraph of gossip to prove the same thing from the outside.

The two brothers "had always loved each other," and she says the sentence that dissolves them into each other, that she has "married both brothers," that in mourning the first she lost the second. Two men, one marriage, and a widow who can no longer keep them apart. It is Peron and Joachim in another town, one brother dead and the other uncertain which he is, except that here the confusion is the wife's rather than the man's. "You would think she was married to Rudolph," the gossip says. "She never speaks of Josh." She grieves the dead brother through the living one and then through no one, exactly as Catherine grieves a composite of lost men and pours the tea for the one she cannot recognize.

What she holds onto is the name, and the name is the point. She was Mrs. Hathaway, she became Mrs. Hathaway, and "now she is Mrs. Hathaway who was twice widowed." The men change and die and the title stays, a fixed label over a shifting referent, which is Lisa Lunde's blackboard law walking around a small town, "all a's are c's." Hathaway is the constant that lets one brother stand for another, the way the black coachman could be "any old coachman" and the wrong passenger could ride in the right coach and death would not check the fare. She is not loyal to a husband. She is loyal to a name, and the name is loyal to no one, which is why it can outlast both men who wore it.

The turn for a writer is how much of a self can be carried by a single refused sentence. Mrs. Hathaway never explains, never confesses, never grieves out loud. She says five words, "I'll still be Mrs. Hathaway," and the five words hold everything, the murder she will not name, the brothers she cannot separate, the identity she has decided to keep no matter which man has to die to leave it intact. Young gives her no interior, because the gossip has no access to one, and the withholding is the character. A writer learns here that a figure glimpsed only in rumor can be built as precisely as one rendered from the inside, if the one thing she is allowed to say is chosen well enough. The whole Spitzer section circles the question of whether a person is one or two. Mrs. Hathaway answers it in a doorway, in a borrowed name, over a muffled body, and the answer is that a person can be neither, only a title that stays while the people underneath it keep changing places and dying.
master-class-character-the-chicago-detec:
The Chicago Detective: The Looker Who Saw a Corpse

← Joe Goldberg · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Little Toy Salesman →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Esther Longtree · Lisa Lunde · Mr. Weed · The Chicago Detective

He is the one whose whole profession is seeing, and he looks straight at the living woman and sees a dead one. Three winters running, a "Chicago detective and specialist in murder mysteries" comes to the frozen meadows hunting an escaped killer, a man who murdered his wives "because of the cracked church bells always ringing" and someone calling him yellow, and three times he fails to find the murderer and finds instead Esther Longtree lying on the cold ground with her eyes wide open, "whom he had always taken to be a corpse." He kneels to examine the body. His rimless eyeglasses drop from his nose. And by her account he "raped her mysteriously" there on the ground he took for a death scene, and went away leaving more clues than the killer he came for, "his eye-glasses, his calling card, a bone button, the frozen conception, a thread, and a single spot of brown blood."

He is the anti-witness in his coldest form, and the book has been building toward him. Mr. Weed reduces the living to weights and never meets them; Lisa Lunde sees through people and so never sees them; the detective looks with the trained, professional eye whose entire job is to see what is really there, and he mistakes a sleeping woman for a murdered one because he arrived with the case already framed. His eyes are "pale, unastonished." Nothing surprises him, which sounds like mastery and is the disease, because a man who cannot be surprised has stopped looking and started confirming. He steps over the real mystery, the living, grieving, uncatalogued woman at his feet, to keep hunting the abstract murderer who fits his file, and in doing so he becomes a criminal in a case he does not know he is in, "the beginning of another mystery."

He cannot solve the one that matters, and the book says he is the one "who could solve all murder mysteries but his own." He is also, of all Esther's fathers, the most plural, "partly wax and partly human," "always in disguise," arriving "once as a wandering locksmith, his pockets full of keys and locks, once as a soap salesman," once as himself, so that the man whose trade is fixing identity, naming the culprit, pinning the fact, is himself the least fixed and most waxen figure in the chapter. He is the official reality walking, the law that decides what counts as a crime and a victim, and he is Esther's father's kind, the policeman's kind, the law that looks and does not see. There is "nothing about her case in the law books." The keeper of the record has no category for her, so he files her as a corpse and moves on.

And here is the wound under all of it. Esther wanted him to detect her. "If he had only detected her, this could not have happened." "Something in her had yearned to be questioned by him, to be dragged forth," to be truly investigated, truly seen, made real by the cross-examination she both dreaded and craved. She would have answered nothing, and still she longed to be asked. And he was "indifferent to the mystery." The one figure whose job was to look hard at her looked past her. The subject offered herself to the witness, and the witness was bored. That is the deepest cruelty in the chapter, almost worse than the rape, that the man of attention had no attention to spare for the actual person, only for the escaped abstraction he never caught.

The turn for a writer is the sharpest indictment in the set, because the Chicago detective is the writer who believes he stands outside the material, cool and expert, detecting the truth of a scene he did not disturb. He arrives with his frame, decides the living woman is a corpse in someone else's story, and steps over the real thing to chase the plot he came for. He is "unastonished," which for a maker is fatal, the incapacity to ever be surprised by what is actually on the ground. And in the act of investigating from his imagined outside, he turns out to be inside, complicit, leaving his own evidence, fathering his own stillborn, generating the next mystery he will fail to solve. Set him beside Weed the procedural killer, and beside the hangman's certainty that the imagined thing leaves a real body. The detective is the looker whose looking is itself the violation, the writer who reduces a person to a scene, who solves everyone and cannot solve himself, "partly wax," and the wax is the thing a writer must not let harden over the looking. The book leaves him wiping his hands, walking away into the winter, still looking for the wrong body, having stepped over the one that was alive and asking to be found.
master-class-character-jacqueline-jackie:
Jacqueline / Jackie White: The Life Made From a Name

← Homer Capehorn · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Tavern Landlord →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Homer Capehorn · Jacqueline White · Madge Capehorn · Vera Cartwheel

Madge is built from a face. Jacqueline is built from less than that. She is the dead girl inside the invented marriage, the rival Homer loved and never won, and she is never once on the bus. Vera invents Madge out of a sleeping stranger, and then, inside that invention, Madge invents Jacqueline out of a name Homer cries in his sleep. She is a ghost at two removes, a made-up woman's made-up rival, and the novel gives her more ache and more shine than either of the sleepers who dreamed her.

On the surface she is the county's golden girl. She could “skate like a comet,” and she was “not afraid to skate where the ice was thinnest,” which is also the shape of her dying. She was the cheerleader, the best dancer, first in every sport and every prize, the one carried on shoulders while the boys who loved her fought in the grass and never won her. Now, in the cold dead spring of the story, she is going to her grave of “galloping consumption,” coughing blood, spreading it through the town like a rumor, while her father turns her plate face-down at the family table among the plates of the other dead. Every fact about her is a fact someone else supplies. She never speaks. She never appears. She is entirely reported, and most of the reporting is invented on the spot.

This is where Jacqueline pushes the book's deepest claim past where Madge left it. The Madge piece said that to see a stranger is already to make her up. Jacqueline is the case with nothing to see. Homer swears he had not thought of her in years. It is Madge who says the name first, Madge who “resurrected Jacqueline,” Madge who keeps “blowing the dead sparks to life and making the dead ashes glow,” and only then does Homer begin to remember. The haunting is manufactured. Homer even states the law out loud, that “women dreamed too much, imagining things which were not there, and sometimes they brought them to life,” which is Radical Immanence spoken by a man who is himself being imagined as he speaks it. And Madge, the guilty one, admits her own method without flinching: “Things that people tell me, and the rest I can imagine.” A stranger on a bus invents a husband, the husband's invented wife invents his dead sweetheart, and the dead sweetheart aches. Reality is made rather than found, and here it is made out of jealousy and a cried name.

Because Jacqueline has no inside, she becomes a mirror, and the mirror shows Madge. “No one ever read Jacqueline's mind or knew what she thought,” and “she had never spoken, and so they had all loved her.” She is a blank the whole county writes itself onto, which is exactly why Madge cannot keep herself separate from her. Jacqueline is light, fast, unpregnant, unmarried, adored, everything Madge was before the child and the ruin, so the rival is really the lost self, the girl Madge should have been, “so light, so light on her feet.” Homer, half asleep, tries to hold them apart with a broken geometry lesson, insisting “You can't be she, Madge. She can't be you,” that two bodies cannot occupy the same place in space, but the passage keeps melting them together anyway, and he finally lands the truth by accident: “It's you who think too much of her, too much of Jacqueline.” The jealous woman and the girl she envies are one heart split in two, which is the oldest law of this novel, that every heart is the other heart.

Her death is not private either. When Jacqueline coughs, the whole town coughs, the preacher in the pulpit and the horses on the road and the fiddler in the saloon, a chorus of contagion, as if one girl's dying could be shared out among everyone who ever loved her. The men line up to drink from her glass to prove they are good sports. The sister who kissed her on the lips caught it and followed her down. Grief in this book does not stay where it starts, and it does not resolve. It spreads, it accumulates, and it takes the living along with the dead.

This is the strange dignity the novel hands its most invented character. Homer gives it the plainest words anyone gives anything: “She was all of us, and she was none of us. We elected her to be immortal.” That is consensus reality set down in a single sentence. Jacqueline is real the way the shared world is real, not because anyone found her but because enough people agreed to. She even chose the class motto, “To thine own self be true,” which is the book's quiet joke, since she is the one figure with no self to be true to, a girl who is all of us and none of us being handed the oldest line about the solid inner core this whole novel denies anyone has.

The lesson for a writer sits one layer deeper than it did with Madge. A careful writer keeps invention tethered to something seen. Young cuts the tether entirely. Jacqueline is invented out of a name, by a character who is herself invented out of a face, and she is still the most vivid person in the chapter: aching, skating, dying, adored. The novel is showing that a made thing does not need a real thing under it to be real. The girl assembled from a cried name and another woman's jealousy carries as much weight as anyone who was actually there, because in this book being made up by someone who loves you, or envies you, is not the opposite of existing. It is how existing works.
master-class-character-jock-cartwheel:
Jock Cartwheel: The One Nobody Could Name

← Miss Georgia MacIntosh · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Old Clam Digger →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Jock Cartwheel · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

You do not meet him. That is the meeting. Jock Cartwheel is named once in the whole book, in a garbled newspaper notice, and otherwise he is a hole in the shape of a man because being barely there, being a name other people fill in however they need to, is the whole of what he is.

Here is nearly everything the book will tell you about him, and watch how little it holds still. A Boston paper, recalling a social season that never happened, calls Vera's mother the late Mrs. Catherine Cartwheel, widow of Jock, the fashionable dog fancier, the fabulous yachtsman, the great mountain-climber who had disappeared when the mountains moved like waves. Three men in one clause, and the clause is a mistake. The notice was jumbled by a printer's devil, and Mr. Spitzer, reading it, decided not to correct it, on the grounds that he could not say which of the world's errors were worth fixing and this one hardly seemed to be. Vera, his daughter, whispers to her imaginary horse the secret that she never knew her father. Catherine, his wife, cannot say who her husband was. She was married on a tennis court by passing a few balls, she was married on an archery range by shooting a golden arrow through a cloud, she was married to a sailboat that lifted its wings and sailed away, to a porpoise and a star, to an iceberg, to a church bell, to a phantom whose face she never saw, to all the fading images of this world. Every fact about Jock is somebody else's guess, and no two guesses agree.

Ask the wrong question and Jock is simply underwritten, a minor dead husband the book never got around to fleshing out. Ask the right one and he is the theme carried to its far edge. The question Radical Immanence puts to him is not why is he so thin, but what is a person who is never present, never single, never known, assembled entirely from the outside? Every figure in this novel is a self that will not stay one. Jock is that idea pushed until it vanishes: a self so plural, so absent, that it never gathers into a body at all.

He is the other end of the scale from Mr. Spitzer, and the two of them frame the book's whole picture of the divided self. Spitzer gets the longest section in the novel to hold his split identity, the man you can watch pace around Boston in a cape, two watches in his pockets, unable to say whether he is himself or his dead twin. Jock gets one jumbled sentence. They prove the same thing by opposite means. Spitzer proves that a person is not one by being given more room than anyone and still not cohering. Jock proves it by never showing up, so that the only way to see him at all is to look at the shape of the hole he left in the people who loved him. One is the plural self drawn from the inside, at enormous length. The other is the plural self seen only as an absence, in a single line.

It would be easy to call his thinness a flaw and move on. The opposite is true. A Jock who was fully drawn, handed a face and a settled history and one dependable identity, would quietly contradict everything the novel believes about people. Instead he is drawn the way the book thinks everyone actually is, with the usual illusion of solidity stripped off: a set of images held in other minds, different in each mind, never the same twice, and gone the instant you reach past them for the man himself. The great lover, the book says of Catherine's phantom bridegroom, is always the absent one, one whom no one has ever known or loved. Jock is that sentence turned into a character.

And he does not stay dead in the tidy way the dead are supposed to. Catherine mourns him alongside Peron and the others, and in her dreaming world the husband she could not name blurs into the lover she could not keep, until the two dead men become one changing beloved she grieves without being able to tell them apart. It is her picture of how love works, aimed at a composite of the lost that keeps swapping its mask. Jock's part in that composite is to be the one who was already absent before he died, the husband who was a phantom at the altar, so that losing him to death only finished a disappearance that had started on their wedding day. He was gone before he was gone. That is how a woman who can barely remember he existed can mourn him so completely.

For Vera the absence cuts deeper, because it sits at her own root. The father is the answer to the oldest question about who she is, and he is the one blank the whole long book cannot fill. The novel never lets him resolve into a single knowable man, never even settles which dead man stands at her origin, the phantom husband or the lover in the next room, so that her beginning refuses, like everything else here, to be single and given. She is the daughter of an uncertainty in parentage. Her search for the dead, which fills the entire novel, starts from a father who was never there to lose in the first place.

The lesson for a writer is that a character does not have to appear in order to be present. Jock never enters a room, never speaks, is dead before the first page and was barely alive to anyone before that, and he still pulls on the story, because presence on the page is not the same as time on the page. It is the size and shape of the hole a person leaves in other people. A writer can build a figure out of nothing but the contradictory things others say about him and the space he takes up in their grief, and if the contradictions are precise enough, the absence itself becomes a person. Jock is the proof that the book can make, out of almost nothing, exactly the character it intends: a man who was never one man, never fully there, and mourned all the harder for it.
master-class-character-the-black-coachma:
The Black Coachman: The Life Made From a Face Turned Away

← James the Chauffeur · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Sea-House Servants →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Jacqueline White · Joachim Spitzer · Madge Capehorn

If James is the invented driver the mother can describe down to his crimes, the black coachman is the one she cannot describe at all. He has no face she has ever seen, barely a name she can recall, and almost no history beyond the driving itself, and he is the one on whom, she insists, everything depends. He is her other chauffeur, older and deeper than James, and where James turned out not to matter, the book says plainly of this one that "it was the black coachman upon whom all things depended." The emptier he is, the more he carries.

What little is known of him is loss. He drove her father and a whole vanished family on their daily circuit, the father, his blind mother, his unmarried sister, his blind wife, and he "survived them all, just by a shade," and then he died too. Now he is dead and still driving. She never sees his face. Through years of dreaming she sees only "the back of the coachman's head," nodding as if in sleep under a high silk hat, and she asks the question she can never answer, "Why did the black coachman never turn his face toward her?" He does not turn, does not answer, does not stop. The carriage never waits and never arrives. He is fused to the thing he drives, so that "horses and coach and coachman were one entity," a driver who cannot climb down from his own box because there is no separate man to climb down.

She keeps him past death the way she keeps everything, by arranging it. She wrote him into her will and left him the carriage, the four white horses, his livery and silver buttons and plume, and asked to have him buried in all of it so that he could go on "driving the horses under the earth." The idea, she is careful to say, was his, not hers. He "wanted the carriage and the horses, just so that he might continue his old employment," a servant who applied to keep working after he was in the ground. His grave, meanwhile, is "hypothetical and changing," never visited, maybe never real, and she has arranged instead that "the black coachman should visit her." The dead man is on call. In this house the dead do not leave, and this one she has put under contract not to.

The reason he matters more than James is that he is not really a servant at all. He is an allegory she rides inside. "Her body was the carriage," her soul was the passenger, "her horses were her will, and the coachman was her conscience." He is the faceless thing that steers her, the part of her that knows where the journey goes and will not turn around to tell her. That is why locating him becomes the whole problem of her nights: "If she could find him, she could perhaps find herself, the bewildered passenger." She is a passenger in the carriage of her own body, driven by her own conscience, and she cannot see either the driver or the road, only that the wheels keep turning on a circular avenue where the end is the beginning.

The construction is so complete that it finally swallows her. Riding behind him she loses track of whose carriage it is, whether the coachman is her coachman or "any old coachman" picked up somewhere, whether the passenger in her seat is even herself, "who was this passenger in her carriage, she would shrilly ask, and who had taken her place?" The invention has grown larger than the woman who made it. When Mr. Spitzer ends up in the seat, he is "the wrong passenger" in the wrong coach, and the coachman "did not know," being now a skeleton driving toward a funeral whose name has been forgotten. Death drives whoever climbs in. The coachman does not check the fare.

This is the strange rule the coachman reveals, and it is the reverse of what James suggested. James was drawn in full, an ex-convict with a rap sheet and a moose to shoot, and the book set him aside in one line, "It had not been her chauffeur upon whom her life depended, however." The coachman is drawn as nothing, no face, no name, no story, and everything depends on him. The more a made figure can be seen, the more it can be checked and found unnecessary. The less it can be seen, the more weight it holds, because a conscience with a face would only be a man, and a driver with a name could be replaced. He carries the whole journey precisely because there is nothing to him but the driving. "Her drugged vision provided more of reality than reality provided," and the most real thing in it is the one she can least make out.

The lesson that gathers here is the darkest of the set. Madge and Jacqueline and James are built for company, to be quarreled with and grieved and loved. The black coachman is built for something else. He is the driver every passenger in this book turns out to have, the invented figure at the reins of a life that is going somewhere its owner cannot see, and the honest thing, the thing the mother does and cannot stop doing, is to keep riding behind him with her eyes open. She never makes him turn around. She only asks, again and again, why he will not, which is the same as asking where the carriage is going, which is the one question the faceless driver she built will never answer and she will never stop needing to ask.
master-class-character-musidora:
Musidora: The One They Looked At and Did Not Know

← Mrs. Tidings · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Mrs. Hathaway →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Gertrude Hathaway Tidings · Musidora Tidings · Peron Spitzer

The town builds whole lives out of nothing, a husband no one saw, a murder no one witnessed, and it cannot recognize the one woman standing in plain sight. Musidora is the daughter of Mrs. Tidings and the sister of Gertrude, and she is the character the gossip of the town circles without ever seeing her.

What the town knows of her is all disgust and distance. She "grew up with the water on her brain." She pushes "a battered baby carriage" from house to house to pick rags, and no one knows why, and she throws the rags into the river so the water might carry them away. She works "off and on at the Tavern," "crawling on all fours," "cleaning the slop out," for "scraps of the landlord's bread." She is barefoot, "those big, bare feet with the blackened soles," "marble-colored eyes," "mottled skin," "grey, ragged curls, water running down her legs." She is "always a baby inside, always another outside." And she "never speaks." When someone wonders why, the answer the book allows is the plainest one: "Maybe she had nothing to say."

Ask the wrong question and Musidora is grotesque, a bit of squalor at the edge of the tavern talk. Ask the right one and she is the fourth claim of Radical Immanence carried past where the clam-digger left it. The truth is not at the shining center but at the margin, in the person nobody watches, and Musidora is the margin of the margin, a mute rag-picker even the other marginal figures step over.

Her own family cannot place her. She begs at Gertrude's and at her mother's, and the two of them will not speak to each other, and she "does not seem to know them," and they "do not act as if they ever saw her before." This is the book's deepest wound worn by its lowest figure. Everyone here loves a composite of the lost and cannot see the living person in the room. Catherine grieves Peron and pours his tea without knowing him. The mother rides behind a coachman whose face never turns. Musidora is that failure of recognition made total and made mutual, a woman unknown to the two people who made her and raised her, standing in their doorways with her hand out, a stranger to her own blood.

She is Esther Longtree's sister in kind. Both are the town's perpetually pregnant woman, "always a baby inside, always another outside," bearing what will not stop coming and mourned by no one. But where Esther is given a whole book of interior, her losses named and counted, Musidora is given nothing from the inside at all. She is Esther seen only from the street, the same everlasting grief with the door to it locked, a silence the town fills with revulsion because it will not fill it with attention. And her silence is not empty. Like the clam-digger, whose closed mouth is the shape his knowing takes, Musidora's wordlessness may be the last dignity she has. "Maybe she's sane," the gossip admits, twice, unable to decide, and the doubt is the point. The town needs her to be an idiot because an idiot can be dismissed, and it cannot quite manage the dismissal, because something in the silent woman crawling on the floor will not reduce all the way to nothing.

The turn for a writer is the hardest one to practice, because Musidora is the person a writer is most tempted to skip. The town invents a husband for Mrs. Tidings and a murder for Mrs. Hathaway and a whole biography for the mother's absent chauffeur, and it does all that inventing while a real woman gathers rags in the actual street and is seen by no one. That is the writer's ordinary sin, to lavish invention on the vivid and the absent while the present, unglamorous, silent person goes unwritten. Young plants Musidora at the very bottom of the book to catch the reader in exactly that reflex, to let the gossip skate over her and the reader skate with it, and then to let the plainest sentence in the passage stop the skating: "Maybe she had nothing to say." The lesson is that the figure beneath even the town's tireless inventing, the one so overlooked that no one troubles to make up a story worthy of her, is the one who most needs the writer to stay. To witness Musidora is to write the person the story was built to walk past, and to refuse, for once, to walk past her.
master-class-character-miss-georgia-maci:
Miss Georgia MacIntosh: The Sensible Woman in the Wig

← Vera Cartwheel · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Jock Cartwheel →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

You meet her as the correction. She is hired. Into the great sea-blackened house where the mother dreams her life away on opium, someone sends a plain, sensible nursemaid to raise the child the dreamer will not, and that is Miss MacIntosh, arriving with her black umbrella and her Pilgrim's Progress and her rule that there is a place for everything because being the correction, the answer, the solid ground the others are measured against, is the role she plays and the role the novel is built to take away from her.

The facts of her are all plain, and the plainness is the point. She is Georgia MacIntosh of What Cheer, Iowa, the middle child of a poor but honest family, daughter of a little shoemaker who also built coffins for other people. There was no room for her at home, no nest. She worked her way through two years at the University of Iowa waiting tables and washing and ironing the shirts of the men students, and learned little more than she already knew from the Farmers' Almanac, how to plow stony ground, how to protect cherry buds from frost, how to break ice for water. No young man ever looked at her twice. Beauty was not hers. She has a broken nose, a whale-boned corset, rimless glasses, no paint on her face, and red hair the color of an August sunset. Her religion is truth to nature and nothing else. She wears blinders on purpose. Once, walking with Vera, she covers the girl's eyes rather than let her carry away the memory of sleigh bells hung in a blossoming cherry tree, because such confusion, she says, is not the mirror of truth. Sleigh bells belong in a world of snow. There is a place for everything.

Ask the wrong question and she is simply the sane one, the standard, the character with no mystery because she is the thing mystery is measured against. Ask the right one and she is the deepest problem in the book. The question Radical Immanence puts to her is not why is she so plain, but what becomes of a person who insists that reality is single, given, found, and never made? Every other figure in the novel lives as though reality is something you build and move into. Miss MacIntosh alone denies it. She is the one who insists the real is simply there, the same for everyone, waiting to be reported and not composed. The whole book is arranged to answer what happens to such a person, and the answer is a wig.

Read one way, she is the cure. She is brought in as Catherine's correction, the discipline set against the dream, the daylight sent into the opium house, the sensible woman against the addict. She is the title character, the one the whole book is named for and aimed at, the visible center everyone watches. Marguerite Young called her the hub. She is reality itself, walking around in sensible shoes, there to save the child from the mother's madness.

Then, at midnight, Vera sees her bald. The red hair is gone, the whole great dome shorn and shining and sweating, the body flat and shorn beneath it, and Vera, horrified, screams "Miss MacIntosh, you are a man!" The wig is a wig. The solidity is a costume. The one person in the house who policed the real, turns out to be the most disguised soul in it, the bald pretender who had been pulling the wool over everyone's eyes for years. It would be easy to file this as an unmasking, the sensible woman exposed as a fraud, and to feel the cheap superiority of having caught her. The novel refuses to be read that way in a single stroke. The child, who might have recoiled, says instead that Miss MacIntosh was more real now than she had ever been. The disguise coming off does not make her false. It makes her true.

That is the reversal the whole book turns on, and it is the same discovery Catherine's story makes from the other side. Catherine built a dream world out of opium and the illustrious dead and moved into it for good. Miss MacIntosh built a sensible world out of a wig and a corset and a book of maxims and moved into that. Both are constructed realities. Both are a self assembled to bear a life that could not otherwise be borne, a poor plain unloved woman making, out of discipline and false hair, a person solid enough that a whole household could lean on her and call her the ground. The only difference between the two women is that Catherine knew hers was a dream and Miss MacIntosh insisted hers was the given world. That insistence is the one thing she is wrong about, and it is the one thing she cannot let go of, because it is load-bearing. To admit the wig is a wig is to admit that her reality was made, like everyone else's, and that admission is the single truth her whole life was built to keep out.

This is why she is sympathetic and wrong at once, and why the novel loves her exactly where it corrects her. Her construction is the bravest kind, a self hammered together by a woman who had nothing, no beauty, no love, no room at home, and held up steady enough to raise another woman's child. Her error is not a lie she told the world. It is the one confession she could not make to herself. And she cannot survive being seen without the disguise. She walks into the loud sea and leaves everything in wild confusion, her galoshes thrown back water-logged by the tide, her Pilgrim's Progress swollen with salt, she who believed there was a place for everything. The woman who preached truth to nature drowns herself rather than be witnessed as she is. She could not live inside the single given reality she preached, because it was never there, and the moment the child saw through the wig, the ground went out from under her too.

Her disappearance is where the whole book begins. Vera's bus is aimed at her, the long search for the lost love who may or may not be dead. The body is never found, which is why Mr. Spitzer, keeping faith with the missing as he keeps faith with all the dead, will not sign her into the grave. Until the body is found, he says, we cannot assume that she is dead. So the woman who insisted the real was a matter of found facts becomes the one fact that can never be found, the missing corpus delicti, the case that stays open forever. Even her ending refuses to be single and given. She spent her life reporting a world of settled facts and left the book a world in which the central fact, her own death, cannot be settled at all.

The lesson for a writer is in how Young builds the character who is wrong without turning her into a fool or a villain. Miss MacIntosh is the most beloved person in the house, the one the child would die or run away for, and the novel never argues against her. It simply springs the wig and lets the reader feel, in the same instant, the horror and the tenderness, and then, worse and better than either, the recognition that this brave assembled woman was doing all along the very thing she denied anyone could do, making a reality to stand up in. You refute a character most completely not by defeating her in an argument but by revealing that she and her opposite were performing the same act the whole time. The sensible woman and the dreamer were both building somewhere to live. One of them just refused, to the end, to call it a building.
master-class-character-esther-longtrees-:
Esther Longtree's Parents: The Watchman and the Mourner

← The Little Toy Salesman · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Mrs. Tidings →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Esther Longtree · Rosemary

Esther Longtree was made by two failures of attention, and between them they explain her. Her father is "the passive policeman," "the night policeman who separated loving couples in the graveyard and always whistled to warn them when he came." He is the law that refuses to catch anyone. He "had even let the bank-robber slip through his fingers." He climbs the graveyard hill in the moonlight "swinging his stick against the tombs so he would catch no guilty one." He is big-boned and gentle, and his gentleness is a form of absence: even if he had known his daughter was endlessly, secretly pregnant, "he might have said nothing." He keeps his watch among the dead while the living crisis happens behind his back, and he hears, at the crucial hour, "only the tooting of the river boat."

Her mother is the opposite kind of failure. She sees too much of the wrong thing. She is frail, with "small, delicate veins, so frail and recessive a heart," who nearly died bearing Esther and never forgave her for it. And she is the keeper of Rosemary, the perfect stillborn twin, whom she mourns by turning the grief into a weapon. She "constantly reminded" Esther, "ever since she could remember, that one was missing, that she had killed it with her big feet threshing in the womb." On the shared birthday "her mother had baked two cakes or none." She loves the dead child she built out of words and cannot love the living one she got, and she tells her so, in a thousand small ways her gentle husband never notices.

So the daughter grows up unseen by one parent and misseen by the other. The father who will not look and the mother who looks only at the dead perfect version make, between them, a child who is invisible as herself and hyper-visible as a murderer. "Little did her parents ever realize what was ever unrealized." They register "her weight and her fluctuations and her voice," and they miss the whole truth of her. "They should have seen, if they had had eyes to see with."
