This is the book's steady charge against everyone who fails its one commandment, and here it falls on the two people who were supposed to be the first witnesses of a life and were the first to look away.

The horror underneath them is that they repeat, one generation up, the very pattern that will define Esther. The mother's own pregnancy was not from the passive policeman but at the old mule farm, from "the other woman" who "was, it seemed in that terrible minute, a man against whom her struggles were all useless," "cold as stone." A legal father who is not the real one, a conception with a stone stranger, a child who is a reproach and looks "like the old go-between." Esther will do it all again with the little toy salesman she chooses as "the legal father." The past is not behind her, it is beneath her, and she claims to have witnessed it, "present" at her own conception, having "seen the whole transaction with her little eyes before her eyes were blinded by the light." The thing that made her is buried under her and pressing up, and she was there for it.

The turn for a writer is the one that closes the whole set, because these two are the making of the maker. The father is the guardian who will not look, who whistles so he catches no one, who keeps his watch among the tombs while the real thing happens behind him, complicit by his gentleness. The mother is the one who loves the perfect dead version over the living flawed one, who builds her grief into an accusation and hands it to the child as an identity. Between the watchman who refuses to witness and the mourner who witnesses only the ideal, they make a daughter who spends her whole life trying to give birth to the child who would finally be seen and finally be loved. This is how makers get made, the book quietly says, out of the two ways of not being witnessed, and the maker's whole work afterward is the attempt to do for her creatures what was never done for her, to stay in the room, to look at the living one, to love the thing that actually came rather than the perfect thing that did not. Esther, endlessly pregnant behind her counter, is what the two failures of attention produce, and she is trying, delivery after delivery, to correct them.
master-class-character-beatrice-fitzgera:
Beatrice Fitzgerald: The Guide at the Washtub

← Mrs. Hathaway · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Stone Deaf Man →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Beatrice Fitzgerald · Homer Capehorn · Jock Cartwheel · Justice O’Leary · Madge Capehorn · Moses Hunnecker · Musidora Tidings · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

She hauls the town's dirty linen through the snow on a child's red sled, half blind and turning more blind, while two strangers on a bus argue about whether she is clean or filthy, beloved or a hag, a mother or a woman who never had a son. Beatrice Fitzgerald is the laundress of the Indiana town, and she is assembled entirely out of that argument, because being made of two accounts that cannot both be true, by people who never once looked at her.

Homer's Beatrice is a saint of labor. "She's clean," he says. She "washes the clothes so clean," and "no one ever worked so hard," and in winter she drags the wash "on a little red sled over the snow," "up the hill and down the hill," until "her face turns blue." Madge's Beatrice is the reverse. She is "one-eyed," "the ugliest old hag for miles," "nearly blind, so what can she see," her clothes "streaked with dirt." She is "losing the other eye," and "she never did want anybody to see her," and so "she turns out the light." Both are speaking of the same old woman dragging the same sled, and the book lets neither win.

Ask the wrong question and Beatrice is a scrap of local color, a poor laundress the bus passes in the dark. Ask the right one and she carries two of the book's claims at once. She is the second pillar of Radical Immanence, reality constructed rather than found, built out of contradictory rumor the way Mrs. Tidings is built out of an invented and murdered husband. And she is the fourth, the truth at the margin, the person beneath all notice, sister to Musidora and to the clam-digger, the one who does the lowest work and is discounted for doing it.

Her name is where the book plays its flat joke and its deepest one, the way it does with Justice O'Leary and Moses Hunnecker. Beatrice is Dante's guide, the beloved who leads the pilgrim up out of the dark and into Paradise, and an engraving of "Dante wooing Beatrice" hangs in the baby doctor's room, over the bed. Here the guide to the light is a half-blind old laundress in the dark who "turns out the light" so no one will see her. The book is saying, in a name, that if the celestial guide came to this town she would come as the woman nobody looks at, hauling wet sheets uphill in the cold, and that the way to find Beatrice is to look at the drudge and see the guide.

Her blindness belongs to the book's strange company of the sightless who perceive. Friday the blind dog sees the angel his clear-eyed mistress cannot, the stone deaf man "heard with his eyes," and Beatrice, losing both eyes, is dismissed by Madge with "so what can she see," as if the one who cannot see does not count. But she is the keeper of the town's soil. She takes in what everyone wants made clean and unseen, the streaked and stained and private linen, and gives it back white, and drags the burden herself. She knows the town the way a launderer knows it, by its dirt, and she asks nothing, and no one ever sends her beautiful clothes. She washes the world and stays in rags. Hers is witnessing without the reward of being witnessed, the pillar Spitzer performs with his cheroots and Vera performs with her looking, worn now by an old woman at a washtub who serves the whole town and turns out the light rather than be seen serving it.

Around her the book grows its usual tangle of uncertain sons. Homer swears she had a boy who "joined the Navy and went to sea," who "sends her postal cards from all over the world," who "has seen all the world's great ports," Borneo and Singapore and Gibraltar, who "never forgot her," and whose "little red sled she dragged through the snow." Madge swears the son never existed. A third account makes him "young Doc," fathered by "old Doc" who "never claimed him" and "never knew that he was a father," though "it could have been anybody's son." Even Moses the bus-driver, stopping near her place, is proposed for a moment as "a faithful son" come for his mother's clean clothes. She is Jock's counterpart in the register of motherhood, a woman whose child is assembled from postcards and denials and may be three men or none, and the red sled is the emblem of it, a boy's toy become an old woman's labor, the absent son present only as the thing she still drags through the snow.

The turn for a writer is that Beatrice is made the way the whole book says people are made, out of the testimony of those who did not look. Two riders who have never spoken to her build her on a bus, one giving her cleanliness and a devoted world-traveling son, the other giving her filth and blindness and no son at all, and the character is neither report and both, alive in the gap between them exactly as a real person is. And the name is the instruction. A writer can hang the highest figure in literature, the guide who leads to Paradise, on the lowest laborer in the county, and let the irony carry the argument, that the guide, if she is anywhere, is at the washtub, blue-faced in the cold, dragging the clean and the soiled up the same hill, turning out the light because she does not want to be seen. To write Beatrice is to refuse the town's two easy verdicts, saint and hag, and to see instead the plain old woman who takes in what everyone wants hidden and hands it back clean, and to understand that finding the guide in the drudge is not a trick of the name.
master-class-character-the-tavern-landla:
The Tavern Landlady: The Life Spoken For

← The Tavern Landlord · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Mr. Weed →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Jacqueline White · Madge Capehorn · Vera Cartwheel

After the landlord, who talks more than anyone in the book, comes the woman he married, and she is his exact reverse. He owns almost nothing and says everything. She owns everything and says nothing. She never appears at the counter, never climbs the stairs, never gets a line of her own. She is the thinnest figure in this whole set, a woman known only as a phrase in her husband's mouth, and the thinness is not an oversight.

Everything known about her arrives secondhand, through the landlord's talk. She had been "a circus fat lady," a body that people once paid to look at, and by the time he found her she was "losing weight," "down to two hundred pounds now in her stocking feet," a spectacle already in the act of shrinking. She owned the Tavern. "It was she who had owned this hotel," he says, "a good enough port for a man in a storm," and that single fact turns out to hold up the entire building the book takes place in.

She is the ground. The Tavern is where the bus stops and where all these people converge, Madge and the football boy and the hangman and Vera, and the Tavern is hers. The landlord married into her house. Every tall tale he tells at the counter, every shipwreck and jungle and knot, is told standing on real estate she holds the deed to. He is the performance and she is the floor it happens on. The book is full of people who float, the sleeping, the dreaming, the summoned, the drowned, and she is the rare one who owns something solid, and she is barely visible for owning it.

She is also the rescue. The landlord had gone down on four ships and brought such bad luck that "none but a mad captain would sign me on," rejected by the sea that kept trying to drown him and by every crew that heard about it. Then, in his own telling, "my wife signed me on." She took the jinxed man the ocean would not keep and the captains would not have, and gave him a berth on dry land. The harbor in the storm is not a metaphor he reaches for. It is the actual woman who owned the actual roof, and who signed the papers that made a drowning man into a landlord.

What she says, she is never allowed to say herself. Every word of hers in the book is relayed, quoted, carried secondhand by the man who talks over her. She is the one who "reminded him" that God said in the Bible no one had ever seen the thing he claimed to have seen. She is the "my wife says" who thinks he should see America before he brags about the rest of the world. She is the "as my wife says" behind the half-price room given to the legless man with no legs to stand on. She is sense, scripture, and charity, the whole domestic counterweight to his tall tales, and she is present only as a clause inside them. The ventriloquist, who made coffee cups and empty rocking chairs speak, is married to the one person at the Tavern who is never given her own voice.

So she stands at the far edge of everything the set has shown. Madge and Jacqueline and James and the coachman were given too much life, whole marriages and murders and consciences built onto strangers and absences. The landlady is given too little. She is real, she owns the house, she saved the man, and the book lets her exist only as something he says. She is not a person invented out of nothing. She is a person talked over until almost nothing is left showing, which is the same power running the other direction.

The connection for a writer is the one the landlord's chapter was too cheerful to mention. Making a person up is only half of what a teller does. The other half is deciding who does not get to speak, whose life gets folded into a clause, whose ownership of the actual house goes unremarked while the talker performs on top of it. Young sets the loudest voice in the book beside the most silenced one and marries them, and she does not soften it. The landlady is what the method costs. Every time a writer gives a sleeping stranger a marriage or a dead girl a whole biography, some real person at the edge of the frame is being handed a smaller share of the telling, owning the floor and saying nothing on it. The honest writer keeps one eye on her, the woman who signed the drowning man on and holds the deed to the house where the story happens, and remembers that she had sense and scripture and mercy of her own, and a voice, and that the only reason it is never heard is that someone else was doing all the talking.
master-class-character-mrs-tidings:
Mrs. Tidings: The Woman Who Invented Her Own Dead

← Esther Longtree's Parents · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Musidora →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Gertrude Hathaway Tidings · Musidora Tidings · Rosemary

She keeps a parrot in the window, and the town says "the things that parrot could tell if that parrot could talk," which is the town admitting it knows nothing for certain and suspects everything. Mrs. Tidings is the mother of Musidora and Gertrude, and she is the household in the gossip that most exactly rhymes with the great house by the sea, because inventing the people she needs and keeping the ones she killed.

The stories about her will not agree with themselves, and the disagreement is the portrait. There never was a Mr. Tidings that anybody knew, no one ever saw him, and "they say she just invented him." And in the same breath, there was a Mr. Tidings, and "they say she killed him." Both are held at once, a husband who never existed and a husband she murdered, and no one can say which. What is agreed is the relic. She "kept his old coats and his old hats," and she "would not bury" the skull, "some old rabbit-hunter's skull," which was "all that was ever found of him," and she let the children play with it on the floor and set it on the mantelpiece. She is "a pillar of the church," the gossip adds, "though I don't know which church."

Ask the wrong question and Mrs. Tidings is a witch out of a cautionary tale, the murderer with the skull. Ask the right one and she is the second pillar of Radical Immanence told in the register of a crime the town cannot prove. Reality is constructed rather than found, and Mrs. Tidings is the town's Catherine, a woman who built the husband she required and moved him into the house, coats and hats and all.

The invented Mr. Tidings is the gossip's version of the mother's James, the chauffeur built out of an absence, kept present precisely by never arriving. Mrs. Tidings does the same domestic magic in a poorer house. Whether the man was ever there hardly matters to the result, because the coats hang in the closet either way and the skull sits on the mantel either way, and a husband made of relics keeps as well as a husband made of memory. The mother kept James by never letting him come back. Mrs. Tidings keeps Mr. Tidings by never letting him be buried. Both refuse the one thing that would end it, which is admitting the man is gone.

And she carries the book's other obsession, the wrong one lost. She meant to kill "the one she thought was weak-minded," and "aimed for the wrong one," and killed instead "the baby that was never named," while Musidora, the weak-minded one, is "the one that lived." "She always did know she had killed the wrong one." This is the Rosemary knot, the perfect child dead and the wrong child surviving, and it is the Hathaway knot, the wrong brother lost, sounded a third time. Everywhere in this book someone is left with the survivor they did not choose and the loss they did not intend, and Mrs. Tidings is the coldest instance, a mother who priced her weak daughter's life and missed. For she did price it. The old man "bought her from her mother for sixteen dollars" and a new roof he promised, paid "twelve dollars down," "still owes four," never built the roof, and Mrs. Tidings "was going to sue." That is the whole economy of the marginal women laid bare in one transaction, a daughter traded for four dollars and a roof that never came, the invented husband and the sold daughter kept in the same ledger.

The turn for a writer is in the contradiction the book refuses to fix. A careful storyteller resolves the record, decides whether Mr. Tidings was invented or murdered, and reports the finding. Young leaves both standing, because the town leaves both standing, and the doubled, self-canceling rumor is truer to how a person is actually known than any settled fact would be. Mrs. Tidings exists in the space between she made him up and she killed him, and the space is not a gap in the story, it is the story. A writer can build a whole character out of two accounts that cannot both be true, and the character will be more alive for the impossibility, because a real person is the one the evidence keeps disagreeing about. The skull on the mantel is the emblem of the method, a thing that is either all that remains of a husband or with no husband behind it, played with on the floor by children who do not care which, kept by a woman who needed a dead man in the house and made sure she had one.
master-class-11-the-main-idea:
The Main Idea

← Regions of the United States · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Style →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The simplest way to state what Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is about is to say it is about the difference between reality and illusion. That is true, and it is the first thing readers reach for, and it is not quite right, because it implies the novel is trying to tell the two apart. It is not. The novel raises the distinction between the real and the dreamed only to dissolve it, and the dissolving is the point. The main idea is not that we must learn to separate reality from illusion. It is that the separation cannot be made, and that a human life is the work of living honestly inside that impossibility.

The book states its own question outright: "What shall we do when, fleeing from illusion, we are confronted by illusion?" Notice the shape of it. It is not "how do we escape illusion for reality." It assumes there is no clear ground to flee to, that the person running from the dream runs straight into another dream. That is the whole novel in one sentence. Vera flees her mother's opium world toward the plain reality Miss MacIntosh promises, and finds that the plain reality was a construction too. There is no exit from the maze into open air. There is only a further room of the maze, and the honest response is not to keep hunting for the door but to learn how to live in the room.

Young inherits the frame from Calderón, whose Life Is a Dream (1636) she echoes in the novel's pervasive treatment of existence as a dream one cannot wake from. Calderón's play sets free will against fate and lets truth and falsehood intermingle until understanding comes only from embracing experience whole, mysteries and all. Young keeps the premise, life as a dream, and drops the consolation. Calderón's prince wakes and learns to act rightly whether life is a dream or not. Young's characters do not wake. They stay inside the dream, and the book's wisdom is about how to conduct oneself there, not how to get out.

This is where the usual reading of the novel goes wrong, and it is worth correcting here because it is the most common mistake made about the book. Miss MacIntosh is habitually described as the novel's rock, the emblem of common sense and grounded reality, the sane standard against which the dreamers are measured, and her plain virtues, honesty, self-reliance, practical knowledge over fanciful dreaming, are taken to be the values the novel endorses. That reading takes her at her own word, and the novel does not. She is not the real thing set against the illusions. She is the most disguised person in the book, bald beneath a wig, her solidity a costume assembled by a poor plain woman to survive a life that offered her nothing. Her insistence that reality is single, given, and simply there is the one thing the novel proves her wrong about. She is sympathetic and she is mistaken, and treating her as the book's answer misreads the book's whole argument. The novel does not resolve the tension between her austere reality and Catherine's dream by siding with reality. It shows that both women built a place to live and moved into it, and that the only difference is that Catherine knew hers was a dream. If the novel has a verdict, it is that Miss MacIntosh's plainness was as constructed as any vision, which is the opposite of holding her up as the ground.

What survives, once that false comfort is removed, is a set of harder things the novel does affirm, and they are the real main ideas.

The first is that the self is not one. The novel's crowd of doubled and dissolving identities, the twin brothers who trade places, the mother's invented servants, Esther and her dead twin, is not a gallery of curiosities but a sustained argument that a person is plural, made of turning contradictions that never settle into a single center. The book's recurring motif of obsession and repetition serves this: life is "filled with repetitions and variations," patterns that cycle rather than progress, because a self that is many does not advance in a line. It revolves.

The second is that grief does not end and is not meant to. The novel reflects continually on death, loss, and the fading of dreams and loves, and it declines the usual arc in which mourning is processed and released. Spitzer never stops mourning his brother. Esther is perpetually pregnant and never delivered. The dead attend the living as freely as the living attend each other. Acceptance, in this book, does not mean getting over loss. It means learning to carry what does not go away, which is a form of maturity but not a form of relief.

The third is that witnessing others is the core ethical act, and that it is harder than judgment or rescue. Vera's taking time to look, her refusal to fix or condemn the adults she examines, is the novel's model of how to live among people you cannot resolve. The book's compassion, its insistence that "every soul is connected" and that understanding comes from entering another's experience, is not sentiment. It is the practical ethic of a world where no one can be finally known and the only honest thing is to keep looking anyway.

These three, the plural self, the grief that stays, the ethic of witness, are what the novel builds once it has knocked away the promise that reality can be told from dream. They do not resolve the central contradiction; they are how one lives inside it. The characters, gathered from the whole range of American type, the mystical traveler, the militant suffragist, the featherweight champion, the waitress, the deaf man, are not there to celebrate folklore for its own sake. They are the many ways a person tries to bear an unresolvable life, and the novel sets them level with one another, dreamers and realists alike, because it will not rank one strategy above the rest.

So the main idea, stated fully, is this. Life is both a dream and a real thing, and the two cannot be pulled apart, and the search for the point where they separate is itself the last illusion the novel takes away. What it leaves in place is not an answer but a way of standing: to accept that the self is many, that the losses accumulate and stay, and that the only ethical response to a world that will not resolve is to witness it closely and love it anyway. The book does not ask the reader to escape the maze of illusion. It asks the reader to live well inside it, which is harder, and which is what it means to be, in Young's world, awake.
master-class-character-catherine-snowden:
Catherine Snowden Cartwheel: The Woman to Whom Everything Happens

← Mr. Peron/Joachim Spitzer · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Vera Cartwheel →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Jock Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

She is in a bed, and she will be in that bed for almost the whole book. That is how you meet Catherine Cartwheel, and it is the right way to meet her, because stillness on the outside and a whole turning world on the inside is the entire fact of her.

Catherine Cartwheel, maiden name Snowden, is Vera's mother. She lives under opium, in what the novel itself calls an opium paradise, a world of dreams that run almost on schedule, tended by imaginary guests and the phantoms of the men she has lost. She rarely leaves the bed. She talks for hours to people who are not in the room and does not always notice the one person who is. She mourns a dead husband, Jock, a fashionable dog fancier, and a dead lover, Peron, and she waits on a surviving brother, Joachim, whom she believes attends her. When the ordinary daylight world presses on her, she answers it by becoming someone else: Catherine the Great, sleeping in a bed with pillars of twisted amethyst.

If Mr. Spitzer is the man to whom nothing happens, Catherine is the woman to whom everything happens, and everything happens on the inside. She is all interior. He is looked past; she does not look out at all. He cannot throw anything away; she cannot stop making things up. They are the two still figures the first half of the book rests on, and they are opposite in the way a photograph and its negative are opposite, which is to say they are the same image.

Catherine looks like the book's cautionary tale: the addict who chose the dream over her own child, who let a governess raise her daughter while she rose and plunged through the years like a rider who will not dismount. Miss MacIntosh, the sensible one, is hired precisely as her correction, the discipline set against the dream, the daylight sent into the opium house. Read this way, Catherine is the problem and Miss MacIntosh is the cure.

The disproportion that undoes that reading is quiet, the novel does not finally take Miss MacIntosh's side. It gives Catherine the richer, truer perceptions and lets the sensible cure turn out to be the deeper illusion. Catherine, dismissed as the one who lost hold of reality, is the one who sees. She is convinced, long before anyone else, that Spitzer is already dead, married to the worm or to his brother, a pale version of himself. Her opium sight looks straight through his living flesh to the dead man inside it. She is right. The confession at the end confirms what the addict perceived decades early and the rational people around her could not. So the novel performs Radical Immanence’s second pillar, that reality is constructed rather than found, from the direction no one expects: it is not the dreamer who is fooled and the sensible woman who keeps hold of the real. The dreamer is the accurate witness, and the sensible woman is wearing a wig.

The opium paradise is a world Catherine built and moved into for good, which makes her the clearest case in the book of a person who treats reality as something you construct and inhabit rather than something you submit to. The imaginary guests, the crowd of illustrious dead in her rooms, are not lapses; they are her holding the lost in the present, the same refusal to let the dead be gone that Spitzer performs with his cheap cheroots. The many dead lovers who blur into one are not confusion; they are her picture of how love actually works, aimed at a composite of the lost that keeps changing its mask. She is not one thing dreaming she is many. She is many, and the dreaming is what the many does.

The living man she cannot see is inside the very blur she mourns. The Peron she grieves and the Spitzer she ignores are one body. Her dream has the right man in it and cannot recognize him, because it holds him under a dead name. She dreams of her love while her love pours her tea. And at the end Spitzer carries her dying body into the garden by the sea and begins at last to tell her the truth, that he is Peron, that he loves her, that he stayed. She dies an hour before, at the start of his whispers. The one recognition the whole counterpart was built toward does not happen. The dreamer who saw everything true does not get to hear the one true thing said aloud.

What stays standing, once the dream and the dreamer come apart, is that Young will not let the collapse become a verdict. Catherine is not simply the addict who wasted a life, any more than the confession simply solves Spitzer. The book treats her constructed world with something closer to respect than to pity, because her way of bearing the unbearable, dreaming the dead into a single deathless beloved, is set exactly level with Spitzer's way, keeping the archive and paying the debts. Two techniques for one task, which is bearing what keeps leaving. Neither works. Both are love. The reality she built was false and it was also the only place she could survive her losses, and the difficulty, which is the whole of Young's honesty, is that both are true at once.

Catherine is the hardest kind of character to write without condescending to her, because everything about her invites the easy verdict: the drug, the neglected child, the retreat from the real. Young's solution is structural. She does not defend Catherine in argument. She simply arranges the book so that the dreamer's perceptions come true and the sensible woman's solidity comes off with her wig, and lets the reader discover, too late to feel superior, that the person they were prepared to pity was the person seeing clearly the whole time. The lesson for a writer is that you can overturn a reader's judgment of a character without ever arguing against it, if you are patient enough to let the plot do the correcting. You withhold the defense and spring it as recognition, which is the same move the novel makes on Catherine herself, and just as merciless about its timing.
master-class-character-mr-peron-joachim-:
Mr. Peron/Joachim Spitzer: The Axle the Book Turns On

← The Characters · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Catherine Snowden Cartwheel →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

He came to handle the body that was never found. That is how Mr. Spitzer enters the part of this reading that matters most: sideways, on someone else's emergency, doing the paperwork of a disappearance. It is the right way to meet him, because sideways and on someone else's business is how he does everything.

He is an aging, portly gentleman, elegant in an old-fashioned way that does not match the shabbiness he lives in: a high silk hat, a soft cape, an ivory-headed cane, a waxed mustache over a double chin. One ear is dead, so he is forever turning the live side toward whoever speaks. He is a lawyer of a particular kind, tracing lost heirs of lost estates, some of which may never have existed. He is an executor of the dead. He is a composer, though his music is silence, written down and never meant to be played. He is a bachelor who once offered marriage to Catherine, Vera's mother, and was refused, partly because she loved his brother and partly because she could never be certain which brother he was. His twin is dead. He carries two watches, one ticking and one long stopped, and is not always sure which of them is his.

Every item about him is strange, and every item is delivered as a plain fact. That combination, strangeness stated flatly, is the characterization of the man, and it is the first clue to why he matters.

Nothing happens to him. Around him, everything happens. Catherine dreams her life away on opium and mourns her dead. Esther is pregnant for years and never delivers. Miss MacIntosh wears a lifelong disguise and then walks into the sea. And Mr. Spitzer sits at the foot of the bed, consults his watch, is scolded for his slowness, reddens, waits, and goes home. Things are done to him. He does very little back. Sort the characters by dramatic event and he comes in last. He is the still one.

And Young gives him more of the book than anyone else. In a novel crowded with drowning nursemaids and everlasting pregnancies and opium visions, the most pages by far are spent on a quiet lawyer sitting in a chair. This is the disproportion, and the disproportion is the argument. The book is not really about events; events are weather, and they blow across a life and move on. It is an argument about what a person is, and to show what a person is one does not point at the people things happen to. One points at the one who stays, who holds still, through whom all the weather passes. Length, here, is just the book telling a reader where to look.

It would be easy to hear that and decide we have simply found a second hub, another still center to set beside Miss MacIntosh. That is the wrong lesson, and the difference is the whole point. Miss MacIntosh was a hub, just as Marguerite Young said,the thing at the visible center that everyone watches. A hub can be removed; hers came off with her wig, and the wheel kept turning. Mr. Spitzer is not watched. He is looked past. Nobody leans on him; they lean past him, toward the dead, toward the dream, toward the lost estate. He is not the thing at the center everyone sees. He is the thing running through the center that nobody sees. That is an axle, not a hub, and the difference is total. Pull the hub and the wheel keeps turning. Pull the axle and there is no wheel.

The two watches: time reaches him only through the dead, his brother's accurate watch running beside his own broken one. The twin: Peron is noise and appetite and the body, Joachim is silence and restraint and the law, and Young puts them in one womb to make her picture of a single consciousness split against itself. The executor's work: he pays a dead man's debts out of his own torn pockets, keeps faith with the dead, refuses to let their affairs be closed, which is exactly what the novel does on every page and what Vera does as she narrates. The circling prose: he cannot take the shortest line between two points, he makes long navigations around and around a subject, and Young's sentences are built the same way, so that in Mr. Spitzer style and psychology are the same thing. Each facet is the plural self, the person who is not one, drawn from another angle. He is the theme walking around Boston in a cape.

At the very end, carrying the dying Catherine into the garden by the sea, Mr. Spitzer confesses that he is Peron, and that it was Joachim, the lawyer and musician, who died. He says the reason no one has heard his music since Peron's death is that he was Peron all along, that he was never a musician and never a lawyer, that he knew not one note from another and scarcely the plaintiff from the accused, and that the whole Joachim identity was almost a celestial joke. And it comes too late. Catherine has already died, an hour before, at the start of his whispers. She will never know he was not Joachim.

Young does not certify the confession. Her phrase is that all had been deception, even to him. Even to him. The man who spent the longest section of the book unable to say whether he was alive or dead, himself or his brother, ends by naming himself the twin everyone thought was in the grave, and the naming is just one more bet from a gambler who cannot see his own cards. The crossing point does not resolve into a single name. It confesses that it never had one. The plural self does not get solved at the end. It makes its final move.

Mr. Spitzer refuses the processed grief that would let him heal, because Young writes that if his grief left him, stole out like a tenant from an old house, he would no longer be Mr. Spitzer; the grief is not something he has, it is what he is made of. He witnesses the dead without concluding they are gone, provisions them with cheap cheroots while he smokes his own perfumed brand, greets them good-night and good-morning. He builds the unheard music anyway, drowned by his brother's noise through a wall thin as a membrane. Grief that will not end, witnessing without the reward of being witnessed, building without arrival: the Radical Immanence pillars are not illustrated by him one at a time. They live in one threadbare gentleman at once, which is why his section is the longest. He is the crossing point, and a crossing point is where a structure needs the most material to hold.

Young could have told us Spitzer was uncertain of himself. Instead she built the uncertainty into the prose, so that reading him is the closest the novel comes to explaining, from the inside, why it is written the way it is. The circling, the deferral, the clause added to clause and arriving late or not at all, is not a description of his mind. It is his mind. That is the lesson hiding in the length: when style and character become the same thing, you cannot render the man briefly, because brevity would assume a stable subject standing behind the sentence, and he has none. The size of the section is not a flaw to explain away. It is the finger pointing.
master-class-character-vera-cartwheel:
Vera Cartwheel: The One Who Watches and Will Not Fix Them

← Catherine Snowden Cartwheel · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Miss Georgia MacIntosh →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

She is on a bus in the mist, looking at a stranger she will never be able to name, and she is already telling his story. That is how you meet Vera Cartwheel because looking hard at people she cannot hold onto and telling their stories anyway is the whole of what she does. The double-headed man by the roadside, the pregnant girl in her painted silk, the whiskey-drinking driver going home to a wife who may not exist: she will never learn one of their names, and she keeps every one of them. He would remain, she says, engraved on memory's whirling disc. She does not act on these people. She does not save them or sort them or decide what they mean. She witnesses them, and she refuses to let them go.

She is Catherine's daughter, the pale rejected child whose eyes, her mother believed, had not craved reality. She was raised not by that mother, who kept to her bed and her dreams, but by a red-headed nursemaid with a broken nose who preached truth to nature and then walked into the sea. Now grown, Vera travels alone, by train and plane and evening comet plane and at last this erratic bus, into interior America, searching for one who is already dead. Every fact of her life is a fact of loss, and every fact is delivered in the same searching, circling voice, so that her grief and her looking are not two things. The looking is what the grief does.

Ask the wrong question and Vera is the weakest figure in the book: the passive narrator, the lonely watcher, the empty frame around vivid people. Ask the right one and she is the center of the novel's ethics. The question Radical Immanence puts to her is not why is she so alone, but what is a person doing when she stays present with someone she cannot resolve? Vera's answer, page after page, is to witness, and witnessing turns out to be the hardest and most active thing anyone in the book does.

Consider what she actually does with the adults around her. She examines her mother without curing her and without condemning her. She examines Mr. Spitzer without deciding whether he is alive or dead, himself or his brother, and she leaves him uncertain because uncertain is what he is. She examines Miss MacIntosh, the woman she loved and lost, without ever shrinking her to the lesson she was hired to be. She examines Esther Longtree, pregnant for years, and does not look away from a grief that will not deliver. In every case she comes close, stays long, and declines to fix. She does not turn a person into a verdict. This is not weakness of will. It is a discipline, and it is rarer than any action in the book.

She is the frame around the two still figures the first half rests on, and she holds them both without ranking them. Mr. Spitzer cannot throw anything away. Catherine cannot stop making things up. Vera watches the man to whom nothing happens and the woman to whom everything happens, and she refuses to choose between them, refuses to call one sane and one lost. Spitzer keeps the dead by paying their debts, Catherine keeps them by dreaming them into her rooms, and Vera keeps them by narrating them, which is why the whole novel is her voice. Her witnessing is not a stance she takes inside the book. It is the book. One woman recalling the dead into the present tense and refusing to let them be gone, is the third technique for the one task the other two are also performing, which is bearing what keeps leaving.

The easy reading calls all of this alienation. Vera walks alone, she says so herself, the seeker through mazes of sorrow, cut off, half sleeping, reaching all her life for the tangible and watching it fade. It is tempting to take her at her most despairing word and file her as the isolated modern soul. The novel does not let that stand. The same narrator who mourns that every dream must fail also writes that every heart is the other heart, that the individual is the one illusion. Her loneliness is not the last word about her. It is the condition out of which she does her real work, which is to find, in strangers she will never meet again, the secret relationship, deep calling to deep. She is not cut off from the others. She is the one who insists, against all the evidence of separateness, that the others are hers.

And then she does the thing none of the resolved characters can do. She set out to find Miss MacIntosh, or the truth behind her, a quest with a destination. She does not reach it. She lands in southern Indiana, a state as yet unknown to her, in the mist, on a road that seems to go back the way it came. The book that was supposed to arrive somewhere arrives here, in the ordinary here-and-now of a bus that plows nowhere, and treats the failure to arrive as the point rather than the defeat. There is no What Cheer at the end of the line. There is only the actual place the traveler is standing, which is the only place anyone is ever standing.

What she builds there, she builds knowing it cannot last. She loves the stone deaf man, the one who heard with his eyes, who could not hear her voice and never would. She marries him anyway, and she conceives a child in a silent world. This is not a rescue and not a perfect union. It is love chosen inside a limitation that will not lift, communion built across a silence, love that comes, in his words, before words were or ever will be. She does not wait for the whole man, or the moment when nothing is broken. She builds in the only conditions there are, which are broken ones, and she builds anyway.

What stays standing is that Vera's stillness was never emptiness. The reader arrives expecting the narrator to be a window, a clear pane the vivid people are seen through, and leaves having watched that window turn out to be the most active thing in the house. She does not resolve her mother, or Spitzer, or Miss MacIntosh, because resolving them would be the failure. To witness a person without concluding her, to stay in the presence of a contradiction and neither flee it nor solve it, is the whole ethical labor the novel is asking for, and Vera is the one who performs it start to finish. The lesson for a writer is that a narrator does not need a plot to be the strongest figure on the page. She needs only to refuse the two easy exits, judgment and rescue, and to keep looking. Presence, held long enough and honestly enough, is an action. It may be the only one the book finally trusts.
