master-class-character-madge-capehorn-ed:
Madge Capehorn Edwards: The Life Made From a Sleeping Stranger

← Moses Hunnecker · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Homer Capehorn →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Homer Capehorn · Jacqueline White · Madge Capehorn · Vera Cartwheel

She is asleep on a bus, a stranger, and before she wakes the narrator has given her a husband, a rival, a jealousy, and a whole ruined marriage because being a face someone else builds a life onto is the entirety of what she is.

A thin, faded girl, prematurely old, pregnant and resisting the pregnancy as if it were a deformity, her tiny face hidden under a mask of heavy makeup streaked with grey, her colorless eyes not filled with the light which comes from love. She is dressed in her finest, and her finest is an accidental chaos, cheap cameos and colored glass, brass and wooden bracelets, cascades of ten-cent-store pearls dripping from her ears, velvet slippers on glass heels which should not carry her far, a stuffed bird nodding on her hat, and among all the rings no wedding ring. Her orange silk dress is painted all over with little sailboats and red football players and white skiers, a whole world of images running across her body. She sleeps sitting stiffly upright so her hair will not be disarranged, and she cries in her sleep. Vera, a few seats away, watches, and out of the mask and the painted dress and the missing ring she builds her.

Radical Immanence holds two things that look separate. It says witnessing others is the central ethical act, and it says reality is made rather than found. Madge is where the book shows they are one thing. She is a stranger Vera will never speak to, Madge Capehorn, poor little Madge Edwards that has a husband called Homer, a dead rival called Jacqueline, a jealousy, a wedding, a grief. The question the book asks through her is whether that is witnessing or invention, and the answer it gives is that there is no difference. To see a stranger truly, in this book, is already to make her up.

Madge’s marriage is the proof. None of it is reported. All of it is built, in what the novel calls a border world between the waking and the sleeping, out of one sleeping woman's face. Homer Capehorn, the faded all-star athlete, lies dreaming of the dead girl he loved and never won, the ice-skater who could skate like a comet, and calls her name in his sleep. Madge lies beside him, older than the others, the fast one, heavy with another man's child, fiercely jealous of a rival who is already in the grave, insisting that the dead girl is nothing, that the bridegroom is the skeleton. Vera invents every word of this, and the book gives the invented marriage as much weight, as much detail, and as much ache as any marriage Vera knew about. The made-up Madge suffers as fully as the real Catherine.

There is a doubling worth noticing. Inside Vera's invention, Madge's own life is ruled by a dead woman. Homer's love for the dead Jacqueline is more alive than his marriage to the living Madge, so that even the constructed stranger is built around the book's oldest law, that the dead do not leave. Vera invents for Madge the exact haunting Vera herself lives under, the dead crowding out the living, which is a quiet sign that the life she builds for the stranger is a mirror held up to her own. The invention is a confession. Handed a blank face on a bus, the narrator fills it with her own grief and calls the result another woman.

And where Catherine is the woman to whom everything happens on the inside, Madge is the woman to whom everything happens on the outside, in a body, in a single lurching moment on a flooded road. She is pregnant and married and betrayed and coming to her early grave all at once, this dead center of life, about to be delivered of herself or of a stranger. She resists all of it, resists the child, resists sleep, wishes she were already in the ground with her little hands reaching above the earth. Catherine escaped into the dream and could not be reached. Madge cannot escape her body and cannot get out of the one terrible instant. The book sets the two women at opposite poles of the same helplessness, the one who is all hidden interior and the one who is all exposed surface, and it grants them equal seriousness, though it had to invent almost the whole of Madge to do it.

The lesson for a writer lives at the edge of what a narrator can know. A careful writer might keep a first-person narrator honest by letting her report only what she could actually learn, and fall silent before the stranger on the bus. Young does the opposite. She lets Vera build the stranger an entire life, and by refusing to mark that life as any less real than the reported ones, she makes her deepest claim in the plainest possible place. Every person anyone knows is partly built by the knower. The line between seeing someone and inventing her is itself a fiction. The honest response is not to stop inventing but to admit that seeing was always an invention, and then to do it with love. Madge is a woman made out of a sleeping face on a bus, and she is as real as anyone in the novel, because in this novel that is the only way anyone is real.
master-class-character-the-sea-house-ser:
The Sea-House Servants: The Sane Ones Who Caught the Dream

← The Black Coachman · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Mr. Res Tacamah →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

They are the ones who keep the great sea-blackened house running while its mistress dreams her life away upstairs, the real maids and cooks and valets on Mr. Spitzer's payroll, and by the time the novel looks at them closely they have caught what she has, so that the people hired to hold the line against the dream are living inside it too. Being the sane, waking, wage-earning staff of a house and having gone as imaginary as its phantom guests is what they are.

They run the book's central move backward. The mother dreams companions into being, a chauffeur, a coachman, a man of letters in a medicine bottle, and treats the invented as real. The servants are the reverse operation, real people turning imaginary from the inside. They are "quite comme il faut as to their unusual environment, taking it all for granted," and what they take for granted is a house full of the dead. They hear "the carriage wheels in the driveway" and "the neighings of the dead horses" in the long nights. They discuss the phantom callers the way one discusses the neighbors, "the latest doings of this fine gentleman or that," one who discovered a new planet, one who believes he dwells on Uranus. One of them "did nothing but polish the shoes left out each evening" by guests who were never there, and grumbles about their muddy boots. Another is sure he lives in "a forest of cuckoo clocks." Another imagines he is "Hannibal driving the elephants over the Alps." Just to hear the servants talk, the book says, anyone might have thought the opium dreams were all real, "especially when they were unreal."

Ask the wrong question and this is just atmosphere, a spooky staff for a spooky house. Ask the right one and the servants carry the second pillar of Radical Immanence somewhere it has not yet gone. Reality is constructed rather than found, the book keeps saying, and every version of the claim so far has lived inside one head, the mother's or Vera's or Miss MacIntosh's. The servants prove it is contagious. The construction does not stay sealed in the dreamer who built it. It spreads to the sane people brought in to keep the house, colonizes their waking hours, hands them invented errands and invented selves, until the proof of the made world is not that its author believes in it but that the hired help have caught it like a fever and gone to work inside it.

The figure who keeps them a portrait instead of a blur is Wellington. He is an old valet with "no man to whom he should serve as valet," no master anywhere in the house, and rather than stand idle he has decided he waits on the Duke of Wellington. The other servants call him Wellington. The mother calls him Wellington and asks after "Wellington's appetites." A real servant handed a false identity not by the dreamer but by his own need and the household's habit, given a self out of nothing and answering to it, is the exact mirror of James, the false servant handed a real biography from the outside. James is an absence dressed as a man. Wellington is a man dressed as an absence. Between them they close the circuit the whole section has been drawing, the invented made into something solid and the solid invented, and it is fitting that both should be servants, since a servant is already a person a household would rather see as a function than a face.

What keeps them their own case, and not merely more of Catherine's dreaming, is that they keep one foot in the daylight the phantoms never touch. Their bedrooms hold clocks that tell the real hour, because "it was not the illusion of servants," who must wake and work while every other clock in the house stands stopped. They gamble in the housekeeper's parlor. Mr. Spitzer pays their wages out of his own thinning pockets, keeping a full staff for a woman who is, he half believes, already dead. And they are afraid. They fear she walks at night, having found "a bare footprint on a marble stair" and "the streak of her long white nightgown in the dust." They fear her wine is drugged with a "nepenthe" that would take their "personal sorrows, their corporeal senses, and their powers of reason," put them to sleep in the dream for good, and leave their carriages standing forever in the drive. They are the crossing point between the opium economy upstairs and the real one, people who punch a clock and draw a wage and nonetheless serve tea to the dead, and who know, better than their mistress, exactly how much they stand to lose to the dream, and go on losing it.

The turn for a writer is that a made world is not kept behind the eyes of the one who made it. It leaks. Build a house of the dead convincingly enough and the living people hired to sweep its floors will begin to hear the carriages, polish the phantom boots, answer to borrowed names, and take the whole impossible arrangement for granted. That is the deepest and least comfortable form of the book's claim, and it is the one a writer performs on a reader without meaning to. The invention does not stay on the page. It recruits. The maid trailing her lace petticoats in the dust and the valet waiting on a dead general are what happens to anyone who lives long enough inside someone else's dream, which is a fair description of reading, and of writing, and of the household staff who keep both going, on wages, by a clock that still tells time, in a house where nothing else does.
master-class-character-solomon:
Solomon: The Slow Wisdom Under the Bed

← Mr. Bonebreaker · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Friday →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

He is a turtle, and he is one of the few companions Vera has in the schoolroom by the sea. Her mother gave him to her "on my twelfth birthday," having received him herself "from one of her dead guests," and named him Solomon, a name the governess "did not approve of but which she could do nothing to change." Solomon is "quite ancient," "a great giant turtle who might have carried, as in some legendary preadamite time, the whole world on his back." Now he carries only "a clay flower pot in which I had planted a red geranium which smelled like tobacco," and wearing his small absurd crown he takes "his meditative constitutional" across the bare floor, scraping, slow, his own castle, drawing head and tail and legs into his shell "as if it carried its own bed covers always."

The two grown women read him in exactly opposite ways, and the split is an example of the whole book in miniature. Miss MacIntosh, the rationalist governess, "could see no wisdom in a turtle," only sloth, "an old turtle sleeping its life away and unaware of happenings on Wall Street or Threadneedle Street." A turtle, she rules, "should be no example for me." Vera's mother, the dreamer, gave him the name of the wisest king. Between the woman who trusts only the visible ledger and the woman who trusts the dream, the slow creature carrying his house is either nothing or everything. The book, which loves the axis that holds still while the wheel turns, is quietly on the turtle's side. Solomon is the vertical line made a small animal, unhurried, self-contained, carrying his whole world and his whole shelter with him, indifferent to the market, wise in the way the philosophy calls wise, by staying in slow contact with what he is made of.

He is also the sacred ordinary, the precious thing you do not notice until it is gone. When Miss MacIntosh "put him out-of-doors where he belongs," she tells Vera, "you will never miss him." She is wrong. His absence is "the absence of something which, though very precious, I had never appreciated before," and the bedroom without his soft padded footsteps is "filled with emptiness." He "had never done very much but push his head in and out of a hard shell," and that turns out to have been a companionship, a presence, a slow heartbeat in the room, and Vera sinks to her knees when he is taken away.

The turn for a writer is a small, steadying one. Solomon is the pace the work actually requires, the slow wisdom, the rationalist mistakes for sloth, the willingness to carry the whole weight and go at a scrape, "unaware of happenings on Wall Street," untroubled by the news and the noise. He is his own castle, needing little, wise by patience rather than by speed. And he is the ordinary companion that is not valued until the brisk sensible voice puts him out the door and the room fills with emptiness. The book lets the governess be wrong about him. The slow thing is not missed until it is gone. It should have been appreciated while it scraped across the floor, carrying its geranium, in no hurry at all.
master-class-character-lucie-bell:
Lucie Bell: The Girl Who Was Too Loud

← The Stone Deaf Man · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Characters as Representations →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Lucie Bell · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

Before Vera came, the stone deaf man loved a woman named Lucie Bell, and Lucie Bell was noise. Vera never sees or hears her, "she had left him before I ever came," and everything we know of her comes through his all-night lament against her, which is really a lament that she could not be silent. He loved silence, and she was "an alarm clock to awaken a man," "a four o'clock train," "a loud noise jangling in my ear," "too noisy a girl." "Be thou the silent bell," he begs the memory of her, but her whole nature was to ring.

She was a runaway and a hitchhiker, a woman who "waited by the side of the road" and held up her little thumb, who had been "running away from an old husband, an old man," and who would run again, "hitch-hiking on, Lucie Bell, come some other dawn." He cannot trust her because she is made of leaving: "if you was running away from an old husband, an old man, why should I think you would be faithful to me?" She loved noisy things, "a jukebox more than she loved" him, "a tired marathon skater" she would "hang around his neck like an albatross." She is the loud, living, faithless girl, the one who could not hold still in the silent world he wanted to keep her in.

There is a cruelty in his verdict that the book does not hide. He decides she "never" loved, that she was only "a loud noise," because she would not be quiet, because she woke him when he wanted "not awakening." He wants a woman who "slept in my arms when the cry was gone," and Lucie Bell was the cry. So he lets her go down the road and turns his love toward silence itself, toward Vera, who will spell her name on his hand and make no sound. Lucie Bell is what the silence-lover cannot keep, the one who is too alive, too loud, too much herself to be folded into his stillness.

The turn for a writer is quick and rueful. Lucie Bell is the living, jangling material that will not be quiet, that will not stay where the maker wants it, that loves the jukebox and the skater and the open road and moves on at dawn. The artist who is in love with silence, with the perfected still thing, loses her, and half-persuades himself she was never worth keeping, "a loud noise," never really loved. But she is the noise of a life that refused to be arranged, and the book lets her keep her thumb out by the side of the road, going somewhere, while the man who could not bear her ringing settles down with silence and calls it love. She is a small figure and a sharp one, the reminder that the thing too loud to keep may have been the living thing, and that calling it noise is how the maker forgives himself for letting it go.
master-class-06-paradox-what-the-dialect:
Paradox: What the Dialectic Leaves Behind

← Dialectics and the Refusal of Synthesis · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Characters →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer

If the dialectic is the system Young invokes and refuses, paradox is the state she leaves it in. A dialectic that is denied its synthesis does not disappear; it settles into paradox, two opposed things held together without resolution, each true, neither cancelling the other. The novel is saturated with paradoxes for exactly this reason. Paradox is not one device among many in the book. It is the residue of every system the novel has put under load and watched fail to resolve, and it becomes the fundamental structural and thematic condition of the work, blurring the lines between opposed concepts and unsettling the ordinary understanding of reality, identity, time, and existence.

A reader might reach for the Zen koan as a comparison, the paradoxical statement that stops rational thought and forces a different kind of seeing, and the comparison is useful as a reader's tool. The novel itself contains no Buddhism; the koan is an analogy we might bring to the book, not a source Young worked from. What the two share is the refusal of the tidy answer. Where they part is that the koan aims at an awakening beyond the paradox, and Young's paradoxes aim at nothing beyond themselves. They are where the reader is asked to stay.

The principal paradoxes are these.

Reality and Illusion. This is the central one. The novel questions what is real and what is not, and repeatedly suggests that illusion is more potent and more meaningful than the objective fact it is supposed to be measured against. Catherine's opium visions are dismissed as unreal and are also the richest, most densely inhabited world in the book. The paradox is not resolved in either direction. The novel does not finally rule the visions false, nor does it endorse them as true. It holds the real and the illusory in a suspension it never lifts.

Life and Death. The boundary between the living and the dead is porous and often, in the novel's own phrasing, not to be drawn at all: "no great distinction should be made between the living and the dead." Death is not an endpoint but a state that coexists with life and extends it. The dead visit, advise, and are loved; Mr. Spitzer lives inside a dead brother's memory. The paradox is that death does not end the relations the living have with the dead, and the novel treats this not as metaphor but as the plain condition of its world.

Identity and Multiplicity. The singular, stable self is undermined at every turn. Characters are perceived as several beings at once, lose track of who they are, or absorb aspects of one another. The twin brothers are the sharpest case: the confession that the surviving brother is Peron and the dead one Joachim does not resolve their identities but dissolves the question, leaving two men who were never cleanly two. Identity here is not a fact to be uncovered but a paradox to be inhabited.

Appearance and Underlying Truth. What looks obvious hides depth, and what looks fantastical carries the deeper reality. Miss MacIntosh is the plain, sensible surface under which the novel's most guarded secret waits; the opium visions, the least credible thing in the book, hold some of its truest perceptions. The novel keeps inverting the expected relation between the apparent and the real without ever settling which is which.

Time and Space. Time in the novel is not linear or fixed but fluid, cyclical, and sometimes simultaneous, the past pressing into the present and events recurring rather than passing. Space is no more stable; rooms shift, distances expand and contract, the house relocates in the night. Neither dimension offers the reader a fixed coordinate to stand on, and the novel never restores one.

Order and Chaos. Characters seek and impose order and are perpetually overwhelmed by the chaos it was meant to contain. Miss MacIntosh's facts and schedules, Mr. Spitzer's measured paces, are efforts at control that the novel's disordered world dissolves. The order is real and the failure is certain, and the novel presents both at once.

Tangible and Intangible. The material world is repeatedly made to seem elusive, less solid than the non-material world of thought, dream, and spirit. Objects lose their fixity; the felt weight of a memory or a phantom exceeds the weight of the physical thing. The novel does not choose the immaterial over the material so much as refuse the assumption that the tangible is the more real of the two.

Love and Absence. Love in the novel is sought most powerfully where it cannot be had, and directed toward the dead or the unreal. The novel states the paradox in its own voice: a love "which never was, yet was more powerful than any love which should be realized in this mortal" world. Catherine loves a dead man precisely because the dead cannot disappoint; Mr. Spitzer's devotion is never declared and never returned. Love is realized here as absence, and the absence is not a lack of love but its intensest form.

These paradoxes are not stylistic ornament. They are what the novel is left holding once it has invoked the systems that promise to resolve contradictions and shown that they cannot. They create a disorienting but richly textured world in which the interior life is constantly projected onto and tangled with the exterior one, so that the reading experience is itself a passage through ambiguity. The novel's language, spiraling and repetitive, enacts the same refusal at the level of the sentence: a prose that will not resolve into simple definition or linear progression because the reality it describes does not. Literary Devices, a later section, will provide examples of the same suspension performed inside single sentences.
master-class-14-the-american-literary-tr:
The American Literary Tradition

← The Context · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Symbolism →

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is hard to place because it belongs to several traditions at once and sits comfortably inside none of them. It is a picaresque, a novel of the road, and yet almost nothing happens on the road; the journey is a voyage of the spirit through illusion rather than a sequence of adventures. It is a psychological novel of extraordinary interiority, and yet its interior is rendered in prose so incantatory and image-drenched that it reads closer to poetry than to the realist psychology the term usually implies. It is experimental and modernist in method, built on multi-level consciousness and the refusal of linear time, and yet its raw material is the plainest American folk life. The book's place in the tradition is precisely this refusal to settle into one lane, and the ambition that refusal serves.

What roots it firmly in American letters is its subject and its ground. Young's inspiration is explicitly the down-to-earth Middle West, and her achievement is to grant that ordinary interior the permanence of myth. Her cast of American types, the bus driver, the suffragist, the old maid, the clam-digger, the gambler, is rendered with a humor and extravagance that are distinctively American, and elevated to mythic scale much as Joyce elevated his Dubliners, though Young's soil is native and her comedy her own. The book has been likened to an American Arabian Nights, an epic that fuses myth and reality out of homegrown material, and the comparison is apt in one specific way: like that collection, the novel is a nesting of tales, a frame that keeps opening onto further stories, and it treats the tall tale and the folk type as vehicles for something far larger than local color.

Its thematic range looks, at first, like a catalogue of sensational subjects, drug addiction, suffrage, murder, suicide, real and imaginary pregnancy, schizophrenia, gambling, perfectionism. But these are not the novel's concerns so much as its instruments. Every one of them serves the single question the book keeps asking: "What shall we do when, fleeing from illusion, we are confronted by illusion?" The addiction, the doubled identities, the pregnancies that never deliver are all ways of pressing the one problem of a reality that will not separate from dream. In this the novel speaks directly to the central preoccupations of American modernism and anticipates the postmodern, the fractured self, the unreliable real, the collapse of linear time, while grounding those abstractions in flesh and folk.

Young's technique is the source of both the difficulty and the reward. She builds by what has been called a cellular expansion, unbroken bridges from word to word and image to image, so that the prose accumulates into a dense, immersive fabric rather than advancing by plot. The imagery is so pictorial it invites comparison to painting, and Young herself admired Chagall, whose floating figures and dream logic are a fair visual analogue to her pages. The events themselves resist explanation, staying ambiguous by design, which is why the book rewards and arguably requires a second reading. What keeps all this from collapsing into mere difficulty is the vision underneath it, which is human, compassionate, and often funny. The novel is hard, but it is not cold.

Its reception has matched its strangeness. At publication in 1965 the reviews were sharply divided, put off by the novel's extraordinary length and complexity and by the fact that Young had published little else to prepare readers for it. It has since been recovered and reassessed as a major, if demanding, American accomplishment, valued for exactly the qualities that once repelled: its ambition, its emotional force, its fusion of the mythic and the mundane. It stands now as a pioneering work that expanded what the American novel could attempt in scope, form, and subject, a book that made room for things the tradition had not previously held.
master-class-12-the-style:
The Style

← The Main Idea · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Context →

Characters: Mr. Chandelier · Mr. Res Tacamah · Vera Cartwheel

Most descriptions of Young's prose reach quickly for the same words: lyrical, dense, poetic, hypnotic, difficult. All of that is accurate, and none of it distinguishes her from a dozen other ambitious stylists. What makes the style hers is not that it is beautiful but that it is doing the novel's philosophical work at the level of the sentence. The prose does not describe a world where reality and illusion will not separate, where the self is plural, where nothing resolves. It enacts that world in its grammar, its shape, and its smallest connective choices. To read Young's sentences carefully is to watch the book's argument happen in the syntax before it ever happens in the plot. Four features carry most of that work.

The grammar undermines what it states

This is the most important and least obvious feature of the style, and it is easy to miss because it hides inside sentences that seem merely descriptive. Young repeatedly builds a clause that asserts something and then, within the same breath, takes the assertion back, so that the sentence arrives nowhere it can be pinned. A character is "the illusion of the illusion and the spectre of the spectre in a mirrorless world." Read that slowly. Each noun is qualified by its own double, and the world that might have reflected and confirmed either one is removed at the end. The sentence offers a thing, then the copy of the thing, then denies the mirror that would let you check which was real. It is a grammar of retraction, and it is everywhere.

The effect is that her sentences will not let the reader stand on them. A statement is made and then hedged, doubled, or reversed before the period, so that certainty never quite forms. This is not vagueness. It is precise. Young is refusing, at the level of the clause, to do the thing prose normally does, which is to fix a fact and move on. Her prose describes a world that cannot be fixed, and it describes it in sentences that cannot be fixed either. The reader who wants a solid handhold is denied one on purpose, sentence after sentence, because a solid handhold would be a lie about the reality the book is rendering. The style is honest by being unstable.

"And" where another writer would put "but"

The smallest instance of that same refusal is a single word, and it is the most transferable thing a writer can take from her. Young overwhelmingly joins her clauses with "and" rather than "but." Where ordinary prose sets one thing against another, this happened, but that undercut it, Young lays the two side by side and lets them both stand, joined by the flat, non-hierarchical "and." The living and the dead, the real and the illusory, the beautiful and the ruined are strung together on "and," never sorted by "but" into the true one and the false one.

This is grammar as philosophy. "But" is the conjunction of resolution; it tells the reader which clause wins. "And" is the conjunction of coexistence; it refuses to rank. A novel whose whole argument is that opposites do not resolve into synthesis, that the dialectic is denied its arrival, could hardly choose otherwise. Every "and" where the ear expects "but" is a tiny enactment of the book's central refusal. The prose does not argue that contradictions coexist. It coordinates them with "and" and lets them lie there together, unresolved, which is a stronger claim than any argument because it is built into the sentence's spine rather than stated as a theme.

The recursive structure

Young's sentences do not advance so much as circle. A phrase generates a variation of itself, which generates another, so that the sentence turns around its subject rather than moving past it, "fading ripples begetting fading ripples," "the music becoming the unconscious music... So the conscious music became the unconscious." Clauses fold back on their own words; the end of one phrase becomes the beginning of the next; images recur slightly altered a few lines on. The unit of her prose is not the line that gets somewhere but the loop that deepens where it already is.

This recursion is the sentence-level version of the novel's whole architecture. The book does not build toward a climax; it accumulates revolutions, a spoke rotating rather than a line traveling. The prose is built the same way. A recursive sentence is a wheel turning in miniature, and a paragraph of them is the novel's structure rendered small enough to hold in one breath. This is also why the book can be so long without going anywhere in the ordinary sense: the sentences are not designed to progress, so the reader who reads them expecting progress fights the prose the whole way. Read for the turning instead, and the difficulty resolves into rhythm. The style teaches the reader how to read the book, if the reader will let the sentence circle instead of demanding it arrive.

Language as construction

The fourth feature connects the style directly to the novel's belief that reality is made rather than found. Young's prose is visibly building its world out of words, and it lets the seams show. Her characters are conjured by naming, a chandelier becomes Mr. Chandelier, a drug bottle becomes Mr. Res Tacamah, "the author of so many fantasies," the instant they are named. The prose does the same thing openly, assembling a person or a place out of accumulated clauses and never pretending the accumulation is anything but made. The famous cumulative sentences, the ones that pile detail on detail through a character's attire or a room's contents until the thing stands fully built, are demonstrations of construction. You watch the sentence make the object. It does not report a dress that exists; it builds a dress out of clauses, and the building is on display.

This is why the density is not decoration and cannot be trimmed without loss. In a novel arguing that the world is constructed by the people who need it, prose that constructs its world in plain sight is the argument in action. The reader is made complicit in the making, assembling each phantasmal figure and shifting house out of the words Young lays down, which is exactly what Vera does on the bus and the mother does in her bed. To read the style is to perform the novel's thesis about reality. The sentence is a small machine for building something that was not there, and letting you see it built.

The surface features, in service of the four

The qualities usually named as Young's style are real, and they all serve the four functions above rather than standing on their own. The sophisticated, surreal vocabulary, "phantasmagoric," "miasmic," "Stygian," "empearled," works by blending the tangible with the ethereal, a "gold chain" beside "ghostly tides," so that diction itself refuses to separate the solid from the dreamed. The pervasive metaphors and personification, "the rain falling like blows," "the moon shining at noon as a distant street lamp," give agency to the inanimate and blur the line between animate and not, which is the reality-illusion collapse worked in imagery. The sound devices, the consonant and vowel repetition that make the prose "billowing before her eyes and blotting out visibility," produce the hypnotic quality that carries a reader through recursion without resistance. The recurring, slightly varied images that make the novel "a canto to obsession" are recursion operating across the whole book rather than within a sentence. And Vera's narrating voice, by turns intimate and cosmic, compassionate and melancholy, is the instrument that holds all of this in one register, close enough to enter a character and distant enough to witness the whole turning world at once.

None of these is the point by itself. Each is a means to the four ends: a grammar that will not let a statement stand, an "and" that refuses to rank, a sentence that circles instead of arriving, and a prose that builds its world in the open. Together they make a style that does not talk about Young's philosophy but performs it, so that a reader who understands how her sentences work has already understood the novel, whether or not a single theme has been named.

The lesson for a writer is the largest the book offers about craft: style is not the decoration laid over meaning but the place where meaning is enacted. Young could have written about a world where reality and illusion will not part, in clear declarative prose, and the book would have been a lesser thing, a description of a philosophy rather than an experience of one. Instead she built the philosophy into the grammar, so that the refusal to resolve, the coexistence of opposites, the turning rather than arriving, the making of reality out of language, all happen to the reader in the act of reading rather than being reported to the reader after the fact. A writer who wants a theme to be felt rather than stated should study how Young makes the sentence itself carry the argument, down to the choice of a single conjunction, until there is no gap left between what the prose says and what the prose does.
master-class-character-james-the-chauffe:
James the Chauffeur: The Life Made From an Absence

← Doctor Justice O'Leary · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Black Coachman →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Jacqueline White · Madge Capehorn · Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel

James is the servant who is not there. He is the mother's chauffeur, and by the time the novel introduces him he has been gone for years, having quit without notice and driven off with her car. She keeps him anyway. When she loses patience and dismisses the whole staff, the real maids and cooks and valets, the one servant she refuses to let go is the one who already left. "The real would go with the imaginary," and she chooses the imaginary. James is the clearest case in the book of a person kept alive entirely by the mind that needs him.

The line that holds him together is short: "That James was absent made him always present." A real chauffeur can quit. An imagined one cannot, because he has already done the only leaving he will ever do, and now he is fixed at the wheel forever, exactly where she wants him. He never turns around. He never speaks. She rides behind him for years giving orders into an imaginary horn, and the whole time he answers nothing, until her commands curdle into a kind of prayer, "James, why have you not answered me through all these years?" He is pure function, a driver with no face left, carrying her on a journey that has no arrival.

The journey is to Alaska, and they never reach it. "Home, James," she says, and then asks where home is, because there is no home and no turning, only the same barber pole and the same bridge crossed again and again in a frozen city. She tells him to run the red lights and stop at the green ones, the logic of someone who has stopped believing arrival is possible and drives on anyway. This is the mother's whole condition rendered as a car ride: a woman who cannot get out, steered by a man who is not there, toward a place that recedes as fast as they approach it.

What makes James more than a symptom is that she builds him a life, and keeps building. She gives him a history, an ex-convict falsely accused and unjustly sentenced, a man who broke rocks on a state road and dreams of open country and can drop a seagull on the wing. Then she gives him the most extraordinary detail of all. He is planning to kill her. When they reach Alaska he means to shoot her where no one will hear, and to shoot her dead father first for good measure. She knows this, rides with it, and cannot call for help. She has invented not just a companion but her own assassin, installed him at the wheel, and cannot look away from him or make herself get out of the car. The witnessing this book asks for, the refusal to flinch from what is actually in the room, turns literal here. The thing in the room is the driver she made to kill her, and she stays.

He has no fixed self, which is the other thing that marks him as wholly built. For the mother he is at once the killer at the wheel and a servant of impossible courtesy, the one who, when her pearl string breaks and twelve pearls scatter, returns thirteen, and the more she loses the more he brings back, "infinities of pearls." When Mrs. Hogden takes over the house and starts giving James orders of her own, he changes character on command, becoming "the soul of honor," and the novel shrugs that "he deviated from his true character" but calls it "an unimportant difference." He is whatever the dreamer requires. He is a terror and a saint in the same week, because there is no man underneath to contradict either version. He is one of the imaginary servants "in no position to question her reality."

He does not even get to be the center of the delusion he anchors. After all the mileage and the murder plot and the pearls, the book sets him aside in a single sentence: "It had not been her chauffeur upon whom her life depended, however." That turned out to be the canary. James, so carefully built, is demoted in a breath, and later accounts cannot even keep his story straight, so that the man who never reaches Alaska is also, elsewhere, said to be driving a taxi in Nome, having finally gone north to shoot his moose. Both are held at once. A made man does not have to be consistent.

The reason James matters past his own chapters is that he shows where Vera learned her trade. The daughter builds Madge out of a sleeping face, and Madge builds Jacqueline out of a cried name, but before either of them the mother lay in her bed and built James out of an absence, an ex-employee who robbed her turned into the most faithful companion of her life. The novel keeps making the same claim through different mouths, that the figures a mind cannot stop seeing are the ones it makes, and that the making is not a failure of contact but the form contact takes. James is the household version of the whole book. A real chauffeur will drive the mother's coffin to the grave, anonymous, barely described, a clam-digger at the wheel of a rickety Packard. The invented one got the biography, the injustice, the loaded gun, the infinities of pearls. In this novel that is the ordinary order of things. The made thing outlives and outshines the real, because the made thing is the one someone needed.

The turn for a writer is the freeing one. Invention runs freest exactly where there is nothing to check it against, and James is built on the emptiest, and so the most open, ground in the house, a man who had already left. An absence cannot talk back. A real chauffeur could be given almost nothing, because a real chauffeur would quit and prove the dreamer wrong, but the one who was already gone could be handed a rap sheet, a wronged past, a loaded gun, a plan to shoot her dead in Alaska, and "infinities of pearls," and none of it could be refuted, because there was no man left to do the refuting. That is where a writer builds most lavishly, on the blank a person leaves behind. And James teaches the harder second thing, that detail is not the same as weight. He gets the fullest biography of any invented figure in the book and is then set aside in a single line, "It had not been her chauffeur upon whom her life depended, however." A writer can pour a whole life into a figure and find the load resting somewhere unremarked, on a canary in a cage, and the danger is in mistaking the sheer amount of invention for its importance. The made thing does not even have to hold still to be real. James drives north and also, elsewhere, drives a taxi in Nome having finally gone to shoot his moose, and the book keeps both at once, because a figure a mind cannot stop seeing lives by being needed, not by being consistent.
master-class-character-the-stone-deaf-ma:
The Stone Deaf Man: The One Who Heard With His Eyes

← Beatrice Fitzgerald · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Lucie Bell →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Esther Longtree · Lisa Lunde · Mr. Weed · The Chicago Detective · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

He is the answer the whole book has been withholding, the true witness set at last against all the false ones. Vera hears him through the wall before she sees him, a voice "gonging through the dim air" all night, singing to a woman who is not there, and when she meets him at dawn he tells her plainly, "I am a stone deaf man." His face has "the look of one who had already drowned," because "all the waters of creation had smashed against his ears, leaving him stone deaf." And here is the sentence that turns him into the counter-figure for everyone else in these pages: "He heard with his eyes." His ears, he says, "were in his finger-tips, and the light streamed from his fingers."

Everyone else in the book who has the ordinary channels open uses them to avoid seeing. Mr. Weed looks at death for a living and never meets a person. Lisa Lunde sees through people and so never sees them. The Chicago detective looks straight at a living woman and files her as a corpse. The little toy salesman witnesses a drowning world and tips his hat. The stone deaf man has lost the easy way in, and precisely because of that he attends to what no one else will. He hears "what others heard not, the fishes whispering at the bottoms of rivers." He has learned the hard attention that the fully equipped keep refusing.

He came to it through a kind of death. He went deaf at fourteen, after "a sleep of six months, a sleep so near to death that it might almost have been his death," and woke to find that "sound had died when he was sleeping," that the key made no sound in the lock, that the long white curtains blowing made none. "It took him a long time to learn to dream." Then "he became a painter, and he was also the artist of his life." This is the book's Boethius, the one stripped down to the vertical line, who lost the horizontal world of easy noise and found in the silence a whole buried country of attention. What sounds like deprivation is the opening of the deeper sense. He is the sacred ordinary made a person: the silent world, for him, is not empty but full, thick with tongues, "the silences where no speech is," and he is "in love with not awakening," in love with the world that stays still and quiet and complete.

And he shows what the book means when it says language is not where reality actually gets built. He and Vera make their love outside of speech entirely. She "spelled out my name upon my lover's hand, for surely a woman must find some way by which to talk to the silence that she loved." He is "the secret lip-reader"; "thy hand speaks to me." He tells her, "there be words of ours, not in the alphabet of the stars. Flowers spell them out on the earth, and grasses talk." When the official channel is closed, love does not stop being made. It finds the hand, the earth, the flower. An old woman on the road had told him the thing he lives by, that a cut-off white man and a cut-off black woman suffer alike "for something that be not their fault," and that "life is imaginary, and this be an imaginary world," so "dream on." His deafness is not a wall between him and the world. It is the door.

The turn for a writer is the tender one, the single figure in the set who is the maker redeemed instead of the maker indicted. The stone deaf man is what the artist is supposed to become, the one who loses the easy way in and learns to hear with the eyes, to read the hand, to attend to the fishes at the bottom of the river because the surface has gone silent. He "became a painter, and he was also the artist of his life." He misses "much foolish chatter" and catches what the chatterers never will. And Vera, who has spent the whole book among people who could not see her, marries him, the one who "could not hear me" and with whom there is nonetheless "the communication of love." He hears her because he cannot hear. The book offers him as the last correction to all its anti-witnesses, and it plans a wedding at which Esther Longtree, "for she was also our love," and all the stillborn "clapping their hands in clouds," and the flowers and the birds and the old mule are the guests. The child of that marriage, he says, "will be our ear." The future will hear what the present could not, and that, the book says, is the whole hope: to lose the easy sense and gain the hard one, and to pass the hearing forward.
master-class-character-lisa-lunde:
Lisa Lunde: All A's Are C's

← Mrs. Hogden · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Esther Longtree →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Lisa Lunde · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Res Tacamah · Mr. Weed · Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel

The young woman who takes Vera's place, once Vera has packed a suitcase and gone, is Lisa Lunde, "my mother's young companion who took my place when, carrying a large suitcase, I escaped from my mother's house." She is the replacement, the next daughter hired to sit beside the mad mother and hold the household to some measure of sense. She is also a would-be physicist, an amateur scientist working for a living, and she keeps her own mad mother fifteen miles away in a telescope tenement. All through the Mrs. Hogden episode she stands exactly where the book likes to put people, between two versions of the real, and her whole character is a study of what a person does with that position when she has decided in advance what is true.

She is Vera's mirror, and the mirror is exact. Lisa Lunde works "to help support her mother who was poor and mad and dreamed that she was rich, even as my mother dreamed that she was poor." Two daughters, two lost mothers, one dreaming up and one dreaming down, and the sentence hinges them together on the words so that you cannot pull them apart. The dreamer's daughter and the debunker's daughter are the same daughter twice. This is why the confusions gather around her. Mrs. Hogden takes Lisa Lunde "to be the daughter of the house," and at the end, when Vera stands in the deserted playroom looking for whoever passed through, the message left behind was meant for her because Mrs. Hogden "mistakenly supposed" she "was Lisa Lunde." The replacement and the replaced trade names without anyone deciding to.

What she is proud of is seeing through things. She "prided herself on seeing immediately through Mrs. Hogden's pretensions." She is the one in the house who names the drug bottle a drug bottle. When Mrs. Hogden asks after Mr. Res Tacamah, the shy gentleman who will share the arithmetic lessons, Lisa Lunde shouts, "with cruel distinctness, determined to shatter all illusions at one blow," that Res Tacamah "is nothing but a drug bottle." She has the reductionist's good ear for the deflating line. To the mother's soft "a rose by any other name would smell as sweet," she answers, "Would smell as strong." She corrects, she classifies, she debunks. She is the consensus-reality officer of a house that has stopped keeping consensus reality, and she does the job with relish.

But the book puts her in the one job where seeing through is exactly the wrong skill, and watches her fail at it. Her real work in the episode is messenger. She carries the argument back and forth between the mother, who will not come out, and Mrs. Hogden, who will not go home, and she carries it badly on purpose. She "ran back and forth with meaningless messages between the two, and she would do nothing to interpret either character to the other." Handed the exact position of the witness, the go-between who could translate one soul to another, she empties it. She grows "revengeful," and she "began to enjoy the embarrassing situation." Where Mr. Weed is the anti-witness who never once meets the person he kills, Lisa Lunde is the anti-witness who stands directly between two people and refuses to carry either one across. Weed arranged never to look. Lisa Lunde looks, and declines to say what she sees.

Here the book turns her own pride against her. The mother's verdict on Lisa Lunde, relayed through Mrs. Hogden, is that she is "a day-dreamer," that "you never notice anything." The would-be physicist, the one who prides herself on seeing through everyone, is told she is the one who does not see, and the book means it. To see through Mrs. Hogden, to file her as a shoplifter and name her drug bottle, is to not see Mrs. Hogden at all, and Mrs. Hogden is precisely the figure who cannot be filed. She was "hard to classify," "something that evaded definition," a woman it would "take a life time" to pick up off the floor. Seeing through a person is not seeing her. Naming the thing "at one blow" is the opposite of staying in the room with it. Even Lisa Lunde's facts are guesses wearing lab coats: told that James went to Alaska, she shouts a date, "merely guessing at the time," and calls it knowledge.

Then the blackboard. Substitution is the law Lisa Lunde lives by, the physicist's clean confidence that "you could substitute one thing for another and get the same result. Apples, buttons, eggs." Mrs. Hogden believes the same thing about arithmetic, and when she leaves she chalks the law itself onto the little three-legged blackboard, a syllogism: "All a's are b's … all b's are c's … and therefore, dear heart, all a's are c's. You know me." In a physics notebook that is valid and tidy and true. In this house it is the horror. The transitive law that lets a stand for c is the same law by which Lisa Lunde stands for Vera, Mrs. Hogden stands for Miss MacIntosh and for a dead Cousin Hannah, and one Mr. Spitzer stands for another. The debunker's most trusted tool is the very thing dissolving the outlines of everyone, her own included. She thinks substitution is how you reason your way to the truth. The novel shows it is how a self loses its edges. "You know me," the blackboard says, and it is right. The syllogism knows Lisa Lunde better than she knows it, because she is one of its terms.

This is where she matters most against the philosophy the book keeps testing. Its failures are never the ones who suffer. They are the ones who "stop paying honest attention," who "replace real complexity with a simpler story they can manage." That is Lisa Lunde's whole method, raised to a virtue and called science. She meets the least sortable person in the house and spends her strength trying to sort her at one blow. She is handed the crossing point, the place where one life could be carried across to another, and she runs meaningless messages through it and enjoys the gap she keeps open.

The turn for a writer is the sharpest one in the set, because Lisa Lunde is not the writer's enemy but the writer's easiest self. She is the debunker at the desk, the one who reduces the strange character to "nothing but a drug bottle" and calls the reduction clarity, who guesses at a fact and calls it research, who stands between two invented people and carries messages without ever translating either into the other. It is the tidy way to work, and it feels like intelligence, and it is the exact refusal the book keeps naming. Set it beside the other kind of making, the kind that stays with the person who evades definition and does not shatter her at one blow. The novel lets Lisa Lunde have her sharp lines and her clean law, and then it lets her fade out of the playroom under someone else's name, taken for the woman she replaced, while the message on the blackboard spells out, in red chalk, the law she trusted and never once turned on herself. All a's are c's. She knew everyone. She never noticed she was one of them.
