Everyone Here Is Made

Read the section back and a strange thing rises out of it. Line the characters up and try to sort them by how real they are, and the sorting falls apart in the hand.

At one end sit the openly invented, the figures no one pretends are solid: James the chauffeur built out of an absence, the black coachman with no face, Res Tacamah the drug bottle, Mr. Chandelier the light fixture with seven crystal hands. Next to them stand the town's invented dead, Mr. Tidings who never existed and was also murdered, Mrs. Hathaway's two brothers who dissolve into one loved absent man. Then the strangers Vera builds on the bus without ever speaking to them, Madge conjured from a sleeping face, Jacqueline from a name cried in sleep, Homer from a ragged football sweater and a name that is not his wife's. And then, at the end where the ground was supposed to be firm, the ones taken for real, Miss MacIntosh who turns out to be a wig, Cousin Hannah remade on a deathbed no one attended, Jock assembled from a garbled newspaper notice no one troubled to correct. There is no line to draw. The made and the found run into each other with no seam, because the book does not believe there is a seam.

The bus is where it says so plainly. The whole novel is framed by a ride through the mist, a woman looking at people she will never meet and giving them entire lives, husbands and rivals and griefs and dead sweethearts, out of a painted dress and a sleeping face. That is not a flaw in the narration, a narrator overstepping what she could know. It is the argument the whole book is built to make. To see a stranger and to invent one are not two acts. They are the same act, and the bus is the place where the novel stops hiding it.

Young said as much in her own voice. When she had examined all the illusions of life, she told Miriam Fuchs and Ellen Friedman, and knew "there isn't any reality," a person nevertheless goes on, and that going-on is what maturity is: accepting that "it is all mask and illusion" and that people move through the world in disguise. The novel was built to demonstrate it, an opium addict's paradise at the center and, spreading out from it, a whole country of people who are masks worn by the ones who need them.

There is a story told about her, that she would take her writing students out to watch strangers at the bus stop and set them to writing the lives of the people they saw. Whether or not it happened as told, it names exactly the exercise the book performs on every page. A writer looks at a stranger and makes a person. That is the craft stripped to its root, and Young put it at the wheel of her enormous novel and drove it through the mist for more than a 1,198 pages.

Which means this section was never quite a catalog of people. It was a catalog of makings, and sorting them, weighing one against another, deciding that Musidora is more real than Madge and Madge more real than the coachman, is itself the thing the book is about. To analyze these figures is to build them a second time. The reader who has come this far has been doing, all along, what Vera does on the bus and what the mother does in her bed and what the town does over its gossip, taking fragments of the barely seen and assembling whole souls out of them, and grieving the ones that will not hold.

So the section does not end on a verdict about which characters were real. It ends on the recognition that the question was the wrong one. The book never asks whether a person is made. It asks how. Its failures are the ones who are made badly: Weed who reduces the living to weights, the detective who sees a corpse where a woman sleeps, Lisa Lunde who shatters the strange person "at one blow" and calls it clarity, Bonebreaker who flees the real the instant it stands revealed, Mrs. Hogden who dreams other people's private griefs out loud as common stock. And the ones it trusts are the ones who make with attention and will not close the person down: Vera, who looks long and refuses the verdict, the stone deaf man who "heard with his eyes," Beatrice at the washtub named for the guide to Paradise. Making a person is not the sin. Reducing one is.

The last image the book leaves is the first one, a bus plowing nowhere through the mist, a woman looking hard at people she cannot hold onto and telling their stories anyway. The reader closing this section is on that bus too. The people here will not hold still, will not resolve into a single settled fact, will not stay found. They have to be made, with as much attention as the maker can spare, and that turns out to be the only way anyone is ever known, on a bus, in the mist, looking at a stranger, and beginning, already, to tell the story.
master-class-character-cousin-hannah-fre:
Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden: The Life Made From a Real One

← The Canary · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Lorena →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Jacqueline White · Joachim Spitzer · Madge Capehorn · Mrs. Hogden

The others in this set were built out of almost nothing, a sleeping face, a cried name, an absence, a turned-away head. Cousin Hannah is the exception, and that is what makes her the hardest case in the book. She was a real person, a real cousin who really lived and really died, and more than that she was the mother's opposite in every direction, the one who scorned dreams and insisted on the hard world. If the book can fold even her into the dream, it has proved the thing it keeps trying to say.

She was everything the mother was not. Where the mother lay in bed for decades, Hannah crossed the actual earth, "a Captain Derring-Do who engaged in those adventures my mother only dreamed of," a suffragist and duelist and mountaineer who rode by camel where no woman had gone, knew the Alpine and Himalayan passes the way other people know their own street, and turned up prescient, having heard of the archduke's murder hours before the news. She was self-sufficient to the point of being her own pair, able to be "both herself and a gentleman," a woman who needed no fourth at the table because she was already two. The mother looked at her and saw "an emancipated extension of herself," the vertical life she might have led if she had ever stood up and got out of the bed.

And Hannah scorned the whole apparatus the mother lived inside. She "had not been persuaded by dreams and visions." She cut through "those delicate threads binding us to reality" as if they were nothing. She had come to the dark house to drag the mother out of it, to break up the opium dreams, to say plainly that the mother loved only "the mere shadow of a man" and should leave him for the open road. She beat the bridegroom with her white umbrella and tried to carry the bride off. She fought the dream directly, in the open, the way she fought everything, and "the valiant heart had fought her losing battle with shadows." She lost. The dreamer stayed in bed, and the realist could not move her.

What made Hannah easy to keep after death was that she had never been present in life. She was always somewhere else, always leaving, and "Cousin Hannah was never known to leave a forwarding address," so that when she died nothing about her changed for the mother, who goes on telephoning the empty house and inviting her to card games and asking her to search the Alps for the lost husband on her next crossing. The great line of the whole portrait is the quiet one: "Death seemed scarcely a greater absence than life had been." A woman that absent does not need to be alive to be summoned. She had already spent her life being unreachable, so the mother simply keeps reaching, exactly as before.

Then the book does the thing it has been building toward. It rewrites her death. Hannah, who lived by the sword and "should have died by one sharp blow, a martyr to her cause," does not. "She had suffered for years from frostbite. She had died after many years of semi-invalidism," in a bed, slowly, like the mother. And on that bed she recants everything. She confesses that the foreign wars were nothing, mere incidents, that "the greatest battles were fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home," that the man who leaves is the coward and the woman who stays is supreme. The adventurer, dying, hands the dreamer the argument. The one who spent a life proving that reality is out there to be crossed says at the end that the real war was the one the mother was fighting all along, lying still.

The catch is that none of it could have happened. "It was impossible to know how the great captain could have made this death-bed confession," because Hannah never answered the telephone, and the two houses were far apart, and the mother "had visited her only in a dream," carried to the deathbed in the carriage of the dead black coachman. The confession is invented. The mother built Hannah's surrender the way she built James and the coachman, and got her own conscience to drive her there to collect it. Even the secret the portrait circles, the grief that shadowed Hannah's unmarried life, "the great secret of Cousin Hannah's life" that Catherine and Mr. Spitzer bury and "skirt around," stays sealed, an interior no one can open, which is its own admission that a person is never fully found, only partly made by whoever is doing the remembering. And later the mother is not even sure Hannah has stayed one person, wondering whether the stranger Mrs. Hogden "must be my Cousin Hannah." The realist ends as raw material, recycled, reassigned, made and remade.

This is where the set closes, because Hannah is the strongest possible test and she fails it the way everyone does. Madge and Jacqueline and James and the coachman were built from little and fooled no one about it. Hannah was real, and she resisted, and she insisted on the exact opposite of everything the dreamer believed, and the dreamer built her anyway, down to the change of heart on the deathbed she was not there to witness. If the woman who cut the threads to reality can be woven back into someone else's dream, and made to say the dream was right, then the book has said there is no one so real they cannot be made. To be made by someone who loved her, or needed her to be wrong so they could be right, is not the opposite of having lived. It is the ordinary fate of anyone remembered by a person who cannot stop dreaming.

The turn for a writer is the most tempting and the most dangerous in the set. Madge and James were built out of almost nothing and never pretended otherwise. Hannah was real, and she resisted, and she held the exact opposite of everything the dreamer believed, and the dreamer remade her all the same, down to a deathbed recantation she was never there to give. That is the writer's most seductive power, the ability to take the very person who fought the dream and, in the telling, make her come around. The adventurer who scorned every illusion is made to say with her dying breath that the illusion was right, that the woman who never left her bed was the braver of the two. A writer reaches for this move whenever a remembered opponent conveniently softens, concedes, admits at the last that the writer had it right all along, and the convenience is the tell. A confession that happens to hand the teller the argument is the teller's need doing the writing, not the person. What keeps Hannah honest, and what a writer should learn to keep, is the thing that would not come out. "The great secret of Cousin Hannah's life" stays sealed, skirted, buried by the very people remembering her, and that locked place is the proof that a real person was there at all. A made up surrender always flatters the one who made it. A real person is known by the part that cannot be persuaded to speak.
master-class-character-mr-bonebreaker:
Mr. Bonebreaker: The Life Made From a Flight

← Lorena · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Solomon →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Lorena · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Vera Cartwheel

Lorena was the woman Miss MacIntosh loved. Mr. Bonebreaker was the man she was going to marry, and he is the other thing she meant when she said there had been no man in her life, "or else there was but the sorriest pretense, and that was my tragedy." He is the male half of the buried past that Vera draws out of the nursemaid, a Gospel salesman in Chicago who preached that the true self must stand revealed, and who ran the instant she revealed it.

He found her at the lowest point of her life. She had just come through her first operation, "the loss of her left breast," and was back at work setting pins in a bowling alley while the wound was barely healed, weak, reeling in the street with a murky water settled on her sharp mind. Mr. Bonebreaker "saw her reeling" and judged that "she must be a drunken woman or lost soul, such as he was always looking for." He mistook the devastation of a body for the stagger of a sinner, and closed on her, a salvation salesman working a mark. He put his arm through hers over her resistance, told her there was "little time," to "join now," and swept her along in the rain under his umbrella, quoting scripture, gathering "the stray lamb to the fold." The engagement began in his misreading, and in his hurry to close it.

He was a taker before he was anything else. It was his specialty, the book says, to "poke and pry with his long black umbrella, looking for lost souls in shadowed doorways," and also for "stubs of pencils, key rings, keys," because he had "the habit of taking whatever he found." Souls and pencil-stubs were the same catch to him. He gathered everything and could not tell one thing from another, a lost woman from a lost key. Born in the Ozarks, an umbrella-mender's son whose mother died giving him birth, sallow and stoop-shouldered and beaked, he ran the streets crowing the end of the world, always at hand, always "little time," a doom he sold as pressure and was punctual for year after year while it never came.

Then she gave him the truth, and she gave it to him on his own terms. He had preached, from the Bible, that the wife should stand before her husband "as the inner man revealed." So she obeyed him exactly. She invited him to her room and stepped out from behind a curtain with the wig off and her clothes off, bald and one-breasted, "denuded, shining, bare, but real," her fists clutched over the missing breast as if to ward off a blow. This was the inner self revealed, the thing his own gospel demanded. If he had meant a word of what he preached, if he had felt for her the compassion he claimed to feel for drunkards and murderers, he would have declared that "he would love her in the tomb," that "she was beautiful as snow." He did not. He became "like a crazy, snared bird," groaned, turned, and ran.

His flight is the truest sermon he ever gave. He ran down three flights of stairs and out, bareheaded into the falling hailstones "exactly as if it were, after all, creation's end," so that the apocalypse he had been selling arrived at last, and it was only the end of him. The Bible tracts fell out of his coat as he fled, and when she gathered them off the floor she found them mixed with Chamber of Commerce pamphlets, "See Chicago and live," the mayor sweeping the city clean, the new skyscrapers dwarfing the old, so that his gospel and his boosterism were the same paper, salvation and real estate sold out of one coat. The man who preached the revealed soul could not stay in the room for one revealed body.

He left his umbrella on her bed, and that is what remained of him. It was not even his. He had "plucked this umbrella from a dead man," a scavenger's find, and now he abandoned it a second time, fleeing so hard he forgot it. She kept it. Not to remember him, she said, but "to remind her of herself," and she carried that dead man's black umbrella for the rest of her life, the one she is never without. Her whole surface is built of what her lost loves left behind, the wig she wears in Lorena's black and then in memorial red, and the umbrella of the man who ran, a relic twice abandoned that shelters her still. Grief in this book is a thing kept in the hand.

He is Lorena's exact opposite at the one place that matters. Both of them saw the bald head. Lorena "had known, laughing behind her fan," and the love was not what she left over, and Bonebreaker knew and fled at once. The dancer under the spotlight could hold the bare truth, and the salesman of God could not. The bald, one-breasted body is the real thing under every made surface in the book, and Miss MacIntosh stood forth and offered it, and the measure of the two people who loved her is simply which one stayed in the room.

The connection for a writer is written into the scene, because Bonebreaker preaches the very thing the book asks of everyone and then fails it in front of the reader. His gospel, "the inner man revealed," is witnessing the whole ethic of staying with what is actually there and not looking away. The people who fail in this book are never the ones who suffer. They are the ones who stop paying honest attention, who cannot bear the real when it stands in front of them under a bare electric bulb. Bonebreaker is that failure given a name and a Bible. He collected souls the way he collected pencil-stubs, never seeing a single one, and when a real person finally stood revealed exactly as he had demanded, he became a snared bird and ran into the hail. A writer is asked to be the other kind, the one who does not run when the wig comes off, who stays for the bald head and the missing breast and calls them beautiful as snow because they are real. Lorena stayed and laughed. Bonebreaker fled and left a dead man's umbrella. The book knows the difference, and it never once forgives him for being the salesman who sold the revealed soul and could not look at one.
master-class-13-the-context:
The Context

← The Style · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The American Literary Tradition →

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Vera Cartwheel

A book saturated with history invites the reader to treat its historical material as background, the furniture of period and place against which the real story happens. That is the wrong frame for this novel, and getting it wrong flattens the book. History here is not background. It behaves the way everything behaves in Young's world: it does not stay past. The Great Chicago Fire, the suffrage marches, Emperor Constantine, the Jim Crow South, biblical genealogy, and the colonial map all press into the present of the novel as live weather rather than settled record, layering under the characters' lives and refusing to resolve into fixed fact. The context is not the ground the characters stand on. It is one more thing that will not hold still, and reading it that way is what connects this material to the rest of the book rather than leaving it as an appendix of allusions.

The most useful way to see this is that Young does to history exactly what she does to the dead. In this novel "no great distinction should be made between the living and the dead," and no great distinction is made between the historical past and the lived present either. Both coexist, both intrude, both are carried rather than left behind. Vera is drilled in geography, history, and biblical genealogies not so she will know what is over and done, but because in this book the past is never over and done; the genealogies are living pressure, the weight of who came before bearing directly on who a person is now. History layers rather than recedes, which is why the novel's time is not linear but stacked, memory and event and myth pressing into one another until past and present blur. The historical material is the past doing what the dead do: staying.

American ground, mythic scale

Young's inspiration is fundamentally American and specifically Middle Western, the down-to-earth interior, and her ambition is to give that ordinary material the permanence of myth. Her cast is a gallery of American types, the bus driver, the suffragist, the old maid, the clam-digger, the gambler, and she treats them the way Joyce treated his Dubliners, granting mythic immortality to figures rooted in native soil rather than borrowed from the classical past. This is the book's first act of historical layering: it takes the plain American present and reads it at the scale of epic, so that a drunk bus driver carries the freight of Moses and a small-town waitress carries the freight of the biblical Esther. The folklore is not decoration laid over the realism. It is the claim that ordinary American life is already mythic, already continuous with the deep past, if looked at from the right depth.

The sacred, raised and doubted

Christian material runs through the whole novel, baptism, saints, angels and cherubim, moral lessons drawn from scripture, and it operates the way the historical material does, as living pressure rather than inherited settlement. But the novel does not simply inhabit this framework; it holds it and doubts it at once. The religious imagery is repeatedly set against secular and skeptical views, and figures like the head-hunter, half-civilized and confused about the symbols he handles, turn the sacred inheritance ambiguous rather than certain. This is the same refusal the book performs everywhere else: it raises a system that promises meaning and declines to confirm it, keeping faith and doubt coexistent rather than resolving to either.

The world inside the American book

For a novel so committed to the American interior, its reach is strikingly global, and the reach is concentrated in Cousin Hannah. As a militant suffragist carrying the fight for women's liberation across Arabia, China, and New England, she pulls the world's cultures and the history of feminist activism into the book, and she does it in a way that intersects with colonial and cultural encounter rather than treating those places as scenery. Around her the novel accumulates the Middle East, North Africa, China, multiple languages and customs, so that a cosmopolitan awareness sits inside the regional American frame. This is layering again, geographic rather than temporal: the wide world pressed into the interior American life, the global and the local coexisting in one book the way past and present coexist in one sentence.

Class, decay, and the persistence of the old

The novel keeps setting humble origins against opulent ruin, Miss MacIntosh's shoemaker father and flour-sack underclothes against the richly furnished, empty drawing rooms of the great house, and the contrast is not a static tableau of rich and poor. It is about persistence and decay, tradition outlasting its own usefulness, the old orders surviving into a modernity that no longer has a place for them. The grand houses are opulent and dying at once, which is the book's characteristic doubling worked in social terms: the past's grandeur and the past's ruin held in one frame, neither cancelling the other.

The historical record as live memory

The named events and figures, the Great Chicago Fire, floods and earthquakes and plagues and famines, Constantine and Captain Cook and John L. Sullivan, are not there to date the novel or to display learning. They function as motifs of recurrence, catastrophe repeating across history the way obsession repeats across a life, so that the historical record becomes another instance of the book's deep pattern: things happening again, cycles rather than progress. History, in this treatment, is not a line of settled facts receding behind the present. It is a layered memory, always recurring, always pressing up, indistinguishable in kind from the personal memories that flood the characters.

Race and the pressure of the unresolved

The novel's engagement with race is the point where the past-that-will-not-pass becomes most morally charged, and it belongs to the same logic as everything above. Racial segregation and its ideologies surface through figures like Mr. Bonebreaker; Black railroad porters, the violence Esther Longtree's mixed-race child would face, the wrongful hanging the hangman recalls, the devaluation of Black lives by a white detective who counts only white children's deaths, all press into the novel as unresolved, ongoing injury rather than closed history. The book's expressed hope for an end to colonialism, to empire, to racial strife is precisely a hope, held against a present that has not delivered it. This is history as a live, immediate pressure: an injustice that is not past, that layers under the ordinary American scene the novel keeps insisting is home, and that refuses the consolation of being over.

Set all of this together and the context stops being a list of things the novel contains and becomes a single consistent gesture. Young situates the ordinary American interior at the crossroads of world history, deep myth, sacred inheritance, feminist struggle, and racial reckoning, not to show off range but because her whole vision requires that the past be present, that the far be near, that the historical and the mythic and the personal all coexist in one layered now. The elaborate backdrop is not backdrop. It is the past doing in the wide world what the dead do in the great house by the sea, refusing to leave, pressing on the living, and turning what looked like settled history into one more thing the novel will not let resolve.
master-class-01-introduction-to-the-2nd-:
Introduction to the 2nd edition

Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Wheel That Turns Around Nothing →

Marguerite Young was first and foremost a teacher. She taught High School English. She taught at the famous Iowa Writer’s Workshop. She taught at the New School in New York City. Her teaching career spanned decades and from the students who have shared reminiscences, she was a beloved teacher.

Young was asked in an interview if she would write a book about writing and her response is that she wouldn’t live long enough to do so.

However, we have her magnum opus, Miss MacIntosh, My Darling plus her poetry and two other novels. Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is unique in that it is much longer than her previous writings and once we dive into it just looking at what she did with the novel, there is a cornucopia of literary devices, character development, style and architecture to learn from and analyze.

My hope with this book is that the structure and writing knowledge from an overlooked author who was a master of her craft will get the attention that it deserves.

To read on-going writing about her work for free, visit coralrussell.substack.com

To All My Darlings is the definitive exploration of Marguerite Young's magnum opus Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. Inside this massive volume you will find all the research and resources from 2019 to 2025. It is broken down chapter by chapter including: character list, synopsis, themes, Symbols and Imagery, Important Passages, and Resources.

A Guide to Reading Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is a condensed version of To All My Darlings where each chapter entry covers the characters, what happens, the themes and symbols worth tracking, the passages most worth pausing on, and a section called "For the Curious" that opens outward into context and connection. You can read it alongside the novel, chapter by chapter, or come to it after a section when you need someone to say: yes, that happened, here is what I think it means.

The Wheel and The Spokes provides a chapter by chapter guide that argues what we have been missing is a complete philosophical system, embedded in the novel's form and enacted by its prose. I called it Radical Immanence. Radical Immanence is not merely a literary philosophy. The study shows Young to be a systematic thinker whose work speaks directly to our most pressing questions about consciousness, identity, loss, and what it means to be constituted by what came before us while constituting the ground for what comes after.

What this 2nd edition does is correct and expand the material to reflect what this reader believes Young was doing within her novel.
master-class-05-dialectics-and-the-refus:
Dialectics and the Refusal of Synthesis

← The Plot · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Paradox →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

Dialectic, in its origins, names a dialogue between people holding opposing views who reason their way toward a shared truth. It resembles debate but excludes emotional appeal and rhetoric; its aim is arrival. The concept begins in ancient philosophy and develops through the Middle Ages. Hegel refigured it so that it no longer meant a literal dialogue but a process: the development of an idea by way of overcoming its own internal contradictions, thesis and antithesis resolving into synthesis. Marx and Engels adapted this Hegelian dialectic into dialectical materialism, a theory of history driven by material contradiction toward resolution.

What is essential to every version of the dialectic is that it moves. Contradiction is a stage, not a destination; the opposites are overcome, and the movement produces something new. This is exactly what Miss MacIntosh, My Darling withholds. The novel is saturated with opposition, but it does not resolve its oppositions into any synthesis. It holds them in suspension, blurs the line between them, and repeatedly suggests they are not two things at all but one thing seen from two sides. The novel invokes the machinery of the dialectic and then refuses the arrival the dialectic was built to reach. That refusal is not a failure of the form. It is the novel's argument: that the human situation is one of permanent, unresolved contradictions, and that the honest response is to inhabit the contradictions rather than to escape it into synthesis.

The novel says so directly. Of the living and the dead it observes that "no great distinction should be made between the living and the dead, the same cruel winds blowing through both worlds at once." Characters are described as "both living and dead" without contradiction. The opposites do not fight toward resolution; they coexist. What follows are the principal oppositions the novel sustains in this unresolved way.

Reality and Illusion. This is the most pervasive of them, and the words themselves press against each other throughout the book: reality and illusion recur constantly, and the word dream appears nearly fifteen hundred times. The novel questions the nature of the real, suggesting that what looks solid may be illusion and what looks illusory may hold the deeper truth. Catherine's opium world, dismissed as unreal, is more densely populated and in some ways more honest than Miss MacIntosh's flat certainties. The novel does not decide between them. It holds both.

Life and Death. Life and death are not mutually exclusive states in the novel but intertwined, coexistent, and at times reversible. The dead attend Catherine's bedside as freely as the living. Mr. Spitzer lives inside his dead brother's memory, wearing one watch for the living and one for the dead. The boundary is porous by design, and the novel treats crossing it as ordinary rather than exceptional.

Order and Chaos. The narrative sets the human impulse to impose order and meaning against a fundamentally disordered existence. Miss MacIntosh is the novel's great bearer of order, insisting on facts and schedules and the straight line between two points; Mr. Spitzer measures his paces and plans his steps. The order they build never holds against the chaos it is meant to contain. The novel's own structure enacts this tension: shifting perspectives, non-linear time, and associative logic that can feel chaotic, which is among the most discussed features of the book.

Unity and Division. Characters are fragmented, doubled, and uncertain of where they end and another begins. The clearest case is Mr. Spitzer and his twin, whose identities trade places until neither can be finally located; the novel's late confession, that the surviving brother is Peron and the dead one Joachim, does not settle the question so much as dissolve it. This category absorbs what might be called the opposition of male and female, since the novel's blurring of gendered identity, Miss MacIntosh's baldness and mastectomy, Mr. Spitzer imagined as Penelope rather than Ulysses, Cousin Hannah's mannish bearing, is one expression of the larger instability of the divided self rather than a separate dialectic.

Silence and Sound. Communication in the novel fails, distorts, or takes unconventional forms, and silence is made to carry as much meaning as speech, sometimes more. The book is unusually dense with deafness and muteness, and its final image of love is Vera's marriage to a stone deaf man whose "musical voice" rolls through a silence he cannot hear her cross. Mr. Spitzer composes music no living ear will hear. Here the opposition is most fully collapsed: sound becomes a kind of silence, and silence becomes the medium of the deepest expression.

Known and Unknown. The narrative privileges mystery and the unknowable, and repeatedly suggests that the attempt to define or fully understand leads not to clarity but to further confusion. The characters who insist most firmly on certainty, Miss MacIntosh above all, are the ones the novel most thoroughly undoes.

Across all of these, the constant shifting and blurring produce the novel's dreamlike, unsettling, and profoundly philosophical atmosphere. The characters' lives are defined by their attempts to navigate, understand, or escape these contradictions, and the novel leaves open the question of whether any of them ever do. What it does not leave open is its method. Young does not resolve the oppositions she raises. She sustains them, which is why the dialectical tradition, with its promise of synthesis, describes the novel's materials better than it describes the novel's aim. The book keeps the tension and declines the resolution, and asks the reader to live there with it.
master-class-character-the-little-toy-sa:
The Little Toy Salesman: The Lone Survivor Who Tipped His Hat

← The Chicago Detective · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Esther Longtree's Parents →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Esther Longtree · Mr. Weed · The Chicago Detective

Of all the salesmen who passed through Esther Longtree's counter, she chose this one to be "the legal father" of the child she was carrying, and he is the strangest choice in the chapter, because he is not a father and not even a man, but an old baby. The little toy salesman "drank his milk from a baby bottle, and she had to wipe his chin." He "could not tie his own shoe-laces." He is bandy-legged, pot-bellied, goggle-eyed, "in his second childhood or his first," who could tell, wearing "a dead rosebud in his coat lapel and a black mourning band around his sleeve" for a dead mother, and he sells "toys to bereaved parents." He never had a childhood, was "always put to sleep in a dresser drawer or in a dark, cold place," and wants now only "the inside of a good woman," a home, to be rocked to sleep in her arms. He is the perpetual infant, the man who never got born into a life, and Esther, mother of the unborn, takes him for a husband.

He is also, like so many in this book, a man who does not see the woman in front of him. He "did not see her, so obvious, the stain of milk, her swelling breasts," and did not notice she was always pregnant. He came in "quack-quacking with his duck-billed mouth," blowing a tin horn, bouncing a rubber ball, and looked straight past the enormous fact of her. He is another of the book's anti-witnesses, in the softest and most pitiable key, too lost in his own infancy to register anyone else's grief.

And then the thing that makes him unforgivable. The little toy salesman is a murderer, and his murder is that he lived. He was the sole survivor of a shipwreck. In a great storm at sea "all others had drowned, the captain, the crew, the women, the children," and he alone "had been saved," floating "safe in a rubber life boat, gently rocking in the vasty deep, tipping his straw hat to women and children whose faces and hands crowded the sea." He offered his seat to no one. "He had not known how to save anyone, not even a pregnant woman, not even a dove." He is "the lone eye witness," the one who saw the whole catastrophe and could act on none of it, who tipped his hat, smiling, "to those who passed by, for they were far away, and he was safe."

This is the deepest cut of the philosophy the book keeps testing, the demand that a person stay in the room with what is actually there and not look away. The little toy salesman witnessed the drowning of the world and looked past it. He would have "looked beyond" Esther even in the lifeboat. His survival is itself the not-looking, the hat tipped to the dying as they went down. Esther's verdict comes in two beats, and both are true. First, she cannot forgive him "that he had not drowned with the others." Second, and finally, "he should be pitied that he lived." The man who survived by not seeing is both the guilty one and the most piteous, "a cold pigeon," an old baby who lost his tear ducts in the desert and his taste and his reason in the storm and cannot even weep for what he failed to save.

The turn for a writer is one of the hardest in the whole set, because the little toy salesman is the maker who survives his own material. He is the one who floats safe in the boat while the people go down, who witnesses the entire storm and renders it so vividly that "she could imagine it, the tumult of earth and heaven," and saved no one, offered his seat to no one, tipped his hat as the faces passed. He makes small consoling objects, "toys to bereaved parents," which is a fair description of a certain kind of art, the little comfort sold to the grieving. And he does not see the living woman across the counter because he is too busy being his own wound. Set him beside Mr. Weed, who reduces the living to weights, and beside the Chicago detective, who sees a corpse where a woman is sleeping. The toy salesman is the survivor whose survival is the crime, the witness whose witnessing saved nobody, the writer safe in his rubber boat among the drowned. The book gives him Esther's double sentence and lets it stand: he cannot be forgiven that he lived, and he must be pitied that he lived, and there is no third thing to say.
master-class-character-esther-longtree:
Esther Longtree: The Grief That Would Not Deliver

← Lisa Lunde · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Rosemary Longtree →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Esther Longtree · Mr. Weed · Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel

She is the waitress in the desolate Indiana town where Vera comes to rest in the first cold of spring, in a lunchroom called the Greasy Spoon whose window is dressed with "a large spoon, a small coffin, and pots of elephant ears." The place smells "more like a grave than a restaurant," and "a grave, it surely was," because Esther Longtree carries her dead with her wherever she goes, and she has a great many. She is the town's one perpetual event, "known for her everlasting pregnancy and her loving heart which knew no lover and her everlasting loneliness." She is always about to give birth, this month and every month, and she never does, or rather she always does and it is always nothing, and she begins again. She is the sentence in this book that will not end, walking on a deformed foot behind a long counter, immense, swelling, braying softly to the child inside her, forever.

She is unforgettably alive, which is the first one of the novel. In a room full of "pale, wavering figures like ghosts of customers," "who could have been more robustly alive than she," with "vitality breathed in her," her black hair loose and free, her cupid's-bow mouth smiling "from jug ear to jug ear," slapping the blood back into her own red hands. And she is set against the grey mule standing in harness outside, "that being from which no mortal issue comes," stopped "at the dead-end of creation." That is her, and the book means it exactly. The most fiercely living woman in the town is the one who brings nothing to term, who conceives everlastingly and delivers only "an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb, nothing." Her aliveness and her barrenness are the same fact seen twice.

She is grief made into a body. The philosophy this book keeps testing says grief does not process and resolve, that "it accumulates," that "you carry it," and Esther Longtree is that sentence taken past metaphor into flesh. Every loss adds to the last. She never empties out. Her children are "as many as the autumn leaves where no spring ever was, the snowflakes," and she has "dropped them," she says, "everywhere," under the leaves and the snow and in the rivers, and she is the only one who ever mourned them: "none had any funerals or mourners but me." So she still carries them. They come back to tease her and ask who their father was. She keeps their toys, buries their layettes in long white boxes under the persimmon and the peach, and knits a little black suit for the one who will live. She is everlastingly pregnant because she has never once been allowed to finish. The body that will not deliver is the grief that will not close.

And she is the sole witness of the unmade. This is where she stops being only pitiable and becomes something the book honors. The figures who fail in its moral world are the ones who look away, who will not stay in the room with what is actually there. Esther Longtree never looks away from a single loss. She keeps vigil over what never quite came into being, the unformed thing with "no ears and no eyes," and she will not let it go unmourned. When Vera, who came here as "the mourner," orders "seven cups" of coffee, Esther sets out seven white cups "for seven skulls but no coffee for them, the little bird bones." She is the one who counts the uncounted, who lays a place for what has no place, who says to the stillborn what no one said to them. In a book terrified of the imagined thing that leaves a real body, she is the woman who gathers every such body up and carries it and calls it hers.

The cost is that she can no longer find the seam between herself and what she has lost. Her own voice comes back to her as a child's crying for water, "her own voice interrupting her voice." She nurses her clenched right fist "as if her right hand were a new-born baby's head." She keeps lovebirds so their noise will cover the crying only she can hear. The old doctor tells her there is "no form within the form," that "it was a cloud," that she is "the immortal medical case and baffling," and that "there is something about all of us that is unrealized." She is the marginal figure the book keeps pointing to, the one who fits no category and so reveals that the categories were built. There is "nothing about her case in the law books," no name for a woman who is mother and barren at once, pregnant with the snowflakes, "brilliant but dumb." When she imagines the jury of townswomen who will accuse her, the book notes that they are "her pale reflection." She frightens them because she carries in the open what they carry hidden. The worst thing they could say, the one accusation she "could not bear," is not that she killed her children but "that her children were never born and were never conceived." The novel refuses to settle it. She has borne "as many as the stars in the sky," and she has borne no one, and both are held at once, without one being allowed to win.

This is why her one refrain is a question with no floor under it. "Who killed cock robin?" she asks, and answers, "Nobody... All people killed him," he was "killed by the death that was in him from the time of his birth." She has understood the thing the whole book has been circling, that there is "something stillborn in every stream, in every flood, in every rose," that no one is "guiltless of this guilt," that every birth already carries its death. She universalizes the stillborn the way Mrs. Hogden universalized the private dream, and it makes her, too, unbearable, because she is right.

The turn for a writer is the tenderest and hardest in the set, because Esther Longtree is the maker who cannot keep what she makes. Every writer knows her as the thing carried for months that comes out unformed, the book that will not come to term, the figure conceived with the whole heart that arrives as "an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a cobweb, nothing." She is the grief of everything that did not make it, buried and mourned and never let go, and she is the stubbornness that conceives again the next morning. She keeps the vigil no one else keeps, for the unwritten, the abandoned, the stillborn draft, and she alone lays a place for them. Late in her chapters she has passed into the purest form of the work, "knitting without needles or thread," no longer unraveling anything, making for the sake of making with the product long since given up. Set her beside Mr. Weed, who reduces the living to weights, and beside Mrs. Hogden, who dreams other people's lives out loud, and Esther is the third face of the same craft, the one who brings forth and loses and brings forth again and carries every loss in her body as bulk. She is the book's own self-portrait, a thing everlastingly pregnant, a sentence that will not end, and the novel does not rescue her, does not deliver her, does not let cock robin be born. It lets her stand in the beam of yellow light with her hand on her heart, having hope. The sentence hasn't ended. The last sentence of the novel belongs to her and it is that she will go down again and then, after a spell, she will be back.
master-class-character-mr-res-tacamah:
Mr. Res Tacamah: The Author Who Was a Bottle

← The Sea-House Servants · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Mr. Chandelier →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Lisa Lunde · Mr. Chandelier · Mr. Res Tacamah · Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel

He is a drug bottle. In the sealed house by the sea, Vera's mother, the great recluse, holds crowded imaginary evenings, and among her guests is "Mr. Res Tacamah, the drug bottle with ears to hear her ravings, her commands." He is "my mother's only permanent companion," the one who is always there when the fickle others come and go, and the book gives him the most unnerving job description in the whole household: he is "the author of so many fantasies." The bottle that produces the visions is named as the maker of them, promoted from object to gentleman, given ears to listen and a hand in every dream, "any number of forms shifting and merging into each other."

This is the mother's whole method, the constructing of reality by naming, carried to its purest point. She turns her furniture into company. A light fixture becomes a suitor; a medicine bottle becomes a man of letters. And the book, which keeps insisting that language is where the real gets built, lets her be right in her mad way, because Res Tacamah does have an existence once she has named him. He is talked about, waited for, given errands, and years later, in the Mrs. Hogden episode, he is still expected, "the delightful gentleman who intended" to share the arithmetic lessons, until Lisa Lunde shatters him at one blow with the flat true word: "Res Tacamah is nothing but a drug bottle." She is correct, and she has seen nothing, because the point about Res Tacamah is that he is a drug bottle and a permanent companion and the author of the fantasies, all at once, and the flat true word about the bottle misses the man the naming made.

He is, most quietly and most terribly, the figure who can never be met. Vera is told to find out for herself "why it was that he could never meet her." He is forever on an errand toward an inheritance that is not there, a companion with big ears who hears everything and is no one, a gentleman with no face behind the label. He is the source of the mother's whole dreamed world, and there is nothing there to shake hands with.

The turn for a writer is the most unsettling self-portrait in the set. Res Tacamah is the drug bottle named "the author of so many fantasies," which is to say he is the machinery of invention itself, personified and empty, the thing that produces the visions and takes the credit and cannot be met because there is no one there, only the substance and the naming. He has ears to hear every raving and no self behind them.

He is a life spent making fantasies. The writer's Res Tacamah is the suspicion that the author is a bottle, that the maker of the dream world is only the mechanism of the dream, big-eared and faceless, permanently present and impossible to meet. The book sets him beside Mr. Chandelier and lets the mother love them both, the fickle light and the faithful bottle, and does not tell us they are less real than the people, because it has spent its whole length refusing to say that the dreamed is less real than the true.
master-class-08-characters-as-representa:
Characters as Representations: Names as Broken Promises

← Lucie Bell · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Setting →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Moses Hunnecker

Marguerite Young used to call out to famous but dead literary figures in her classroom, Edgar Allan Poe, Henry James, William James, welcoming them in and offering them a seat, addressing them as if they had walked through the door. From students' accounts the habit entertained and enlivened the room.

The section that follows takes a liberty with that vignette and tries the same relationship on the characters in the novel. These are speculations, but they point to something a writer can use. Young does not name a character after a famous figure to flatter the comparison. She does it to make a promise she intends to break. The borrowed name raises an expectation in the reader of the prophet, empress, savior, and then the character is built to defeat it. The allusion is not a resemblance. It is a load the novel places on a familiar shape so it can show the shape failing to hold.

These three comparisons work, and they work because in each one the text itself plants the name as a flag and then labors against it. The reader carries the borrowed figure into the chapter and watches Young dismantle it. That is the craft lesson: a name can function as a controlled subversion, a way of summoning a whole set of expectations in one word so the character can spend the book refusing them.

Moses Hunnecker and the biblical Moses

The bus driver's name is the plainest flag in the novel, and the book makes the connection explicit by mentioning Moses leading the Israelites. Both figures lead a group on a journey across a wilderness. There the promise ends and the inversion begins.

The biblical Moses is a prophet with a clear vision, receiving divine messages and leading his people toward a promised land, delivering the law, moving in a straight line toward freedom. Moses Hunnecker leads toward "the jumping-off place," a place "where creation stops." His vision is fueled by whiskey and personal folklore, his pronouncements rambling and hard to read for any clear direction. He is a self-proclaimed prophet whose prophecies arrive drunk. Where the biblical Moses delivers the law, the driver disregards it, driving erratically and drinking openly. Where the biblical Moses leads out of slavery toward a new beginning, this Moses ferries his passengers toward an end.

Every point of the comparison is a reversal. The name promises a guide to the promised land and delivers a guide to the end of things. Young summons the most familiar deliverer in the culture precisely so she can invert his direction, and the reader feels the inversion because the name did the setup work before a single chapter unfolded.

Catherine Cartwheel and Catherine the Great

This is the strongest of the three because the novel does not merely hint at the name, it has Catherine become Catherine the Great outright, sleeping in a bed with pillars of twisted amethyst. Young plants the flag inside the text and in the character's own imagination.

Both Catherines are figures of influence who reject the limits of the ordinary world, and both exercise control over their environments. But the empress wielded political power to shape Russia, engaging with the world to expand and modernize it. Catherine Cartwheel wields power only over her own reality, retreating from the "brutal world" into an "opium paradise" of dreams and phantoms, "oblivious to the realities of flesh and blood." Her bedroom is "filled with visitors as the Grand Central Station," a court of the dead and the imagined rather than a court of state.

The inversion is the direction of the power. The empress pushed outward to remake a world. Catherine Cartwheel withdraws inward to build one. The name promises worldly command and delivers total retreat, and the comparison holds because Young herself put the empress in Catherine's head, then showed the throne to be a bed she never leaves.

Esther Longtree and the biblical Esther

Both characters carry the name that means "star" in Persian, and the name hints at radiance and significance. Both carry heavy burdens and endure. There the promise breaks.

The biblical Esther has a clear purpose and achieves it: a queen who uses her position and her rhetoric to save her people from destruction, decisive and successful, ascending to power and influence. Esther Longtree has no such purpose and no such ascent. She remains on the margins, a "dumb, brilliant waitress" defined by poverty and isolation, driven by a formless desire for connection she never satisfies. The biblical Esther's sexuality is bound to her royal duty and the saving of a nation. Esther Longtree's is a source of shame and endless ill-fated pregnancy. The biblical Esther has a clear vision; Esther Longtree's is clouded, and she is never sure what she sees. One saves a people. The other saves no one, herself least of all.

The name promises the star who intercedes and delivers a woman who cannot deliver at all. The subversion is the whole point of the borrowing: Young takes the culture's model of the woman whose action redeems her people and builds against it a woman to whom things simply happen, so that the shining name falls on someone the world refuses to see.

For a writer the lesson is when a character has a famous name then the reader is handed an entire set of expectations for free. The interesting work is not honoring them. It is breaking them, on the page, where the reader can feel the promise give way.
master-class-character-mrs-hogden:
Mrs. Hogden: The Woman Who Dreamed Our Dreams Out Loud

← Friday · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Lisa Lunde →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Lisa Lunde · Mr. Weed · Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel

She arrives during Vera's absence, "a faceless woman, a Mrs. Hogden who, though I never saw her, implored my attention." Vera never lays eyes on her. The whole of Mrs. Hogden is assembled from what the servants and Lisa Lunde reported, a phantom pieced together at a distance, and yet she is the most solidly bodied thing in the chapter, "fat, corporeal, moon-eyed," waddling into the hallway under a smashed hat and a wilted ostrich feather, wearing four coats of graduated sizes and carrying every object she owns on her person, an empty bird cage, a fluted teapot, a tape measure around her neck, Javanese temple bells, cardboard boxes tied with string, until she looks "more like a Christmas tree than a human being." She has come to teach arithmetic to a mad woman, two and two making four, forever. She has sold her home and brought her own wet mattress. She was hired for the rest of her natural life "but no longer," and the terms of the job, which delight her, include "a salary, a funeral." She is a woman who has bought a place to die and finds it wonderful.

Her name will not hold still. Hogden, Logden, Fogden, Bogden, Dogden. "Mrs. Hogden or Mrs. Logden? Nobody knew which it was, as nobody thought to ask." She is the teacher who might be a shoplifter, the servant who acts as mistress, the guest who was perhaps invited and perhaps not, alive and yet sleeping "the sleep which seemed like death." Lisa Lunde, whose whole pride is filing people at a glance, cannot file her: she is "hard to classify," "something that evaded definition," "too complex, too separate a person." She is exactly the figure the book keeps pointing to, the one who stands at the edge of every category and makes the seams show. Where a person fits, the category looks natural. Where Mrs. Hogden stands, smiling, unbudgeable, wearing a name that changes by the sentence, it becomes plain that the categories were invented and that she was never going to fit one.

She is the great yes-sayer of the house. Everything pleases her, "immeasurably." Nothing surprises her. She walks in already knowing the place, recognizing the nude javelin-thrower at the gate and the shivering cherub, certain she has dreamed all of it before, sure of "every nook, every cranny, almost every cranny." She finds the desolate, black-curtained, fog-swept house "simply divine." She smiles at an assassination on the radio exactly as she smiles at a garden party, because to her they weigh the same. The philosophy the book keeps testing has its own sense of the sacred, "full attention to the actual world, which turns out to be more than enough," and Mrs. Hogden is the counterfeit of it, the smiling opposite. She finds everything holy by finding everything the same. Her bliss is not attention but its absence. She stands in the moonlit playroom "seeing nothing," or perhaps "seeing everything at a glance," and no one can tell which, because for her there is no difference. "Perhaps she was only amazed that she was not amazed."

Then the offense, which is the real center of her. She knows things she could not know. She knows the head of Alcibiades is in the drainpipe, she knows about James and the whale in the bedroom and the droves of whales dying on the beach, details "which only my mother could have divulged." She was hired to "reflect my mother's every mood," and she does more than reflect it. She dreams it. She takes to bed as a "rival invalid," "the ugly aspect of beauty," and she lies there "dreaming our dreams out loud as if they were hers instead of ours." This is what cannot be forgiven. Each person in this book guards a singular dream, an eccentric grief, one private thing held in "utter silence," and Mrs. Hogden speaks all of it aloud in her fevered, smiling voice as if it were common stock. "She made us vulgar in our own eyes." "Everything rare and individual and hidden became the commonplace." The thing each person prided as "most eccentric" to the self "should suddenly become universalized," and the horror of it is not that she lies but that she is somehow right.

Here she becomes the book's own argument, standing up and waddling around. She is a phantom Vera never saw, and she falls across the soul all the same. She is imagined and she eats real food, occupies the house parasitically, steals a real object, leaves real whiskey bottles and apple cores behind on her island of boxes. She is "the thing which is real and more horrible than anything imaginable," "a mare sticking its head in through the window luring a nightmare." The whole novel insists that the dreamed does not stay in the dream, that a stranger can be given a whole life, that what is made in the mind leaves a body, and Mrs. Hogden is that insistence in a purple lace dress. Vera, who never met her, will not let her go: "how can we confine our life to our actual life? Mrs. Hogden is important to me for her own sake." The woman who was only "a substitute, after all, for the dream life I wanted" turns out to be no less real for being dreamed, and Vera knows it, and says so: "She was my mind's betrayal of my mind."

And under all of it, she is unbearably alone. Of everything in that overloaded house she steals one thing, "an ivory-handed back-scratcher," "an ivory hand at the end of a purple stick," "something she had needed, something she had missed before." It is the perfect object for her, the hand that touches when no other hand will, the companionship of "the right hand loving the left." She sits for hours under the gargoyles scratching her own back among the dead flies, smiling. "I did not have a friend in the world until now," she says into a dark mirror that shows only "the warped ghost of her face." She leaves the playroom door open, the servants think, "because she had wanted somebody to see her, welcome her, but she had remained ignored and unwanted." The woman who is full of everyone's dreams is no one in particular, and the price of being no one in particular is that no one comes. She bought a place to die and no one caught her name. Mr. Spitzer, asked it, only answered, "What's in a name?"

The turn for a writer is the one that should be hardest to admit, because Mrs. Hogden is the writer, undisguised. She is the uninvited woman who arrives in the abandoned playroom of the mind and somehow knows the most private dream of every person in the house, who moves in, eats the food, reflects every mood, and dreams the family's dreams back at them out loud until they no longer recognize them as their own. That is the whole trade. The writer takes the grief each person held in silence, the eccentric hidden thing, and universalizes it, speaks it aloud as common stock, and makes them vulgar in their own eyes. It is theft and it is mercy and it is impossible to tell which. She is nearly a god of the little world, knowing almost everything in it, and she is drunk and fallible and missing exactly one fact, the "one small, warped flower growing" "outside the consciousness of God," "the crucial flower," which is the writer's true condition, to know almost the whole of the made world and never quite all of it. Set her beside Mr. Weed, who reduces people to weights and never sees them, and beside Lisa Lunde, who sees through people and never sees them either. Mrs. Hogden does the opposite and it costs more: she sees everyone so completely that she dreams them out loud, and it makes her a parasite, and a medium, and the loneliest figure in the book. The novel lets her ride off into the mist in her ostrich feather, name uncaught, playroom door standing open behind her, and it does not decide whether she was a thief or a teacher or a ghost, because she was, of course, every one of them at once.
master-class-character-homer-capehorn:
Homer Capehorn: The Champion of a Finished Season

← Madge Capehorn Edwards · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · Jacqueline / Jackie White →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Homer Capehorn · Jacqueline White · Justice O’Leary · Madge Capehorn

He is asleep the whole time. He never wakes, never speaks a waking word, and everything known about him is either dreamed by him or dreamed onto him because he is a man whose whole life has already happened, who is present now only as deep sleep and old glory.

Homer Capehorn, once the captain of the football team, the all-star athlete, the champion carried off the field on his teammates' shoulders, and now a faded figure sleeping his deep sleep on a bus beside a pregnant wife he does not notice, in a football sweater gone to rags with a red-stained letter across the front. Madge, awake and bitter beside him, calls him a human football, always out kicking an old ball on the practice fields of his dreams. The crowds that once roared for him have long gone home. The teammates who carried him are the dead crew now, a team of which he is the only living member, a season that exists only inside his sleep. And in that sleep he calls a name that is not his wife's. Jacqueline. Jacqueline White, the girl cheerleader who cheered when he was captain, the best girl athlete he ever knew, the ice-skater who could skate like a comet, and who at this very hour is breathing her last, or is already being carried up the hill by her pallbearers to her grave.

Radical Immanence holds that the past does not go away, that the dead go on living inside the present and shaping it. Homer is that idea worn as a whole man. The question the book asks through him is not why he sleeps, but what becomes of a person whose life is entirely behind him, whose only real season is a finished one. The answer is that he does not live in the present at all. He lives in the game that ended and the love that never started, and the two together have swallowed everything a present might have held.

His glory is complete and gone, and he cannot leave it. He is the all-star athlete of the past, and the word past has eaten the rest of him. He kicked the ball clear over the stars once, because Jacqueline was cheering, and he has been kicking at that same vanished ball ever since, on practice fields that exist only in his dreams, always the wrong ball, never any goal. A man can be finished while his heart still beats, and Homer is the plainest case in the book: carried forever on the shoulders of a dead crew, captain of a team with no other living member, replaying a season the world stopped watching years ago.

The reason the past will not release him is that the one thing at the center of it was never spoken. He loved Jacqueline and was too shy to say it, was helpless in his love and never once put it into words. No one ever read Jacqueline's mind, and he never let her read his. An unspoken love is the one kind that cannot end, because it had never begun, never answered, never refused, never lived out and used up. It stays open forever, a door no one walked through, and it surfaces now only the way such things surface, as a name cried out in sleep to a woman who is dying and who scarcely remembers him. What Homer never said is exactly what will not pass. The silence that failed him at the one moment that mattered fixed the love in amber, and a love in amber does not age or die. It only waits, in the dark under the deep sleep, and speaks the one word it knows.

He keeps Jacqueline alive by refusing to believe she can truly die. He believes in the best and not the worst, believes in immortality, insists that what he loved was never the body but something the grave cannot reach. Where Madge, bitter at his side, says the bridegroom is the skeleton, that death is the plain end of the flesh, Homer holds the opposite, that the flesh is nothing and the essence goes on. His faith is not wisdom. It is the same refusal to let the dead be gone that runs through the whole book, through Spitzer's cheroots and Catherine's imaginary guests and O'Leary's ghost sister, and Homer performs it in the simplest, most trusting form of all, a boy's belief that the girl he never won is somewhere still skating, that no one he loved is ever really lost. The book neither mocks the belief nor confirms it. It lays the belief down beside Madge's bitterness and lets the reader feel that both are ways of standing the same unbearable fact, that the ones a person loves go into the ground.

Homer and Madge are another example of exact opposites, like Spitzer and Catherine. Madge is all bitter surface and body and the single lurching present moment, unable to escape her own flesh. Homer is all faith and dream and a finished past, never once inside his present. She is awake and raging; he is asleep and serene. Between them they chart the two ways of missing the here-and-now that the whole long bus journey is trying to reach, the one trapped in the body's instant with no future ahead of it, the other gone off into a season that is over. The sleeping couple on the bus, built out of two strangers' faces, turn out to be a small double portrait of the very split the novel is built on.

The lesson for a writer is in how much can be carried by a character who never wakes. Homer speaks not one waking word and performs not one waking act, and he is a complete and moving man all the same, because a person can be built entirely out of what lies behind him and what he could not bring himself to say. Grief for a dead love, glory that has ended, a sentence never spoken: these are not the leftovers of a life. They are a life, and a writer who understands that can make a whole human being out of a man asleep in a bus seat with a name on his lips. Homer is finished before the book begins, and the book loses nothing by it, because here the finished and the unspoken are not the absence of a story. They are the story.
master-class-character-the-tavern-landlo:
The Tavern Landlord: The Life Made From Its Own Telling

← Jacqueline / Jackie White · Teaching a Writing Masterclass · The Tavern Landlady →

Spoiler note: This portrait is written for readers who have finished the novel. It discusses the character’s whole story, including how it ends.

Characters: Homer Capehorn · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Mr. Weed · Vera Cartwheel

The landlord is the man at the door of the whole book. The Tavern is where the bus stops, the hotel where Madge and Homer and Moses and Vera and Mr. Weed all come to rest, and it is the landlord who signs them in, carries the trunks, and hands out the rooms. He is the only figure in the set whose main work is not being made by someone else. His work is telling, and what he tells first and last and always is himself.

He is a former sailor now keeping a hotel, bald, ruddy, deaf in one ear or pretending to be, standing behind his counter in "suppressed power." His whole biography is written on his skin, "hearts and darts and one lonely anchor," a battleship behind the hairs of his chest with "Remember the Marne" under it, a woman's face in his palm that winks when he closes his hand. He wears where he has been the way Madge wore her painted sailboats and skiers, a man turned into a surface of the world he claims to have crossed. And the claim is enormous. He was a candy merchant at ten, a magician who plucked cards off people's sleeves, a soldier, a hunter, a man in Intelligence, a killer of a little black man who had swallowed a diamond. "There is no country I have not seen," he says, "except America," and "there seemed to be nothing he had not experienced." The life is plainly a tall tale, and he tells it, the book notes, "as if he were talking to himself."

What holds the tale together is that he has already survived his own death, several times. He went down on four ships, the Titanic and the Lusitania among them, and was "written up as missing in many a shipwreck," so that he stands at his counter, in his own phrase, "unofficially alive." His mother had told him he was "born to drown, not to hang," and he believes it still, waiting for the sea to finish a job it has four times failed at. He is a man narrating himself out of the graves he was reported into, which is only what everyone in this book does, except that he does it about himself, cheerfully, to a stranger, while carrying her luggage.

His trade is knots, and the trade makes him the exact opposite number of the guest signing in beside him. The other guest is a hangman, and where the hangman ties the knot that ends a man, the landlord ties "lovers' knots, knots which none shall untie until Gabriel blows his horn." He has spliced many a couple into the one knot he swears "cannot be untied," the marital knot, binding them so that "even after death should not part them." The hangman, gloomy, corrects him, "the marital knot can always be untied," which is just what the hangman is there to do. Between the two of them the whole business of the book is laid out at the front desk, one man binding people together past death and the other cutting them loose, and the reader is left to notice that these are the same rope.

Then the landlord does the thing that marks him as the book's own kind of maker. He tells Vera that the talkative, confessing hangman was not the hangman at all. The real hangman is a close-mouthed, respectable dairy farmer who ties the knot only because, as the landlord puts it, "he got paid to tie it." The one who rambled and confessed was "the hangman's shadow, who got loose after every hanging and said the things the hangman never would have said." So the landlord splits a single man into two, the silent farmer and the loosed shadow, and then, carrying the trunk up the stairs, he closes the split back up, because "as if in ocean depths, the two were one." He is a plain working man who casually performs the book's whole doctrine of the divided self, and he does it as a favor, to explain the noise from the next room.

He cannot keep persons and things and names apart, and does not try. Asked about a rustling, he says it is thirty chained turkey buzzards, then that they are canaries big as buzzards, then that they belong to an old woman, then, tapping a wardrobe trunk, "Tillie," a very young girl who will knit a baby hood, and it turns out he means one person by all of it, or none. Asked who Imadaisy is, he confesses, "Nobody." He puts Vera in a room called the Fire Escape and explains it by the bridal suite being taken by a young couple, the same explanation, word for word, he had already given to the hangman's shadow. Names, guests, rooms, buzzards, canaries, girls, nobodies, they run together in his mouth like water, and he hands them out with total confidence, because at his desk the difference between a real guest and an invented one has stopped meaning anything.

The landlord is not haunted the way the mother is, or grieving the way Miss MacIntosh is. He is cheerful, loud, and completely untroubled by the fact that his life will not bear checking, that his hangman has two bodies, that his guests may be nobodies. He is the one person in the book who has made peace with living inside a story, and he keeps the door of the place where all the other stories arrive.

The connection for a writer is the plainest in the book, which is why it comes at the threshold. Among his many trades the landlord names the truest one, ventriloquist, the man who threw his voice into empty rocking chairs, who "made the coffee cups speak with human voices" and "made birds twitter where there were no birds." That is the novel describing itself. Everything in these pages is a coffee cup made to speak and a bird made to sing where there was no bird, a sleeping stranger given a marriage, a cried name given a death, an absent chauffeur given a rap sheet, a faceless coachman given a whole conscience to steer. Young puts her method in the mouth of a bald, deaf, shipwrecked hotel-keeper because the method has no dignity to protect and needs none. A writer is a person who narrates a self that will not bear checking, who ties the living to the dead in knots meant never to come undone, who splits one person into a man and his shadow and then swears the two are one, and who stands at the door of a house where the real guests and the made-up ones sign the same register and are shown to their rooms with equal care. The landlord does all of it for a living and sleeps fine. The honest writer, this book suggests, could do worse than to be him, untroubled at the threshold, generous with the rooms, telling the tale as if talking to himself, and never once pretending that the guests he invented are worth less than the ones who walked in off the bus.

Characters: Mr. Chandelier

He hangs from the ceiling of the mother's sealed room, and in "some slow moment of awakening" she looks up and sees that "the chandelier was Mr. Chandelier, her companion, not always faithful." He is a light fixture made a lover, "with seven lighted candles in his seven crystal hands," "with his seven bent flames lighting, to its four corners, a dark, empty heaven." He is the beautiful one among the mother's imaginary guests, all prisms and reflected fire, and the single word she attaches to him tells his whole character: unfaithful. The light that comes and goes, that flares and dims, that will not stay, she has understood as a fickle companion, and she loves him anyway.

He is the constructed reality at its most gorgeous, the ordinary object charged past bearing with significance. A chandelier is glass and candle and borrowed flame, and the mother has made of it a seven-handed being lighting the void, a suitor with prisms for a face. The philosophy this book keeps testing has a sense of the sacred that points not upward to heaven but deeper into the ordinary thing, and Mr. Chandelier is that exactly, an everyday fixture becomes a small radiant god who lights "a dark, empty heaven" from inside the room. The mother asks "no further verification" than that he shines. His reality is his light, and his light is real while it lasts.

But he is "not always faithful," and that is the truth of him. He is the vision that will not stay, the beauty that flares and goes dark, the companion made of flame that cannot promise to keep burning. The mother, who has lost the visible world and lives among her dreamed guests, has chosen for her most beautiful companion the one who is by nature intermittent, present only while the candles hold, faithless the way light is faithless, here and then gone. She loves the flaring thing knowing it will dim.

The turn for a writer is a small, bright one. Mr. Chandelier is the beautiful image you conjure that will not stay faithful, the vision that lights the empty heaven for a moment and then goes dark, the companion made of glass and borrowed fire. Every maker knows him, the radiance that arrives unbidden and cannot be commanded to remain, that flares through the room and then leaves one in the dark ceiling with the cold prisms.

He is the sacred ordinary at its most seductive and least reliable, the everyday object that becomes, for as long as the flame holds, a seven-handed god, and then is only a chandelier again. The book lets the mother love him without demanding he be constant, "asking no further verification than just that" he shines, which may be the only honest way to love the beautiful thing that comes and goes: to take the light while it burns and forgive it for being light.
